Conflict and Disagreement

Disagree and commit; separate people from positions — and know exactly when that instruction is wrong.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On Thursday, 10 September 2026, Aparna Varadarajan, Chief Product Officer of Zubaan Support Cloud in Bengaluru, sat between two people she had hired herself. Zubaan's AI agent resolves support tickets for forty-one enterprise clients — large e-commerce sellers, two NBFCs, a consumer-durables brand — and its next release would let it grant refunds up to ₹2,000 with no human in the loop. Sameer Qureshi, who leads applied machine learning, had an offline evaluation on eight thousand held-out tickets showing a false-grant rate of 1.4 per cent, and wanted to ship on the 24th. Deepa Rangan, who runs customer success, had hand-audited nine hundred August tickets and found forty-one wrongly granted: 4.6 per cent. Each believed the other had measured the wrong thing.

Six days later, Nikhil Bordoloi, VP of Product at Gagan Payments Network in Pune, faced a different argument. Gagan's 6.2 lakh merchant soundboxes announce roughly 2.4 crore UPI transactions a month. NPCI's settlement callback arrives at a median of 1.9 seconds but a 95th percentile of 8.4 seconds, and a merchant at a busy Kothrud tea stall experiences that tail as a dead device. Nikhil's team had built a local confirmation announcing receipt at 0.4 seconds. Shruti Patwardhan, who runs hardware and field operations, wanted it killed: about 0.07 per cent of locally successful transactions never settle, so the box would tell roughly 16,800 merchants a month that money had arrived when it had not.

Both faced one structural problem in two instances. In Bengaluru the disagreement was about a number a better measurement could settle. In Pune it was about a promise, and no measurement would. That distinction, between disagreements evidence can close and disagreements it cannot, is the spine of everything below.

Fig. 1 — Two live decisions. Both are called conflicts; only one is arbitrable by evidence.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

Define the terms precisely. A position is what a person argues for aloud. An interest is the need the position serves. A prior is the belief about the world that makes the position sensible — what most arguments are actually about and never name. Separating people from positions is taught as a two-layer move: get from positions to interests and the conflict often dissolves. The expert treatment adds the third layer. Sameer and Deepa's interests were not in conflict at all; both wanted the release to succeed. Their positions clashed because their priors about model drift differed, and neither had said so.

The history runs down two channels that rarely cite each other. The negotiation channel begins with Mary Parker Follett's 1925 distinction between domination, compromise and integration, and reaches modern form in Fisher and Ury's Getting to Yes (1981). The organisational channel begins with Andrew Grove at Intel, whose “constructive confrontation” answered a specific pathology: correct objections arriving after the fabrication decision was irreversible. Bezos's 2016 shareholder letter gave the doctrine its name and its escape clause — his example has him committing to someone else's project, not extracting commitment from a subordinate.

A third channel is empirical and less comfortable. Karen Jehn's 1995 study separated task from relationship conflict and found the first sometimes helpful. De Dreu and Weingart's 2003 meta-analysis then found both correlated negatively with performance, task conflict at about −0.23 — never cleanly overturned, and sitting awkwardly under every slide titled “healthy conflict.” A fourth channel, Edmondson's work on psychological safety, puts the constraint upstream: not how you referee disagreement, but whether it reaches you.

Table 1 — What each school will and will not sign. The disagreements are real, not stylistic.
SchoolWill signWill not sign
Interest-based (Follett, Fisher & Ury)Most positional deadlock hides a compatible pair of interests; surface them.That deciding fast is the best path; speed destroys the integrative option.
Constructive confrontation (Grove, Bezos)Argument has a deadline; after it, unanimous execution regardless of belief.That every disagreement deserves resolution. Some deserve a decision and nothing more.
Empirical conflict research (De Dreu & Weingart)Conflict of any type is on average costly; its advocates carry the burden of proof.That task conflict reliably improves outcomes.
Psychological safety (Edmondson)Observed harmony is usually suppression; measure dissent volume first.That a decision-rights framework fixes a team where juniors stay silent.

3. Mechanics: pricing a disagreement before you have it

Experts run a step competent practitioners skip: before scheduling the argument, they estimate what it is worth. Aparna did this on the back of a page.

Start with the stake. Zubaan's forty-one clients generate 1.9 lakh refund-eligible tickets a month; the agent would auto-resolve 62 per cent of them, 117,800. At Sameer's 1.4 per cent false-grant rate and an average wrong refund of ₹1,240, leakage is 117,800 × 0.014 × ₹1,240 = ₹20.4 lakh a month. At Deepa's 4.6 per cent it is ₹67.2 lakh. The disagreement is worth ₹46.8 lakh a month: the beliefs imply outcomes that far apart.

Next, the detection lag. Zubaan's clients reconcile refund ledgers quarterly, so if the team shipped and Deepa were right, three months would pass before anyone noticed: ₹1.40 crore of avoidable loss. Then the price of settling it — a fourteen-day shadow run, the agent scoring live tickets and logging what it would have done. Engineering cost ₹9 lakh; a fortnight's delay defers ₹3.2 crore of annualised expansion revenue by a twenty-sixth of a year, or ₹12.3 lakh. Total: ₹21.3 lakh.

The formal treatment is the expected value of sample information, applied to an argument. Let p be your honest prior that the dissenter is right. Testing pays when p × ₹1.40 crore > ₹21.3 lakh, that is when p exceeds 0.152. Aparna's estimate was 0.35: an expected saving of ₹49.1 lakh against a ₹21.3 lakh cost, net ₹27.8 lakh for holding the argument open a fortnight. The threshold matters more than the number. Most organisations implicitly set that bar near fifty per cent, and so under-buy dissent.

Fig. 2 — The value of holding an argument open, plotted against belief. The line is steep because the detection lag is long; where errors surface within days, the break-even prior rises and shipping to learn beats arguing.

The second-order effects of saying this aloud exceed the calculation. Once Aparna stated p = 0.35 in front of both, Sameer could not treat the objection as obstruction, because the CPO had priced it; Deepa could not treat a decision against her as dismissal, because she had seen the number that would have changed it. Three steps are usually left implicit: name the belief gap rather than the position gap; name a falsifier both sides accept before the result; name who decides if it returns ambiguous.

4. When the doctrine applies, and when it actively misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. First, a decision right exists and both parties know where it sits. Zubaan passes: Aparna decides. Gagan passes partly — firmware touching payment confirmation sits with Nikhil for product behaviour and Shruti for field risk, and no document says which frame governs. Second, the disagreement is arbitrable by evidence obtainable inside the decision window. Zubaan passes; Gagan does not, because Shruti's objection is not a forecast that could be wrong. Third, the loser can execute without violating a professional obligation. Both pass narrowly. Fourth, the decision is reversible at acceptable cost. Zubaan passes: a feature flag. Gagan fails: re-flashing 6.2 lakh devices costs about ₹190 each, or ₹11.8 crore, and merchant trust does not roll back with firmware.

Where the doctrine actively misleads deserves blunt statement, because it is taught as universal. It misleads when the dissent concerns an irreversible harm rather than an uncertain outcome; when the person invoking it holds the decision right and the person expected to commit does not, converting a symmetric norm into an instrument of authority; and when the same disagreement recurs across unrelated features, which usually means a strategy conflict is being fought by proxy where it cannot be resolved.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

In a two-sided marketplace, conflict between two internal teams can be structurally correct rather than a failure of alignment. Godhuli Agri Networks, matching Nashik grape and onion growers to institutional buyers, runs a supply PM and a demand PM whose objectives are opposed by construction: tighter grading raises buyer confidence and cuts farmer realisation. When Godhuli moved its grading threshold from 82 to 88, buyer repeat-purchase rose 6.4 points while lots rejected at the collection centre rose from 9 to 17 per cent, pushing about 1,900 farmers a month back to the APMC mandi. Someone must own that trade-off at the level of platform economics; treating it as a communication problem wastes quarters.

In regulated and hardware-plus-software settings, Gagan's case, the seam runs between people carrying personal regulatory exposure and people carrying none. Shruti's team signs the field-incident reports; Nikhil's does not. Asking her to commit to a behaviour she must defend to NPCI asks her to absorb a risk the decision-maker cannot share. Mature companies handle this structurally: a named veto, bounded in scope, that specific roles may exercise without having to win the debate.

In AI-native products the evidence itself is contested. At Ganak Intelligence Systems in Hyderabad, two staff engineers disagreed for five weeks about whether a retrieval change improved answer quality. Both had evals: one on a 1,200-item benchmark built in March, showing +4.1 points; one on 400 hand-labelled August production queries, showing −2.3. The disagreement was about which distribution counted as reality, which argument cannot settle. Only someone with authority declaring which eval set defines quality this quarter resolves it — a product decision masquerading as a technical one.

At organisational seams generally — product against platform, an India team against a US-based design lead, a squad against shared infrastructure — disagreement surfaces late because neither party can convene the other. What mature companies do, as distinct from what they publish, is keep standing forums whose only purpose is hearing cross-boundary objections weekly, because otherwise objections travel by escalation, which is slow and punishing to whoever escalates.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: commitment is a resource movement, not a sentence. The competent practitioner hears “I'm on board” and closes the meeting; the expert checks within seventy-two hours whether the dissenter moved something they control — a person, a sprint slot, a customer call. The tell of hollow commitment is enthusiasm beside unchanged allocation. Reading it as politics is usually wrong: more often they have simply not re-planned, which one conversation fixes at week one and which looks like sabotage at week six.

Two: the phrase is almost always said by the winner. Audit a quarter's usage and you will find “let's disagree and commit” said by whoever's view prevailed, to whoever's did not; Bezos's own example runs the other way. Hypocrisy is too harsh a reading: it is drift, a symmetric norm decaying into an authority move because the asymmetric version suits whoever holds the gavel, unless someone deliberately models the other direction.

Three: reversibility, not expected value, sets the argument budget. Gagan's optimistic confirmation has overwhelming expected value and still deserved weeks of argument, because the error mode is unrecoverable in merchant memory. The tell is that an expert asks what the rollback costs before asking what the model predicts. Reading this as risk aversion misses that the same expert cuts short an argument over a reversible decision with worse expected value, and ships it to learn.

Four: most disagreements are about priors and get argued as though they were about plans. Sameer and Deepa were not arguing about a refund cap; they were arguing about whether offline model performance survives a policy change. The tell is that neither side can say what would change their mind, because the evidence they need concerns the world, not the proposal. The expert asks both “what would you expect to observe if you were wrong?” before any option is scored.

Five: silence is a read of the decision rights, not agreement. When a senior voice states a position first and the room concurs, the room has judged that objecting is unlikely to change the outcome and certain to cost something. The tell is dissent arriving afterwards — in one-to-ones, on WhatsApp, or in an estimate quietly inflating by thirty per cent. The countermeasure is mechanical, not cultural: ask the most junior relevant person by name, first.

Six: incentives predict a dissenter's objection better than their stated reasoning, and that is information, not cynicism. Deepa's team absorbs every refund dispute, so she weights false grants heavily; Shruti signs the field reports, so she weights false announcements heavily. The tell is an objection mapping exactly onto the objector's metric. Discounting it as self-interested is backwards: organisations route risk knowledge through incentives, and whoever's metric absorbs a harm usually sees it first.

Seven: a commitment without a falsifier is a belief, not a decision. Competent teams end conflicts with a choice; expert teams end them with a choice plus a tripwire — a metric, a threshold and a date at which the decision reopens without anyone losing face. The tell is a memo with no revisit clause. Omitting it leaves the losing party one route back to the question, re-litigation, which the culture has just labelled a failure of commitment.

Eight: some disagreements should be preserved rather than resolved. The tension between Godhuli's supply and demand PMs, or between growth and risk at any lender, is how an organisation keeps two truths in the room. Resolving it durably requires one function to stop arguing, after which the metric it protected degrades quietly for several quarters. Experts manage the cadence and decision rights of such conflicts, and read sudden agreement between opposed functions as a warning.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

Table 2 — Where the difference is real. Where it is not, the row says so.
ContextWhat actually changes
ConsumerArgument budget is short because most decisions are reversible; the failure mode is arguing about what an experiment settles in nine days.
B2B and enterpriseNot very different. A named customer enters as a proxy combatant, but the real question — is one account outweighing the other forty? — is arithmetic.
Platform and marketplaceGenuinely different: opposed objectives are designed in, so the aim is governed tension, not resolution.
Hardware and physical goodsGenuinely different: irreversibility is physical and dated. Argument must finish before tooling or an OTA window; the calendar, not the culture, sets the deadline.
AI productsGenuinely different: the evidence is contested, so someone must own the definition of quality first.
Stage: under 50 peopleThe founder arbitrates by default and speed is free; the risk is that dissent never forms, because the founder's preference is visible.
Stage: 150–600The transition point. Informal arbitration stops scaling, decision rights must be written down, and the new escalation path is tested by the disagreements it was built for.
Stage: 2,000 and aboveConflict turns inter-functional and political; the scarce commodity is not resolution but a forum where two functions meet inside one week.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Zubaan, resolved. The shadow run covered 54,000 live tickets and returned a false-grant rate of 3.1 per cent — above Sameer's number, below Deepa's, inside the ambiguous band defined in advance. The disaggregation was the payoff: errors concentrated in two of nine intent classes, while the other seven, covering 71 per cent of eligible volume, ran at 0.9 per cent. Restricting auto-grant to those seven gave 83,600 tickets a month at 0.9 per cent and ₹1,240 average loss, or ₹9.3 lakh of leakage, a seventh of Deepa's feared case. Neither position survived; both bodies of evidence did.

Gagan, resolved by refusing the framing. The numbers favoured shipping decisively. Downside: 16,800 false announcements a month, about 60 per cent reaching a merchant at day-end reconciliation — 10,080 disputes at ₹340 support cost, or ₹34.3 lakh. Disputed merchants churn at 4.1 per cent in ninety days against a 1.3 per cent baseline; 2.8 points of 10,080 is 282 merchants at ₹8,600 lifetime value, or ₹24.3 lakh. Total downside about ₹58.6 lakh a month. Upside: an eight-week test on 4,200 devices lifted ninety-day retention from 91.2 to 93.8 per cent; across 6.2 lakh devices that is 16,120 retained a quarter, roughly ₹4.6 crore a month — nearly eight to one. Shruti lost on expected value and was right about what expected value did not contain: a device whose purpose is to tell a merchant money arrived must not say so when it has not. Nikhil changed the design rather than the decision — “payment accepted, confirming” at 0.4 seconds, the settled tone at callback — recovering 1.9 of the 2.6 points with no false claim.

Fig. 3 — Gagan logged objections and their authors before each firmware decision. The six decisions of Q2 2026, sorted by whether dissent was written down beforehand.

Zakhira Warehousing Networks, failed. Zakhira runs eleven distribution centres for FMCG and apparel clients out of Gurugram and, in 2025, replatformed its warehouse management system at a budgeted ₹6.4 crore over fourteen months. Balaji Muthiah, the COO, argued that cutting over three high-throughput centres simultaneously in the festive quarter was the wrong sequence, and that centres should migrate one at a time from the smallest. Sunaina Dhall, the CEO, heard him twice and invoked disagree and commit. Balaji committed, visibly and without complaint — which was the problem. Nine months in, the cutover failed at three centres: ₹11.2 crore of shipments ran late over nine days, one FMCG client invoked SLA penalties of ₹1.8 crore, and the rollback cost another ₹2.1 crore.

The post-mortem is instructive because the process was followed correctly and still failed. The decision right was clear, the argument was heard, the loser committed. Missing was the tripwire: nobody had recorded what Balaji expected to observe if he were right, so the early signals — pick accuracy at the pilot centre falling from 99.1 to 96.4 per cent in week three, and 240 hours of unplanned manual reconciliation — were absorbed as teething rather than read as the dissenter's prediction coming true. Zakhira now runs a dissent register: every decision above ₹50 lakh records the strongest objection, its author, the observable that would vindicate it, and a review date. Two calls have since been reversed inside sixty days.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Each failure below is cheap to catch early and expensive afterwards.

Table 3 — The five failures practitioners actually hit, with the question that catches each one early.
Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Compliance without commitmentVerbal agreement, unchanged staffing“What did you move this week because of this decision?”A quarter of drift blamed on execution
Commit with no falsifierDecision memo with no metric, threshold or revisit date“What would we see in three weeks if this were wrong?”Zakhira: ₹3.9 crore against a ₹9 lakh alternative
Authority dressed as normThe phrase is only ever said downward“When did I last commit to a call I argued against?”Dissent stops arriving; the room goes quiet for years
Proxy war in feature reviewsThe same two people disagree about unrelated items“Is this the third instance of one unstated argument?”Decisions that never stick
Premature resolution of structural tensionTwo opposed functions suddenly agree on everything“Whose metric has quietly stopped being defended?”Two or three quarters of silent degradation

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

On whether speed or integration should govern. Constructive confrontation, steelmanned: in fast markets the cost of a delayed decision exceeds that of a slightly wrong one, decisions are mostly reversible, and organisations seeking integrative solutions on every disagreement simply decide less. Its evidence is Intel's and Amazon's execution records. It is wrong if reversibility is rarer than assumed — in hardware, regulated finance and anything touching customer money, it is. The integrative position, steelmanned: Toyota's nemawashi front-loads consensus deliberately, decides slower and executes far faster because nothing must be re-explained downstream. Gagan's 5.7× re-litigation gap is small-sample evidence for that. It is wrong if front-loaded cost scales with headcount faster than the downstream saving.

On whether conflict helps at all. Advocates hold that disagreement surfaces information hierarchy suppresses. Sceptics hold the meta-analytic line: both conflict types correlate negatively with performance, and the cases held up as proof of productive conflict are selected on the outcome. What would settle it is a study separating conflict volume from conflict termination. Nobody has run it cleanly, so the field knows only that both extremes are bad.

On whether structure or safety is the binding constraint. One camp says write the decision rights and behaviour follows; the other says a RACI in a team that fears its director changes nothing but the vocabulary of silence. The first rests on observed speed gains when decision rights are clarified; the second on Edmondson's finding that the teams reporting most errors were the best-performing. The discriminating test — clarify decision rights in a low-safety team and watch dissent volume — has only anecdotal results, and they favour the safety camp.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this runs the ritual: surface interests, timebox the debate, write the memo, ask for commitment. Someone who has internalised it does three things differently. They price the disagreement before scheduling it. They distinguish within ten minutes between a disagreement evidence can close, one only a decision right can close, and one that should be preserved — and say which it is aloud, because naming the type ends half the argument. And they treat their own commitments as the norm's transmission mechanism: the fastest way to make disagree-and-commit real is for the most senior person in the room to visibly execute a decision they argued against.

The competent practitioner referees the argument. The expert decides which arguments are worth having, and then referees those.

12. What they decided

Aparna held the release. The shadow run cost ₹21.3 lakh against an expected ₹49.1 lakh of avoided loss, and produced a design — seven intent classes automated, two routed to humans — that neither Sameer nor Deepa had proposed. She recorded that Deepa's audit was directionally right and Sameer's evaluation sound, which keeps both arguing next quarter.

Nikhil shipped, but not what he had argued for. He treated Shruti's objection as a constraint rather than an input, redesigned around it, and gave up about 0.7 retention points — roughly ₹1.2 crore a quarter — to avoid a claim the company could not stand behind. He also wrote into Gagan's decision log that field operations holds a bounded veto over any firmware behaviour asserting a payment state before settlement, converting a recurring fight into a rule.

Discussion questions

1. Aparna priced Deepa's dissent at a 35 per cent prior. Where did that number come from, and would shipping have been defensible had she estimated 12 per cent?

2. Shruti lost the expected-value argument by nearly eight to one and still changed the product. When is that good governance, and when is it a veto that will paralyse Gagan?

3. Zakhira followed the process correctly and lost ₹3.9 crore. If the dissent register is the fix, what does it cost when the dissenter is wrong, and who decides the tripwire has not been tripped?

13. Going deeper

Difficult conversations is the prerequisite: conflict is the difficult conversation that does not resolve in one sitting. Negotiation for PMs is the harder next step, because it removes the shared finish line — a vendor or regulator owes you no commitment. Influence without authority covers the case this page assumed away: disagreeing with someone who need not listen. What makes a great PM situates judgement about which arguments to have. Building trust with teams supplies the balance arguing draws down. Psychological safety and team health decides whether dissent reaches you at all. Coaching and feedback raises a team's tolerance for being contradicted. Working in diverse and global teams matters because directness is culturally calibrated: vigorous debate in one office reads as an attack in another.

People, Leadership & Organisation · Leadership & Team

Conflict and Disagreement

How do I disagree productively and then commit?

1. A WhatsApp message, three weeks, and two people who are both right

On Tuesday, 22 September 2026, Meera Iyer, VP of Product at Ekagra Health Systems in Bengaluru, found two urgent meetings stacked on her calendar, both about the same feature. Ekagra sells scheduling, sample-routing and reporting software to roughly three hundred independent diagnostic centres across twelve states — labs competing against national chains such as Dr Lal PathLabs and Metropolis Healthcare by being faster and cheaper to book with. The feature would let a patient get their test report on WhatsApp within an hour of it being ready, instead of opening Ekagra’s own app.

Karan Mehta, who runs growth, wanted it shipped in three weeks, ahead of the Diwali surge, at a build cost of about ₹40 lakh, projecting roughly ₹2.4 crore in added annual revenue. Ritu Sabharwal, who runs trust and compliance, wanted it stopped. Diagnostic reports are sensitive personal data under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and sending them over WhatsApp without explicit consent put Ekagra and its clients at real, uncapped risk. Their newest client, a NABL-accredited chain in Pune, was mid-audit for its own accreditation renewal.

Neither was wrong. Karan understood the market; Ritu understood the exposure. Meera’s problem was not deciding who was right — it was that the two had stopped hearing each other, and the sprint calendar gave her eleven days to fix that before the decision made itself by default.

Fig. 1 — Eleven days separate the argument from the sprint calendar deciding by default.

2. The idea: arguing hard and then rowing together

Conflict and disagreement, used the way this page means it, is not a breakdown to be smoothed over. It is information: two capable people have looked at the same situation and reached different conclusions, usually because each is anchored in facts, incentives, or risks the other does not fully weigh. Handled well, that gap is where an organisation finds out which trade-offs matter before the market or regulator does. Handled badly, it explodes into friction or gets buried — and buried disagreement resurfaces later, more expensively, as the topic this one builds on: the difficult conversation that did not resolve the first time.

The discipline has two halves. The first, separating the people from the position, comes from Roger Fisher and William Ury’s Harvard Negotiation Project, published as Getting to Yes in 1981. A position is the stance someone argues for out loud — “ship in three weeks,” “don’t ship at all.” An interest is the need the position tries to satisfy — Karan’s is a seasonal revenue window and a number he has told the board; Ritu’s is the audits and indemnity clauses keeping Ekagra’s biggest contracts alive. Positions are usually mutually exclusive; interests, examined honestly, often are not.

The second half, disagree and commit, is arguing your position hard before a decision, then supporting it fully once made — whether or not it won. The phrase is most associated with Andy Grove’s writing on Intel’s culture in the 1980s and was later written into Amazon’s leadership principles by Jeff Bezos, but the instinct is older: healthy organisations need vigorous dissent before a decision closes, and none after. The sentence Meera could say without sounding glib: “I want your best argument before we decide, and your full effort after — even when it isn’t the argument that won.”

Fig. 2 — The positions clash; the interests underneath, once named, may not.

3. How it actually works

Meera did not run a debate. She ran a sequence, and most of what makes it work is the steps people skip as mere ceremony.

She named the disagreement out loud and dated its resolution — a ninety-minute session Thursday, decision by Monday, tied to the sprint-lock. Left undated, disagreements do not resolve; they metastasise into the ongoing tension the prerequisite to this topic describes: the difficult conversation that never quite happens all at once.

Next, before either side argued its own case, each restated the other’s case well enough that the other agreed it was accurate. Karan explained why an unconsented data flow was a genuine indemnity problem, not compliance theatre; Ritu explained why three weeks mattered commercially. This is the step most conflict conversations skip, and it best predicts whether what follows is a negotiation or a shouting match.

Third, positions and interests went on the whiteboard as two columns, turning “ship now” versus “don’t ship” into “capture the festive window” and “protect the accreditation-linked contracts” — satisfiable, it turned out, by a design neither had proposed yet.

Fourth, the debate was timeboxed and grounded in evidence: counsel stated what a compliant flow required under the DPDP Act; engineering confirmed what WhatsApp’s API already offered.

Fifth, because Ekagra runs a written DACI (Driver, Approver, Contributors, Informed), everyone knew Meera was the Approver if the directors could not converge — escalation meant deferring to a process, not losing to a rival.

Sixth, and least glamorous: the decision would be written in one page, restated publicly by whoever had argued against it, and given a date to revisit — commitment does not mean permanent silence about a call that turns out wrong.

4. A worked example: scoring the options, then re-weighting them

Three options were on the table: A, ship in three weeks with no added consent screen; B, delay eight weeks for a full compliance review; C, ship in four weeks with a lightweight consent gate built first. Meera scored each 1–5 on four criteria and weighted the criteria, so the debate had numbers to push against rather than adjectives.

CriterionA: Ship nowB: Full reviewC: Consent gateWeight, Pass 1Weight, Pass 2
Speed to revenue5130.400.20
Regulatory risk (5 = safest)1540.150.35
Client trust & renewal2440.200.20
Engineering cost (5 = cheapest)5340.250.25

Under the Pass 1 weights — speed weighted heaviest, since that was the number Karan had put before the board — A scores 5(0.40)+1(0.15)+2(0.20)+5(0.25) = 2.00+0.15+0.40+1.25 = 3.80. C scores 3(0.40)+4(0.15)+4(0.20)+4(0.25) = 1.20+0.60+0.80+1.00 = 3.60. B scores 1(0.40)+5(0.15)+4(0.20)+3(0.25) = 0.40+0.75+0.80+0.75 = 2.70. On these weights, A narrowly leads.

Midway through the session, Ritu’s counsel flagged that the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology had that month issued a public show-cause notice to a rival health platform over exactly this kind of unconsented sharing. That changed how much the room believed regulatory risk should weigh — not a new risk, but a newly visible one. Meera re-ran the arithmetic with regulatory risk raised from 0.15 to 0.35 and speed lowered from 0.40 to 0.20. A now scores 5(0.20)+1(0.35)+2(0.20)+5(0.25) = 1.00+0.35+0.40+1.25 = 3.00. C scores 3(0.20)+4(0.35)+4(0.20)+4(0.25) = 0.60+1.40+0.80+1.00 = 3.80. B rises to 3.50. The ranking flips: C leads, A falls last. What mattered was never the score — it was that Ritu’s dissent forced the room to notice the weights had been set before anyone priced the risk properly, which is often what disagreement is for.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

Fig. 3 — Disagree-and-commit sits between two failure modes.

It is not consensus

Consensus needs everyone to agree before acting; disagree-and-commit needs everyone to act after, whether or not they agreed. Confusing the two produces paralysis dressed as inclusiveness.

Separating positions from interests is not ignoring feelings

Interests are not purely rational; fear of being blamed is a legitimate interest, not noise. Treating emotion as illegitimate data is a common misapplication.

It presumes someone holds the decision right

Without a DACI or equivalent, the discipline degrades into whoever is senior, or louder, wins. It works here only because Ekagra had already answered, in writing, who decides if the room cannot.

Timing is the whole mechanism

Arguing hard is expected before the decision, corrosive after. A director who re-litigates a settled call the following week, with no new information, is quietly withdrawing commitment.

It has a floor

Some positions should not be argued down to compromise: a genuine legal or safety red line is not negotiable, and no “commit anyway” culture should ask Ritu to sign off on something unlawful.

It is often confused with conflict avoidance

A team proud of its harmony often has less real disagreement reaching the table, not more resolution of it — visible calm is often evidence that dissent has nowhere safe to go.

It cannot tell you which decision is correct

The process improves the odds that information surfaces before a call is made; it does not guarantee the call is right. Option C could still fail. It buys a team that executes at full speed regardless.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and stage

Fig. 4 — Who the disagreement is between shifts with the business model; how formally it resolves shifts with size.

Inside Ekagra’s consumer app, the Karan-versus-Ritu pattern is the common shape: growth against trust, resolvable in one session because the decision right sits with one person. On the enterprise side, selling to hospital groups, the conflict usually runs between an account team half-promising a custom feature to close a deal, and product holding the roadmap; there, sensibly, product keeps the veto, since one client’s request must be weighed against every other client’s.

In a genuine marketplace — the pattern at platforms like Urban Company or Swiggy, where a partner’s interests and a customer’s are not the same and neither reports to the other — the disagreement is three-sided, and the platform must arbitrate an interest it does not itself hold.

Stage matters as much as model. In Ekagra’s first eighteen months, the founder was the default Approver for everything, so disagree-and-commit was fast and informal — the risk being that dissent gets skipped, since no one is sure arguing is welcome. At a hundred and forty employees, informal no longer scales; the DACI had to be written down so a disagreement did not wait on the founder’s calendar.

7. Common mistakes

The best programmes teach this through role-play and live stakeholder conflict, because every mistake below is invisible on paper and obvious in the room. Cases with “no stakeholder conflict” in them — a repeatedly flagged pitfall — produce graduates who can define disagree-and-commit perfectly and still freeze the first time a peer contradicts them.

MistakeSymptomMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Silent nodding, then sabotageAgreement in the room, work quietly slows for weeks after“Commit” performed in the meeting, not practised after itAsk each person their next action within 48 hours
Endless relitigatingSame debate resurfaces later with no new factsNo revisit trigger, so “decided” never felt finalCheck if the memo names a date or metric to reopen
Personalising disagreementPeople avoid each other, or stop objecting at allAttack on a position read as attack on the personAsk each side to state the other’s interest aloud
False consensus by hierarchyNo one objects once the senior voice speaks firstSilence mistaken for agreement, not deferencePoll juniors by name before the senior voice speaks

8. What good looks like

Fig. 5 — The disagreement compressed into a one-page memo both directors could point to afterward.

The Thursday session ran the sequence in full. Karan restated Ritu’s indemnity concern accurately enough that she agreed with it; Ritu restated the commercial cost of delay the same way. Legal supplied the DPDP requirement; engineering confirmed the consent-template path would cost roughly ₹6 lakh and one extra week. The re-weighted matrix, forced by dissent rather than preference, pointed cleanly at Option C. Meera signed it as Approver; Karan, whose position had lost, presented the consent-gated version as his own recommendation next morning — visible proof commitment had happened, not merely been announced. The feature launched 20 October; Ekagra logged a 78 percent opt-in rate in three weeks, revenue tracking to ₹2.1 crore against the ₹2.4 crore projection, with no compliance exposure.

9. What Meera decided, and what to read next

Meera chose Option C. Her reasoning was not “compliance won” or “growth lost” — the disagreement had been useful: it forced a re-weighting of a risk the plan had quietly under-priced, and produced a design nobody proposed on day one. That is what disagree-and-commit is built to produce, more often than a clean win for either side.

The natural next stop is negotiation for product managers, since this discipline assumes everyone in the room eventually commits. Once the other party is a vendor or regulator who owes you no commitment at all, the same interest-based reasoning must survive without that shared finish line — a harder, different skill.

Sit with these before your next disagreement:

1. The last time you lost an argument, did you actually commit — or did the work you controlled afterward quietly slow down?

2. Whose disagreement most needs to reach you before your next big call, and is there a real mechanism for that — or only an open door you hope someone uses?

Builds on: Difficult conversations. Unlocks: Negotiation for PMs.
case40v1-lead.conflict:
Panghat Dairy Systems · Product Leadership · Case 40

The Score and the Pourer

Ahmedabad, Sunday night, 20 September 2026

The flush season had started early. From her balcony in Bodakdev, Hiral Trivedi could hear the last Navratri rehearsal drums two lanes over, and had on her laptop two documents she could not reconcile. The first was a slide her data lead in Amsterdam had prepared for tomorrow's executive review: Quality Intelligence — 84% precision, ₹1.94 crore recovered, ready to scale to 11,400 centres. The second was a resolution in Gujarati, passed nine days earlier by the board of Panchdhara Milk Union, directing that no deduction be made from any pourer's payment on the basis of “software estimation” until the union's own quality committee had reviewed the matter.

Both documents described the same eight months of work. Hiral had been VP Product at Panghat Dairy Systems for three years, and had learned that in the dairy business the argument is almost never about the milk. At ten she would sit with her head of engineering on a link from Jaipur, her field operations head in from Rajkot, a founder-CEO careful not to say what he thought, and an investor director who had asked twice whether the Quality Intelligence number in the plan was still good. What kept her at the table at eleven at night was a suspicion that all four of her options answered a question nobody in the company had agreed to ask.

1. Company history

Panghat Dairy Systems was founded in Ahmedabad in 2014 by two automation engineers who had spent their twenties commissioning bulk milk coolers across north Gujarat, with a third partner whose father had been secretary of a village dairy cooperative for nineteen years. The product replaced a paper register: a screen at the collection centre recording a pourer's identity, the weight of the milk, the fat and solids-not-fat (SNF) readings from the analyser, and the rupee value owed under the union's rate chart. By 2020 it reached from the village to the union's dairy plant, settling payments every ten days into bank accounts.

The decision that still shapes everything happened in February 2019. Cash was short, and Rasaayan Instruments Group — an Anand-based maker of ultrasonic milk analysers with roughly a third of the domestic installed base — offered a five-year original-equipment agreement. Panghat's software would ship pre-loaded on Rasaayan hardware at ₹340 per centre per month, under a third of Panghat's direct price. In exchange Rasaayan held the customer relationship at bundled sites, took a clause entitling it to “aggregate quality telemetry” from them, and took a right of first refusal on any sale of Panghat. It was renewed in 2024 to 31 March 2027, terminable on ninety days' notice.

It worked. Rasaayan's channel carried Panghat into nine states and past seven thousand centres in four years, and Exhibit 1 shows the shape of the problem: the bundle is most of the installed base and a minority of the revenue. In March 2024 Riyaaz Growth Partners led a ₹210 crore Series B at ₹1,340 crore post-money, with a ratchet if recurring revenue missed ₹90 crore by 31 March 2027 — a number that, on the FY26 run rate, needs either a price increase the bundle forbids or a product it does not cover.

2. The industry

India's organised dairy sector rests on a cooperative architecture that is remarkable and slow to change. Village societies pool milk from smallholders with two or three animals; district unions chill, test and process it; federations market it. The Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation's Amul brand, the Karnataka federation's Nandini, Mother Dairy and processors such as Hatsun and Heritage Foods all buy from networks of this kind, and the National Dairy Development Board in Anand sets much of the vocabulary Panghat's software must speak. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India governs what may be sold; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, now governs the pourer's identity, bank account and, arguably, the fat percentage of her morning's milk.

Three forces bear on Panghat. First, hardware is commoditising: analysers that cost ₹1.1 lakh in 2018 now sell at ₹62,000, and vendors treat software as an inducement rather than a product. Second, a venture-funded cohort — Prahari Agri Cloud of Jaipur is the aggressive one — bundles cattle health, insemination records and procurement into one subscription, priced to win. Third, the Gulf. UAE and Omani buyers of Indian ghee, paneer and milk powder now ask for batch-level traceability to the collection point, and Rabta Dairy Trading LLC of Dubai, supplying retail and hospitality across three Gulf markets, issued an RFP in July 2026 for a collection and traceability platform spanning ninety points in India and the UAE — the first contract in Panghat's history that would be signed in a currency other than the rupee.

3. The situation in detail

The idea was uncontroversial when Zoya Qureshi proposed it in September 2025. Adulteration and dilution cost unions real money; the rate chart penalises low fat and low SNF but cannot distinguish a buffalo in late lactation from water added at the can. Zoya's team in Amsterdam built a model over four years of Panghat's readings — weight, fat, SNF, temperature, pourer history, route, season — returning a per-sample risk score. In the pilot it flagged 1.9% of samples, and on retest 84% of those flags were confirmed. Exhibit 2 is the slide the company has shown since July.

What was believed in July and what is now known differ in three ways. In late July a field engineer's note prompted Ketan Solanki's team to pull the pilot apart by union; Exhibit 3 is that re-cut. The headline precision is a volume-weighted average dominated by Panchdhara Milk Union, whose retest ran the second sample on the same analyser model that produced the first — so a calibration drift common to both would confirm itself. Where retests went to an independent laboratory, confirmation fell to the high sixties. At three unions the retest registers were never digitised.

Second, the ₹1.94 crore is the value of milk for which payment was withheld at flagged samples, never netted against what the rate chart would have deducted anyway for the same low-fat samples. Where that netting was done — at two unions — incremental recovery was ₹29 lakh against ₹85 lakh claimed. Nobody falsified anything; the number had never been asked to mean what the slide implied.

Third, Exhibit 4 shows payment disputes per thousand pourers at pilot and control centres. Read casually it shows a spike and a recovery, which Zoya reads as pourers adjusting. Mrinalini Bose, the principal designer in Berlin, pointed out in August that from April the pilot unions logged a dispute only if it escalated past the chilling-centre in-charge. Ketan's field groups suggest the arguments at the gate did not fall at all.

Then two things arrived in one fortnight. On 4 September Rasaayan wrote invoking the telemetry clause and requesting the pilot dataset, mentioning that its instrumentation division was developing “on-device quality estimation” and that it wished to discuss the 2027 renewal early. On 11 September the Panchdhara resolution reached Hiral's inbox, forwarded by a union secretary with a one-line note.

4. The people

Hiral Trivedi — VP Product, Ahmedabad. Owns Monday's recommendation and, from March, the ₹90 crore number. Believes the disagreement now costs more than any option would. Has not told anyone she thinks the Rasaayan renewal, not the score, is the real decision.

Mihir Dholakia — Head of Engineering, Jaipur. Position: the score must not run at bundled centres, where devices sit on 2G, lose power six hours a day and sync in batches. Incentive: he carries the pager. Not saying: a sync defect caused ₹14 lakh of ledger mis-postings in February, quietly corrected, and any audit of the score will surface it.

Zoya Qureshi — Lead, Data & Machine Learning, Amsterdam. Position: ship it everywhere, payment-linked, before Rasaayan builds its own; an advisory score is one nobody looks at. Incentive: her team of nine is the company's only defensible asset. Not saying: she has accepted a November conference slot on the pilot results, and two of her engineers hold Gulf offers.

Ketan Solanki — Head of Field Operations, Rajkot. Position: advisory only, never linked to payment, anywhere. Incentive: ninety field engineers who stand in front of farmers. Not saying: he assured three union secretaries in February, without telling Hiral, that the score would never touch a pourer's payment.

Purnima Deka — Head of Customer Success, Guwahati. Position: make it configurable per union; north-eastern unions of tiny pourers want it more than Gujarat does. Incentive: renewals at eleven unions. Not saying: she switched it on at an Assam union in June without a signed amendment, and it is still on.

Naushad Merchant — VP Global Sales, New Jersey. Position: the score is why Rabta shortlisted Panghat and must be in the January go-live. Incentive: sixty per cent of his variable pay rides on new-logo value. Not saying: he has verbally given Rabta a January date, and has not read Exhibit 3.

Mrinalini Bose — Principal Designer, Berlin. Position: the disclosure to the pourer — voice call, SMS, slip — must be redesigned and DPDP consent rebuilt first. Incentive: professional conscience. Not saying: she believes a per-sample judgement on an individual farmer is the wrong unit altogether and that the score belongs at route level; she has not said it because she was overruled on a similar point in 2024.

Shalini Kabra — Partner, Riyaaz Growth Partners, Mumbai; board director. Girish Amin, the CFO, has taken no position beyond wanting the Rasaayan question settled before the auditors arrive. Position: Quality Intelligence is the premium tier that closes the gap to ₹90 crore, and delay is the expensive option. Incentive: Riyaaz is raising its next fund. Not saying: Rasaayan has approached Riyaaz about a secondary stake.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — Panghat Dairy Systems: installed base and revenue, FY23–FY26

Exhibit 2 — Quality Intelligence pilot, headline results, six unions, December 2025 – June 2026

Exhibit 3 — The same pilot, re-cut by union (field operations, 8 August 2026)

Flush months are over-represented in the Panchdhara volume, and two unions declined to share rate-chart deduction data.

Exhibit 4 — Payment disputes per 1,000 pourers, pilot versus control centres, January–August 2026. Source: union grievance registers. Exhibit 6 — The decision window. The two dates in red are contractual; the Rabta window was already extended three weeks at Panghat's request.

6. Voices

From the engineering channel, 12 September, 19:40 IST:

Zoya: Precision at Panchdhara is 91%. Pull payment linkage and the score is a decoration. Decorations do not renew.

Mihir: Precision measured against the instrument that made the error is not precision. And you want my firmware holding a model on a device that loses power six hours a day.

Zoya: Then say that. Do not say the model is unsafe when you mean the device is.

Mihir: I mean both. You have never stood at a centre at 5.30 a.m.

The thread ran to 74 messages. Hiral replied once, asking each to send her the other's argument at its strongest. Neither did.

From Ketan Solanki's voice note to Hiral, 13 September:

“Madam, the issue at Panchdhara is not 1,240 pourers. It is one man, Jethabhai, sixty-one, four buffaloes, flagged eleven times in the flush, who came with his son to ask what he had done. The in-charge could not tell him. I could not tell him. If I cannot tell him, we should not be deducting.”

From Naushad Merchant's email, 14 September, 02:10 IST:

“Rabta's procurement head asked one question on Thursday: does your quality layer work at our Sharjah collection points on day one. I said yes. If the answer from Ahmedabad is now no, I need to know what I tell him — the other vendor is quoting 40% below us and has nothing like our score.”

From Mrinalini Bose, in a design review margin, 16 September:

“We keep debating where the score runs. Has anyone asked whether a number attached to one woman's one can of milk is the thing we should be building at all? A route-level anomaly, reviewed by the union's own committee, would recover most of the money and none of the shame.”

From Rasaayan's letter of 4 September:

“We would welcome an early conversation on the 2027 renewal and on how quality estimation is best positioned for the cooperative customer. Pending that, kindly treat this as our formal request under clause 9.3 for the aggregate telemetry described therein, including the pilot period.”

Clause 9.3 has never been tested; counsel's note of 9 September calls its scope “arguable both ways”.

From Shalini Kabra, board group, 18 September:

“I am not asking you to ship something unsafe. I am asking whether we have a premium product by March, or whether we are a ledger with a hardware partner about to become a competitor. Those are different companies.”

7. The options as Hiral sees them

A. Scale the score as designed, payment-linked, default on

Extend it to all 11,400 centres and keep the deduction workflow. Answers Shalini and Naushad, gives Zoya her mandate, and is the only option that plausibly reaches ₹90 crore by March. Needs Rasaayan's consent for premium pricing at 62% of centres, 22 person-months Mihir does not have, and a position on Exhibit 3 Hiral cannot yet defend out loud.

B. Advisory only, everywhere, payment linkage removed

The score becomes a flag for the union's own inspector. Ketan's promise holds, the resolution is moot, DPDP exposure narrows. But Rasaayan can put an advisory flag in firmware within a year, the premium tier disappears, and Zoya will read it — correctly — as the company declining to stand behind her team's work.

C. Configurable per union; the union decides linkage

Ship both modes and let each union's board choose. Superficially the mature answer, and Purnima's unions would switch it on tomorrow. It hands a liability to boards that cannot read Exhibit 3, multiplies support across nine states, and leaves Panghat the data fiduciary whoever flipped the switch.

D. Reserve the score for private dairies and the Gulf

Withdraw it from cooperatives; sell it to Rasdhara Dairy Foods, Rabta and export-facing processors, where the payer is a company rather than a smallholder. Highest margin, cleanest ethics on paper. But a model trained on 29.3 lakh cooperative pourers then earns nothing for them, and the cooperative segment — the founding purpose and 80% of revenue — is conceded to whoever wins the hardware.

Hiral had written the four options on one sheet and noticed, late on Sunday, that every one was a sentence about where the score runs and who it charges. None asked whether a per-sample judgement on an individual pourer is the right instrument at all, and none mentioned 31 December, the date by which Panghat must tell Rasaayan whether it wants to be partner or rival. Mrinalini had raised the first in a margin note; nobody had raised the second in a meeting.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

Monday's review is not the decision; it is where the decision stops being deferrable. The Rabta window closes on 15 October, already extended once. The Panchdhara quality committee meets on 28 October, and two of the three unions Ketan spoke to sit on one federation's technical panel. Ninety days' notice on the Rasaayan agreement falls due on 31 December — so the renewal must be negotiated before Panghat knows whether the score is a premium product. The ratchet bites at ₹90 crore on 31 March 2027; the August run rate is ₹52.9 crore, and Exhibit 5 leaves 34 engineering person-months against 61 requested.

Beyond that: nineteen months of cash; a DPDP obligation to explain automated decisions that Panghat's pourer SMS does not meet in any of the eleven languages it sends; an FSSAI protocol governing what a retest legally demonstrates; and the fact that a pourer's ten-day payment is, for most households on the ledger, the most reliable money in their lives.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. Separate each stakeholder's position from the interest beneath it. Who is arguing about the same thing in different words, and who wants a genuinely different outcome?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 describe the same pilot. What would you need before putting either number in front of a union board, and who here should have produced it?
  3. Exhibit 4 reads as vindication or as an artefact of a definition change. How should a product leader treat a metric whose measurement rule changed midway, for good operational reasons?
  4. Mihir conceals a defect; Ketan made a commitment Hiral did not authorise; Purnima has a union running unamended. Are these failures of one kind, and what does each say about how disagreement is handled at Panghat?
  5. Mrinalini thinks the unit of analysis itself is wrong and has not said so in a meeting. What has that silence cost, and what would have made it speakable in February rather than September?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Hiral decide, what does she leave explicitly open, and what does she tell the board about the ₹90 crore, knowing 31 December forces the question again before anyone has better data?

Sunday, midnight

At a quarter past midnight she closed the laptop without writing the recommendation. The drums had stopped. On the sheet beside her she had drawn, without meaning to, a box around the word pourer, and beside it a question she had asked nobody: if the score were right about Jethabhai eleven times and wrong once, which of those twelve mornings was the product for? At ten, four people would arrive certain, and she would have to decide something before she had decided that.
case20v1-lead.conflict:
Waseela Trade Systems · Product Leadership

The HS-Code Argument

Kochi, Wednesday, 10 September 2025

At 7.40 a.m., Tanvi Balakrishnan was on her terrace overlooking the Vallarpadam container yard, reading the same Slack thread for the third time. It had run to sixty-one messages overnight across three time zones and had not moved an inch. By Friday she owed the founders a single recommendation: what Waseela Trade Systems would tell a large Dubai-based freight forwarder, in a demo now nine days away, about how the company's new classification engine actually worked. Her engineering head in Pune wanted to slow the demo down. Her data science lead in Toronto wanted to speed it up. Both were right about something, and Tanvi could no longer tell whether the argument was about the product at all.

1. Company background

Waseela Trade Systems was founded in 2018 by two former Cochin Customs House Agents who had spent a decade filing Bills of Entry by hand. The company builds cloud software that helps Customs House Agents (CHAs) and exporters prepare and file customs paperwork — Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills, AD Code registrations — and push supporting documents into the government's e-Sanchit repository ahead of ICEGATE submission. It reconciles IGST credits, tracks DGFT licence balances, and flags mismatches before a filing reaches a customs officer, where an error can mean a container losing its Direct Port Delivery (DPD) fast lane, or a demurrage bill running into lakhs a day.

By FY25 the company served roughly 410 CHA firms and 1,150 exporter accounts out of Cochin, Tuticorin, Chennai, Mundra and Nhava Sheva (JNPT), with annual recurring revenue of ₹34 crore. It competes at the edges with Kale Logistics Solutions' port community systems and with freight platforms like Cogoport that are moving into documentation as an add-on; Waseela's pitch has always been narrower and deeper — it only does customs paperwork, and does it in a way a CBIC auditor can follow line by line. That narrowness was why a large win was now on the table: a Jebel Ali-based freight forwarding group had shortlisted Waseela for its Indian customs desk, provided the company could show a faster way to classify goods under the Harmonised System (HS) than its manual process allowed.

2. The situation

Six months earlier, Aakash Devan had built a prototype that read an invoice line item — say, "PVC pipe fittings, threaded, 32mm" — and suggested an eight-digit HS code and duty rate, trained on eleven years of Waseela's own filing history. In a pilot across forty CHA desks in Tuticorin, it matched the CHA's final code 91% of the time and cut the average time to draft a Bill of Entry line from six minutes to ninety seconds. Aakash wanted to put a working version in front of the Dubai client on 19 September, positioned as Waseela's core differentiator.

Her engineering head, Siddharth Rao, had a different number in mind: 9%. That was the share of lines the model got wrong, and under Section 111 of the Customs Act, a wrong HS code is not a UX bug — it can mean a mis-declaration penalty, a redo of the filing, and in repeat cases a flag against the CHA's own licence. Siddharth's team had spent three years building a deterministic rule engine, cross-checked against the CBIC tariff schedule, so that Waseela could tell a customer exactly why a code was suggested. He did not want an unexplainable model near a live filing, least of all in a first demo to a client the company barely knew.

From Singapore, customer-success lead Meenal Fernandes had a third data point: in exit interviews, CHAs who churned most often cited fear of an audit trail they couldn't defend, not slow software. From New Jersey, sales head Arvind Chacko had a fourth: the Dubai group's own RFP asked for "AI-assisted classification," and a rival vendor had already demoed something with that label. The disagreement had stopped being about facts — everyone agreed on the 91% and the 9% — and had become about which risk each was willing to own.

3. The people

Tanvi Balakrishnan — VP Product, Kochi (HQ). Owns Friday's recommendation and the Dubai demo content. Wants a decision the whole team will actually execute, not just accept in the room.

Siddharth Rao — Head of Engineering, Pune. Wants the AI suggestion, if shown at all, kept strictly advisory, with the rule engine as system of record. Fears reputational and legal exposure if a misclassification is traced to Waseela.

Aakash Devan — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Wants the model shown running live — a hedged, buried demo will read as Waseela not believing its own engine — and two of his team have already been approached by a rival startup.

Meenal Fernandes — Head of Customer Success, Singapore. Wants any AI feature to keep the CHA as the final, visible approver on every line, so customers don't feel decisions are being taken from them.

Arvind Chacko — VP Sales, New Jersey. Wants the Dubai deal closed; it is the largest contract in the pipeline and the RFP language explicitly rewards an AI story.

4. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — Waseela Trade Systems, FY25 revenue mix and FY26 plan (₹ crore)
SegmentFY25 ARRFY26 planNotes

Exporter subscriptions9.411.51,150 accounts

Total ARR34.041.7Dubai deal not yet in plan
Dubai forwarder (prospective)—4.8Single largest single-account addition on record

Source: Waseela FY25 management accounts; FY26 figures are the board-approved plan before the Dubai account.

Exhibit 2 — Classification approach compared, Tuticorin pilot (40 CHA desks, 14,000 lines)
ApproachAccuracy vs. final CHA codeAvg. time / lineSample cost of a wrong code
Manual (status quo)~97%*6.0 min₹0 (self-corrected before filing)
