Exhibit 3 — The decision window: five working days between Tanvi's internal call and the Dubai demo.

5. The options

A. Back Aakash: demo the AI suggestion live

Show the model running end to end, positioned as the product's future. It answers the RFP's own language and gives Arvind a strong close. Cost: Siddharth's team cannot yet guarantee an audit trail, and one visible error in front of a new client's compliance team could cost more than the deal is worth.

B. Back Siddharth: keep the rule engine as the only thing shown

Demo the proven, explainable system; mention the AI work as a research direction, nothing more. Safest compliance position, and it protects the CHA trust Meenal has built. Cost: it does not answer what the RFP asked for, and it tells Aakash — and the two engineers he is trying to retain — that eight months of their work is not yet real to the company.

C. Reframe the demo: AI proposes, CHA disposes

Show the model live, but as a visible first draft a CHA reviewer must accept, edit, or override before anything reaches ICEGATE — the configuration Exhibit 2 already supports (98% accuracy, ₹0 recorded loss). Cost: it is a narrower claim than "AI-assisted," it takes real design work to make the review step feel fast rather than bureaucratic, and it asks both Aakash and Siddharth to change their brief before Friday.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does each stakeholder actually want underneath their stated position — is Aakash arguing for the model, or for something else; is Siddharth arguing against AI, or against something else?
  2. Read Exhibit 2 again. Which row would you want your own name attached to, if a penalty notice arrived the week after the demo?
  3. Arvind says the RFP rewards an "AI-assisted" story. Does Option C satisfy that language, or must Tanvi manage what the client hears as much as what the product does?
  4. Tanvi has five working days. What should she decide by Friday, and what should she leave open until after the demo?

7. A note for the learner

This case is a disagreement, not a data dispute — Aakash and Siddharth do not argue about the 91% and the 9%; they argue about which failure they are more afraid of putting their name next to. That is the trap in most stakeholder conflict: two reasonable people, each holding a real piece of the truth, arguing past each other because neither has separated the position ("ship the model" / "don't ship it") from the interest underneath (Aakash: credibility and retention for his team; Siddharth: defensible compliance and Waseela's licence to operate). A PM who referees the positions will produce a compromise nobody executes well; a PM who surfaces the interests can usually find an option neither side has stated yet.

Option C is the defensible path, and it works because it is not a 50-50 split between A and B — it is a different claim that satisfies both interests at once. The pilot data already shows a CHA-reviewed AI suggestion beats the rule engine alone on accuracy (98% vs. 95%) while cutting review time nearly in half; that gives Siddharth an audit trail he can defend to CBIC and gives Aakash a live, credible demo of real model output. It also gives Meenal the visible human approval step her churned customers said they needed, and it still answers Arvind's RFP language, just precisely rather than loosely. Tanvi's remaining work by Friday is not to re-litigate the data — everyone already agrees on Exhibit 2 — but to get Aakash and Siddharth to commit, out loud, to the same demo script, so the disagreement doesn't resurface live in Dubai on the 19th.
exp40v2-lead.pm.skills:
What Makes a Great PM

People, Leadership & Organisation — Leadership & Team. A near-expert treatment: the schools that disagree, the arithmetic underneath “alignment”, the organisational seams, and the failure modes with their diagnostics.

1. Two rooms, one February

On 4 February 2026, Nandita Bose, Director of Product for governance at Fehrist Data Cloud in Bengaluru, opened a spreadsheet she had shown nobody. Fehrist sells a metadata catalogue and data-lineage platform to banks, NBFCs and insurers: ₹86 crore of ARR across forty-one accounts. Three customers — two private-sector banks and a general insurer, ₹19.4 crore of ARR between them — had internal audits landing between April and July, and their auditors now wanted column-level lineage evidence rather than a diagram. Fehrist’s engine reconstructed lineage by parsing SQL, covering about seventy-one per cent of a typical bank’s pipelines and silently omitting the rest: anything moved by a Spark job, a stored procedure or a vendor ETL tool never appeared.

Sharvari Kulkarni, VP of Engineering, wanted fourteen engineer-months to rebuild on runtime instrumentation. Dev Pillai, the CRO, wanted an attestation pack in five weeks. And at a board meeting in November, Fehrist’s CEO had called lineage coverage “essentially complete”. That sentence, not the engineering, was the part Nandita had no obvious tool for.

On 11 February, in Pune, Kabir Anand watched an audiologist wince mid-fitting. Inayat Hearing Devices had spent nineteen months on its first mass-market product: a CDSCO-licensed Class B hearing aid with a fitting app, MRP ₹18,900 per ear against a ₹4,180 bill of materials, sold through 240 partner clinics and committed to the pre-Diwali retail window. Validation on 310 fittings showed the adaptive feedback-cancellation firmware whistling audibly in nine per cent of cases, concentrated in one ear-canal geometry. Tejaswini Rao, who ran hardware, priced the fix at eleven weeks and a ₹38 lakh mould tool. Faraz Sheikh, who ran retail, had a festive quarter. Dr Leena Mathew, the clinical advisor, said the uncomfortable thing: nine per cent of fittings is nine per cent of people who go home and tell other people.

Neither had authority over anyone in the argument. Both had a week. Both would be judged less on the decision than on whether the organisation did it.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define the role by its output. A product manager’s output is not a document, a roadmap or a shipped feature; it is decisions that other people execute. Value then equals decision quality multiplied by the fraction of the organisation that adopts it: call it D × A. Competent PMs are respectable on one term. Great ones keep the product of both high when the problem is ambiguous, the clock short and the room occupied by someone who outranks them. The five capabilities usually listed — a defensible view under incomplete evidence, commitment from non-reports, evidence disciplined enough to change one’s own mind, a narrative that survives retelling, and clarity that reduces rather than adds work — are inputs to D and A, not virtues.

The problem is older than software. In 1931 Neil McElroy proposed a “brand man” at Procter & Gamble, accountable for a brand across manufacturing, advertising and sales — invented because no function owned the outcome and every function owned a piece. What made it hard then makes it hard now: responsibility without a reporting line. Ben Horowitz’s 1996 Netscape memo restated it for software; Marty Cagan’s Inspired (2008, revised 2017) reframed it around empowered teams and discovery. Together they are four traditions, not one, and they disagree about what to hire for.

The judgement school. Greatness is the quality of the call; product sense is the scarce input, the rest hygiene. It would sign: a PM who is systematically right about what to build is great even if abrasive. It would not sign: process can substitute for taste.

The leadership school. Greatness is adoption; since the PM commands nothing, followership binds. It would sign: an eightieth-percentile decision fully executed beats a ninety-ninth-percentile decision half-executed. It would not sign: the PM should be the smartest person in the room.

The systems school. Greatness is a property of the organisation: decision rights, team boundaries and manager quality dominate. It would sign: most PM failure is org design showing through a person. It would not sign: hire better PMs to fix a slow roadmap.

The craft-and-analytics school. Greatness is measurable: instrumented products, pre-registered hypotheses, calibrated forecasts. It would sign: a PM who cannot state a falsifiable prior is not doing the job. It would not sign: vision compensates for un-instrumented shipping. The four do not reduce to a synthesis, and firms that pretend otherwise end up with frameworks that score everything and predict nothing.

3. Mechanics, with the arithmetic

Expert practice has a sequence whose steps leave no trace in the artefacts. Nandita’s first move was to refuse the framing. Sharvari and Dev were arguing rebuild-versus-attestation; she asked instead what does an auditor need to see, at these three accounts, before July. Auditors do not require complete lineage, only that regulated paths be traceable and gaps documented. That produced a third option nobody had tabled: instrument the twelve highest-risk pipelines at those accounts first, lifting coverage on regulated flows to ninety-four per cent in nine weeks on six engineer-months — as increment one of the rebuild rather than a throwaway.

Her second move was to price the options rather than argue them, at Fehrist’s loaded ₹10 lakh per engineer-month. With the customer-success leads she estimated two probabilities: the chance an auditor raises a material finding under each path, and the chance such a finding costs a renewal. The second she put at thirty-five per cent, and wrote down that she was guessing.

Path C dominates, but the number that made it survive cross-examination was not in the table. Dev challenged the thirty-five per cent churn assumption, correctly: it was invented. She had run the sensitivity. The expected-loss gap between A and C is (0.45 − 0.15) × p × ₹19.4 crore = ₹5.82 crore × p, where p is the probability of losing an account given a material finding; the cost gap is ₹10 lakh. They are equal at p = 0.017. Unless a bank handed a material finding on its lineage has under a two per cent chance of not renewing, C wins. The argument stopped there, because the conclusion was insensitive to the assumption under attack. Disciplined evidence is not more numbers; it is the number that would change your mind, computed before the room asks.

Her third move is almost never written down. Nandita had six stakeholders — Sharvari, Dev, two customer-success leads, compliance and the CEO — and six people generate fifteen pairwise relationships, which is why aligning everyone with everyone is a full-time job with no output. She pre-wired the four who could veto, half an hour each before the Thursday review, to surface the objection while it was cheap. Sharvari’s was that Path C would be declared “done” and the remaining eight engineer-months quietly cancelled, which is what usually happens. Nandita could not promise otherwise, so she wrote Path C in as increment one of three with the later increments dated, and had Dev commit the sales-side dependency in the same document.

The second-order effect matters more. Pre-wiring changes what the meeting is for: a review at which objections have surfaced already becomes a ratification, which is boring, which is the point. Executives learn that this PM’s reviews hold no surprises, and begin delegating a class of decision entirely. That authority — never formally granted, never in a job description — is most of what people mean by a great PM.

4. When the model applies, and when it misleads

Claim 1: leverage scales with the number of functions that must move together. Count the functions whose plans change if the decision changes. At Fehrist it is four: engineering, sales, customer success, compliance. At Inayat it is six, adding manufacturing, regulatory affairs and the clinical network. Kabir therefore has more leverage, and a higher cost of error, than his title shows.

Claim 2: adoption dominates where decisions are reversible; decision quality dominates where they are not. Nandita can reverse Path C in six weeks at the cost of work done. Kabir’s mould tool cannot be un-cut: ₹38 lakh and eleven weeks go the moment the order does. Where irreversibility is high the emphasis shifts from bringing people along to being right, and capital is better spent on evidence than on agreement.

Claim 3: the model presupposes slack. Alignment work is unpriced but not free, and a PM covering three squads at a one-to-twelve ratio has no room for four pre-wiring conversations a week. The right response is not five things done badly but two done well: clarity in writing, and one disconfirming metric.

The model misleads in three places. Where the uncertainty is technical: no alignment tells Kabir whether the firmware can work, and treating a physics question as a stakeholder question is an expensive category error. In regulated contexts, where the answer is a licence condition and “bringing people along” means delay. And in founder-led early-stage firms, where a competing PM vision is noise.

5. Hard edge cases at the seams

Multi-product. Imarat Build Cloud, an Ahmedabad construction-software firm, runs four products — procurement, site operations, bills of quantity and contractor payments — each with its own PM. The behaviour that makes a PM great inside one product — taking the call, creating clarity — reads across the seam as a land grab. Simran Kohli, Imarat’s VP of Product, watched two strong PMs each define “the vendor record” and spend five months building incompatible versions. The official remedy was a decision-rights matrix. What worked was a standing Friday slot with one executive empowered to settle data ownership in fifteen minutes. Mature companies put the matrix in the handbook and run the Friday slot.

Two-sided markets. Iravati Freight Exchange, a Nagpur road-freight marketplace matching 11,400 trucks to 3,200 shippers at a 4.1 per cent take rate, faces an alignment problem that is not internal. Clarity given to shippers — guaranteed two-hour pick-up windows — is a constraint on fleet owners, who lose backhaul flexibility. The PM tells two versions of one story to audiences with opposed interests, both true, neither complete. The tell of a weak marketplace PM is a narrative that works only while one side is not listening.

Regulated, and hardware-plus-software. Inayat sits in both. A CDSCO licence fixes claims, labelling and change control in ways no rallying moves, and the cadences mismatch: firmware ships weekly, tooling once. The expert skill is sequencing irreversibility — choosing which irreversible commitments to make early, while information is worst but options widest.

AI-native. Farmaan Credit Systems, a Gurugram underwriting platform, shows the newest seam of all. In a model-driven product a PM cannot promise behaviour, only distributions; the commitment is an error budget, not a specification. Alignment now includes model-risk and governance functions absent from the 2015 org chart, and evals have replaced the feature demo as the contested artefact. A PM who cannot read one is not in the conversation, whatever their influence skills.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

Vision is timing, not invention. The obvious reading is that great PMs originate ideas. Almost none do. They say, a week before anyone else, what a dozen scattered conversations already implied. The tell is repetition: within three weeks others use the PM’s sentence in rooms the PM is not in, unaware they quote.

Alignment is measured in absence. Agreement in a meeting is cheap and usually courteous. The expert test is whether the decision holds in a meeting the PM did not attend. Path C survived a March escalation while Nandita was on leave, because the CS leads could reconstruct the argument — including the crossover at 1.7 per cent — without her. That reconstruction, not the original consent, is the evidence.

Evidence discipline looks like pre-registration. Competent PMs bring data to defend conclusions. Experts state in writing, with a date, what would falsify their recommendation, before it arrives. The tell is archaeological: a document written before the result. Kabir’s was one line to Faraz — above two per cent of fitted units returned inside thirty days, the launch pauses regardless of festive revenue. That converts an argument about loyalty into arithmetic.

Story quality is tested by a hostile listener. The wrong test is whether the story inspires. The right one is whether a finance reviewer who dislikes the plan can restate it accurately. A story surviving only in friendly hands is positioning; one surviving an opponent’s restatement is a shared model.

Clarity has a cost curve and someone pays it. A PM who seems to generate clarity effortlessly is often producing it for one function by pushing ambiguity to another — engineering gets a crisp spec because regulatory was handed an unanswered question. The tell is asymmetric relief: one team calmer, another quietly acquiring undated work.

Credit allocation is an instrument, not manners. The obvious reading is generosity. The mechanism is informational: peers who expect to be named bring bad news earlier, and early bad news largely determines whether a plan survives. The tell is not the all-hands speech; it is whether engineers forward failing tests unasked.

Experts manage what their executives have already said in public. Nandita’s hardest constraint was the CEO’s November sentence, not the engine. A competent PM corrects the record and acquires an enemy. The expert supplies a next line rather than a retraction: coverage is complete for regulated reporting, the remainder instrumented by Q3. Same facts, no reversal, something the executive can say on Monday.

Calibration beats confidence, and it is recorded. Experts keep a private record of their forecasts. Nandita’s last four: catalogue adoption above sixty per cent of seats, stated at 70, missed at 44; the insurer renewing flat or better, 85, hit; an auditor raising the lineage gap in FY25, 55, hit twice over; the rebuild fitting one quarter, 40, missed. Four forecasts prove nothing statistically. The tell is that the probabilities are specific — sixty per cent, not “likely” — and that she cites her misses unprompted.

7. Product type and company stage

Two things do not vary, worth saying plainly because consulting revenue depends on pretending otherwise. Evidence discipline — naming the disconfirming number in advance — is identical in a hearing aid and a data catalogue. And the written close, one decision with one owner and one date, is no large-company ritual: a six-person startup that skips it re-litigates the same decision, faster and with more feeling.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Fehrist, and the audits. Nandita ran Path C. Actual spend was ₹68 lakh against a ₹60 lakh estimate, an overrun she reported in the same sentence as the result. Two audits closed with observations rather than findings; the insurer raised a finding on an unrelated retention control. All three accounts renewed, ₹19.4 crore intact, and increments two and three survived the budget cycle — because Sharvari, who had objected in private, defended the roadmap in a forum Nandita was not in.

Iravati, and the guaranteed pick-up window. Prakash Mohite piloted two-hour guaranteed pick-up on 620 lanes. Adherence rose from 61 to 88 per cent and shipper repeat-booking improved eleven points. It cost something real: utilisation on those lanes fell four points, and Iravati conceded 0.4 percentage points of take rate to fleet owners, ₹1.9 crore annualised. Prakash published both numbers in the same note, which is what made the fleet-side team willing to run phase two.

Farmaan, and the failure. Rhea Venkataraman, Group PM at Farmaan Credit Systems, ran what looked from inside like a textbook case of the whole model. She built a model-driven underwriting flow for small-ticket business loans, aligned risk, credit operations, engineering and the lending partners, told a clean story and shipped on time. Approval rates rose from 31 to 44 per cent; quarterly disbursal rose ₹210 crore. Every meeting was calm. What she lacked was a disconfirming number with a date. The shared metric was approval rate — an output everyone liked — rather than a vintage curve, which would have shown the new cohort’s 90-day delinquency at 5.8 per cent against a 2.1 per cent book average. By the time the second vintage matured, ₹310 crore had gone out and expected credit loss was about ₹18 crore. Alignment had been perfect and pointed at the wrong quantity, the most dangerous configuration in the role, because nothing feels wrong until it is expensive.

The recovery took eleven weeks and was structural rather than personal. Rhea made the vintage curve the single shared metric, published monthly to the audience that had been reading approval rates; wrote a model-change protocol requiring risk co-signature on any shift in approval thresholds; and reset approvals to 37 per cent, which cost the quarter. The part she later called the actual fix felt like punishment: she lost the ability to ship a policy change unilaterally. Adoption had been her strongest term all along, and constraining it restored the other one.

9. Failure modes and diagnostics

All five first present as scheduling problems — the team is behind, the vendor is slow — which is why they persist. Only the diagnostic question separates a delay from a missing step, and each takes a minute to ask.

10. Where the field genuinely disagrees

Individual or organisational? The systems position, steelmanned: measured PM performance tracks team autonomy, manager quality and the number of sign-offs a decision needs, and firms that replaced PMs without changing decision rights saw no improvement. Opponents point to individuals who turned around two unrelated teams at two unrelated firms. The systems view fails if such transfers are common rather than anecdotal; the individual view fails if output swings threefold on reorganisation alone. Both observations exist; nobody has run the study that settles it.

Does vision matter in enterprise software? One camp holds that in B2B the job is discovery and execution, and vision a consumer affectation; buyers want a roadmap matching a procurement cycle. The counter-position is that enterprise buyers make five-year bets and are purchasing a view of where the category goes. What would settle it is whether win rates move with stated direction at constant feature parity; the evidence is self-reported.

Domain expertise or general craft? In regulated and AI-native products — Inayat and Farmaan both — the generalist is now punished, because the load-bearing judgements concern licence conditions and error distributions. In consumer, outsider intuition remains an asset. The expertise claim fails if domain-naive PMs keep succeeding in regulated categories; the generalist claim fails if expert-led consumer products outperform. Neither has been shown cleanly.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in ways visible within a fortnight. They arrive at contested meetings having had the argument already, in private, so the meeting is short and slightly dull. They volunteer the number that would make them wrong before anyone asks. They write the decision down within the hour and name the owner, including when the owner is not them. They give away authorship of the framing and keep responsibility for the outcome, which is the opposite of the instinct. They can say what the sharpest opponent of their plan would argue and why it is not stupid. And under pressure, where the competent version reaches for more agreement, they reach for more evidence.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Nandita recommended Path C, framed as increment one of three with the later increments dated, and handed her CEO a forward-looking sentence rather than a correction. She said in writing that the 0.35 churn figure was a guess and that the recommendation held down to p = 0.017. Kabir made the harder call. He shipped into the festive window for the ninety-one per cent of fittings that worked, added a ninety-second in-clinic canal check routing the affected geometry to a deferred Mark II, committed the ₹38 lakh mould tool that same week, and gave Faraz the number that would stop everything: two per cent thirty-day returns. He made the irreversible decision early, when information was poorest, because the option would not exist later.

Three questions worth arguing. First: Kabir shipped a device he knew failed for nine per cent of patients, in a clinical category, behind a mitigation that depends on clinic staff performing a check correctly — a control, or a way of making a revenue decision feel clinical? Second: Nandita’s reframing was accurate and also convenient; where is the line between supplying a next line and laundering a mistake? Third: Rhea was, by the leadership school’s standards, doing the job superbly until the vintages matured — if a PM can be excellent on adoption and catastrophic on outcome, what should a firm promote on?

13. Going deeper

  1. Influence without authority — the mechanism under the adoption term; taught properly only through role-play with real conflict.
  2. Telling the customer story — how a narrative survives retelling, which is what makes alignment portable.
  3. Creating clarity and energy — the same discipline applied to a team rather than a decision.
  4. Resilience and handling failure — the Farmaan recovery in general form.
  5. PM interviews — how these capabilities are probed, and which signals predict.
  6. Executive presence and credibility — what accumulates once your reviews stop producing surprises.
  7. Conflict and disagreement — Sharvari’s objection was the quarter’s cheapest information; how to make that routine.
  8. Negotiation for PMs — Iravati’s take-rate concession was a negotiation; trading across functions without escalating.
  9. Building trust with teams — why engineers forward failing tests early.
  10. Psychological safety and team health — the precondition for anyone telling you the metric is wrong.
  11. Coaching and feedback — transmitting pre-registration and calibration to a team.
  12. Working in diverse and global teams — pre-wiring and story across time zones.

Product Management Teaching Case · People, Leadership & Organisation

Eighty-Seven Months of Want: Pranali Kothari and the Xetra Plan

An ambiguous case for the module on leadership and team, Indian School of Business

1. Opening: Sunday night, Vadodara

At twenty minutes to ten on the night of Sunday, 27 September 2026, Pranali Kothari sat at the dining table of her flat off Gotri Road in Vadodara with a laptop, a printed sprint ledger and a cold cup of tea, unable to decide whether the slide in front of her was honest.

The slide was titled H2 FY27: One Sequenced Plan. It had four rows. Pranali, Vice-President of Product at Xetra Site Systems, had built it for the leadership call at ten the next morning, and it would go almost unchanged into the board pre-read due Wednesday for the 9 October meeting. Each row was something the company had already told somebody it would do. Together the four asked for eighty-seven engineer-months in a half-year that could fund forty-eight, and the arithmetic had not moved in three weeks of trying.

What made the night long was not the shortfall. It was a sentence Jaideep Chauhan, the co-founder and chief executive, had dropped into her review on Friday evening with no apparent edge to it: “Pranali, you are running this like a very good programme manager. I don't need a programme manager for the next two quarters.” She had asked what he did need. He had said he was hoping she would tell him on Monday.

On her screen, unsent, was a message to Anirban Sen in Kolkata asking whether the re-platforming could pause for six weeks without losing the year. Beside it, also unsent, a reply to the finance head of Xetra's largest customer, who had written that his board was “reviewing all software vendors” and needed the RERA quarterly-report module working by 15 October.

2. Company history: the promise of March 2019

Xetra Site Systems was founded in Vadodara in 2017 by Jaideep Chauhan, formerly a planning engineer on transmission projects, and Urvi Pandya, who had built billing software for a Gujarat electrical-contracting group. Their premise was mundane and correct: Indian construction ran on a measurement book, a running-account bill and a WhatsApp group, and nobody had joined the three. Xetra's app let a site engineer geo-stamp progress against a bill of quantities; its billing engine turned those measurements into subcontractor running-account bills with retention, steel and cement rate variation and tax deducted at source; its reporting layer produced the quarterly project-progress statements developers must file with their state Real Estate Regulatory Authority.

By September 2026 Xetra had 208 customers, 3,140 live projects, 296 employees and ₹47 crore of annual recurring revenue, against ₹41 crore at the close of FY26. A Series B of ₹210 crore in August 2024 had been raised on one sentence — the operating system for Indian construction — and ₹96 crore of it remained.

One decision from March 2019 shaped everything after it. To win Shilanyas Developers, a Surat residential developer then building eleven towers, Xetra agreed to a dedicated single-tenant deployment with a bespoke measurement-book schema, and to a clause barring any use of Shilanyas data outside the Shilanyas account. It closed the deal, and became the template every large customer asked for. Seven years on, twelve enterprise tenants ran on forks carrying ₹19.4 crore of ARR and consuming eleven of the eighteen engineer-months a quarter Xetra spent merely keeping things running. Nothing shipped platform-wide in one pass; almost nothing could be analysed across customers.

3. The industry

Indian construction software in 2026 was crowded at the cheap end and thin at the expensive one. Powerplay and a dozen smaller field apps served contractors at a few thousand rupees a month; Autodesk Construction Cloud and Oracle's Primavera held the design and schedule layers of the largest projects; groups of the scale of Larsen & Toubro or Tata Projects ran their own SAP-adjacent stacks. Xetra's territory was the middle: developers of the Godrej Properties or Kalpataru shape but three tiers smaller, and the engineering-procurement-construction contractors who served them. Most kept accounts in Tally or Zoho Books, which is why Xetra's billing exports mattered more than its dashboards.

Two competitive facts were newer. Sarvekshan Survey Systems, a Noida firm that had raised ₹180 crore on drone photogrammetry, now bundled free RERA quarterly filing with its survey subscription — a wedge into accounts where progress capture, not survey, was the real workflow. And Sanad Records Cloud of Gurugram, which sold compliance documentation, had pitched Shilanyas in August with a proposal Xetra had not seen.

Regulation moved in the same weeks. On 14 September the Gujarat Real Estate Regulatory Authority published a consultation paper proposing machine-readable quarterly project filings from April 2027, with Maharashtra's authority thought to be considering something similar. Ganesh Iyer in New Jersey read this as the best commercial gift of the year; Pranali read it as a date she could not control. Separately, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act meant site photographs containing identifiable workers — the raw material of Xetra's most promising prototype — needed a consent basis nobody in the company could yet describe on one page.

Abroad, Xetra had one opening: Sadaf Contracting LLC, a Dubai fit-out and civil contractor turning over ₹1,900 crore a year, had piloted four projects since August and offered ₹6.4 crore over three years, conditional on a Gulf edition by 1 February 2027.

Illustration. Xetra's product organisation and the two customers that dominate the H2 FY27 debate. The only hour at which all seven locations are awake is 7:00 p.m. IST.

4. The situation in detail

In April 2026, three weeks after Pranali was promoted to Vice-President of Product, the leadership team approved a programme called One Xetra: collapse the twelve enterprise forks onto one multi-tenant data model, then build once. The plan assumed two enterprise tenants would migrate voluntarily in the first quarter, proving the path. Xiti Realty Partners, a nine-project developer working across Vadodara and Rajkot, moved in June and was glad it had. Shilanyas declined, citing the 2019 schema clause and a Diwali possession commitment on four towers. By mid-September migration stood at 38 per cent of tenants by count and 21 per cent by revenue, and Anirban's team was maintaining three code paths where there had been two.

In June, Mrinalini Raghavan's team in Toronto shipped a prototype that read progress photographs against the bill of quantities and flagged material variance — shuttering counted twice, steel booked against an uncast slab. Run for a quarter on Xiti's nine projects, it surfaced ₹68 lakh of questionable billing. Everyone repeated the number. It appears as Exhibit 5, where the footnote matters more than the figure.

In August the Sadaf pilot went live and Ines Vogel flew from Berlin to Dubai for four days of site observation. She returned with a re-estimate nobody wanted: the Gulf edition was not a translation job. Variation orders, retention practice and payment under the Wage Protection System differed enough that the billing engine needed surgery. Six engineer-months became twenty-two.

Then three things landed in one week of September. The consultation paper on the 14th, which made Xetra's reporting layer either a moat or a commodity depending on who moved first. Rizwan Shaikh's field audit on the 18th, which is Exhibit 4, and which says something the dashboards do not. And on the 22nd, Bhavesh Sanghvi's email giving 15 October as the date by which the rebuilt quarterly-report module and a two-level running-account approval workflow had to be in production, mentioning in a subordinate clause that his board had asked for a vendor review.

April's belief was that One Xetra would pay for itself within two quarters by freeing sustaining capacity. What was visible now was that it consumed capacity first and freed it later, and that the customer whose fork cost most was the one least willing to move and most able to leave.

5. The people

Jaideep Chauhan

Co-founder and Chief Executive · Vadodara

Wants a plan he can defend on 9 October and a Series C story by mid-2027. Says he will back whatever Pranali decides. Has not said that he told the board in July the reconciliation work would be investor-ready by January, or that he has shown it to two funds.

Anirban Sen

Vice-President, Engineering · Kolkata

Position: finish One Xetra or abandon it, but stop half-doing it. Incentive: attrition at 22 per cent, and three senior engineers have told him the fork work is why. Not saying: he doubts the remaining seven tenants can be migrated without a commercial concession he has no authority to offer, and he has not re-run the estimate since June.

Mrinalini Raghavan

Principal Data Scientist · Toronto

Position: the reconciliation model is the only thing competitors cannot copy in a quarter. Incentive: her team of four was hired for it and she has a standing offer elsewhere. Not saying: 63 per cent of her labelled training data comes from the twelve walled tenants, and she has not asked legal whether the 2019 clause permits what she has already done.

Ines Vogel

Design Director · Berlin

Position: adoption, not features, is the gap; a site engineer in Vapi and a foreman in Dubai both abandon the app at the measurement screen. Incentive: she has argued for a research-led quarter for a year and lost. Not saying: her Dubai findings imply the Indian measurement flow is wrong too, making the Gulf work a rewrite of something Xetra sells as finished.

Shabana Qureshi

Director, Customer Success, APAC and Gulf · Singapore

Position: sign Sadaf, because two further Gulf prospects worth ₹11 crore are watching. Incentive: her variable pay is tied to the Gulf book she built. Not saying: Sadaf's projects director has twice asked in writing for the Arabic interface and she has answered “in the plan” without a date.

Ganesh Iyer

Senior Vice-President, Sales · Newark, New Jersey

Position: the RERA reporting module wins India, and the consultation paper is a nine-month window. Incentive: 70 per cent of his quota is Indian mid-market, where Sarvekshan's free filing tool now appears in deals. Not saying: he has demonstrated the reconciliation prototype in sales calls since July, and four signed customers expect it.

Rizwan Shaikh

Head of Field Implementation · Jaipur

Position: none of the four proposals matters if a clerk is still re-typing WhatsApp photos. Incentive: his team absorbs every adoption failure as manual service work. Not saying: his own people do that re-typing for three enterprise accounts to hold satisfaction scores up, which is part of why Exhibit 2 looks healthy.

Bhavesh Sanghvi

Chief Financial Officer, Shilanyas Developers · Surat (external)

Position: 15 October, or a vendor review. Incentive: four towers to hand over before Diwali and a filing that must not be late. Not saying whether the Sanad Records Cloud proposal on his desk is a real alternative or a negotiating instrument.

7. Voices

“We are three code paths deep. Every fortnight we pay interest on a decision made in 2019 and call it maintenance. If we stop the migration now I lose two more people by December, and they are the two who understand billing.”

Anirban Sen, engineering review, 16 September, 7:10 p.m. IST

“Eighty-two per cent weekly active measures phones being switched on. In Vapi I watched a clerk retype a week of photographs on a Saturday. We are not fighting Sarvekshan. We are fighting WhatsApp, and WhatsApp is winning because it works with one hand and a torch.”

Ines Vogel, email from Berlin, 19 September

“₹68 lakh on nine projects. Multiply by 3,140. Nobody else in this market can even see it. And I would like to know why the thing I was hired to build is row three of four.”

Mrinalini Raghavan, product forum chat thread, 23 September

“India pays the salaries. Every mid-market deal I lost this quarter, I lost on filing. The authority has just told us what the next two years look like. Spend this window rebuilding plumbing no customer can see and we will own the best architecture in a smaller market.”

Ganesh Iyer, pipeline review, 25 September, 9:30 p.m. IST

8. The options as Pranali sees them

She wrote them as four rows because the leadership call needs a table.

A. Finish One Xetra

Seventy engineer-months to collapse the forks: the only option that makes every later option cheaper, and the only one with nothing a customer can see before March. It assumes the remaining seven enterprise tenants can be moved — which Anirban privately doubts, and which the 2019 clause does not oblige them to accept.

B. Build the Gulf edition

Twenty-two engineer-months secures ₹6.4 crore and opens ₹11 crore of pipeline, but it sits on the old billing engine, so it gets built twice if A ever happens. Ines's finding — that the measurement flow itself is wrong — would make it a rewrite at the wrong layer.

C. Ship material reconciliation

Sixteen engineer-months and ₹1.1 crore a year of compute for the one capability competitors cannot match in a quarter, and which four signed customers and two prospective investors believe exists. Its training data sits behind the 2019 clause; its DPDP consent basis has never been written down.

D. Honour the enterprise commitments

Fourteen engineer-months protects ₹19.4 crore of renewals, ₹3.9 crore of it due in March, and meets 15 October. It is also the row conceding that the twelve costliest tenants go on setting the roadmap — the condition A exists to end.

Pranali has noticed, and not said out loud, that A and D overlap: the quarterly-report rebuild Shilanyas wants is the data model One Xetra needs, if built on the new schema rather than the fork. Anirban costed them separately because they arrived as separate requests from separate people. Nobody has asked Bhavesh Sanghvi what he needs in production on 15 October as against the March specification, or asked Sadaf whether Arabic screens alone would hold the signature.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Monday's call at ten, the pre-read on Wednesday, the board on 9 October. Cash of ₹96 crore against ₹4.2 crore a month; the board's July resolution asked for ₹75 crore of ARR by March 2028 with burn under ₹3 crore a month, and approved four engineering additions worth ₹1.9 crore a year that Anirban says cannot be productive before February. Nalini Ranganathan, the investor director, wants one slide showing what Xetra will not do.

What cannot be negotiated in a fortnight: the 2019 data-use clause, reaffirmed twice by Shilanyas's counsel; the DPDP consent question on worker photographs; 15 October, tied to a statutory filing and a Diwali handover; the 1 February lapse of Sadaf's offer; and the fact that a senior engineer in Kolkata costs ₹38 lakh a year while Mrinalini's four-person Toronto team costs more than eleven Indian engineers — a comparison Anirban has put in writing twice and Jaideep has not answered.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Reading Exhibits 2 and 4 together, what does Xetra actually know about whether its product is used?
  2. Exhibit 5 was quoted in a board pack as ₹68 lakh. What is the defensible number, and what does the gap imply for how Pranali handles option C before the board?
  3. Each stakeholder holds one piece of a good decision and one piece of self-interest. Which unstated position, if surfaced on Monday, would most change the answer — and what does surfacing it cost Pranali?
  4. The 2019 promise bought Xetra its largest customer and its hardest constraint. On what basis could that trade have been judged at the time, and what does that suggest about the commitments being made this week?
  5. Is the four-row framing of Exhibit 3 the right frame at all? Construct an alternative that changes what eighty-seven against forty-eight engineer-months means, and say what it gives up.
  6. What should Pranali do on Monday morning — concretely, in the first two hours — and what exactly should she say to the board on 9 October about the half-year she is not going to have?

The rest of the night

At ten past eleven Pranali deleted the fourth row of the slide, looked at three rows for a while, and put it back. She typed a new title — What we will not do — and had nothing to write under it that she could also say to Mrinalini at seven the next evening without losing her.

Her phone showed a message from Rizwan in Jaipur, sent at 10:52: a photograph of a measurement book from a site in Vapi, columns filled in by hand, dated that morning, the app's reference number written neatly in the margin afterwards. No text with it. She looked at it for some time, then at the two unsent drafts, then at the clock, which said the leadership call was eleven hours away.

What Makes a Great PM

People, Leadership & Organisation — Leadership & Team. On the question of what separates a great product manager from a merely competent one: vision, alignment, data, story, bringing people along, and clarity.

Six weeks to renewal

On the third Monday of September, Ananya Rao, Group Product Manager for Checkout at Onkar Commerce Cloud in Bengaluru, opened her laptop to a dashboard she did not want to see. Card-payment failure rates had climbed from a steady 4.1% to 11.3% over ten days, coinciding with the RBI's tokenisation-refresh mandate, which required every payment aggregator to re-tokenise stored card credentials by a fixed cut-over date. Onkar routed checkout for roughly 1,400 D2C merchants and ₹640 crore of monthly GMV, of which ₹180 crore ran through the tokenised flows now failing.

The number that mattered most sat in one row: Onkar's largest customer, a national fashion-and-lifestyle brand doing roughly ₹40 crore a month through the platform, had a renewal due in six weeks and an ops manager who had already escalated twice. By ten that morning Ananya was in a war room with three people who each wanted something different. Karthik, VP of Engineering, wanted a month to rebuild the vault properly. Meera, who ran Customer Success, wanted an apology and a workaround by Wednesday. Rajiv, the CEO, wanted a number for the board and, more quietly, wanted to know whether Ananya could run this. Trade press covering Indian fintech, quick to praise Razorpay's and Cashfree's uptime through the mandate, would notice if Onkar's largest account walked. What Ananya produced over the next four days is the case this page uses to work through what "great," as opposed to "competent," means in practice.

What "great" actually means

Strip away the adjectives attached to product management — visionary, data-driven, customer-obsessed — and the distinction is narrower and more testable. A great PM, unlike a competent one, can take a genuinely ambiguous, cross-functional problem and reliably produce five things at once: a defensible point of view when evidence is incomplete (vision); real commitment from people who do not report to them (alignment); evidence disciplined enough to change their own mind, not merely persuade a room (data); a narrative someone who was not in the room can understand and repeat (story); and a level of clarity — one decision, one owner, one deadline — that lowers anxiety rather than adding a meeting to the calendar. Competent PMs usually manage one or two of these under pressure. Great ones produce all five, in sequence, in the same week, without becoming exhausting to work with.

The distinction was written down earlier than most assume. In 1996, Ben Horowitz, then a product manager at Netscape, wrote an internal memo, "Good Product Manager, Bad Product Manager," later republished by his firm, Andreessen Horowitz: a good PM is the CEO of the product not by title but by the discipline of setting a direction others choose to follow. A decade on, Marty Cagan's writing for the Silicon Valley Product Group, and his book Inspired (2008, revised 2017), made the same case differently: judgment and followership matter more than authority, because the role carries almost none. The sentence Ananya could repeat on Thursday without sounding glib was this: "My job isn't to have the best answer — it's to make the hard call something the five of us can execute without me in the room."

The loop, step by step

What Ananya did between Monday and Friday maps onto a sequence great PMs run out of habit. First, she separated the presented symptom from the real problem: the spike was the symptom; the real problem was a fix sequence that protected revenue without permanently under-investing in the vault Karthik had flagged for a year. Second, she formed a provisional point of view before the data was complete — a one-page draft marked, visibly, "draft" — because waiting for complete data means waiting forever, and a draft gives colleagues something concrete to push against.

Third, she quantified the trade-off with her analyst, sizing leakage by merchant tier rather than platform average, producing the arithmetic below. Fourth — the step most competent PMs skip — she pre-wired alignment: short one-on-ones with Karthik and Meera before Thursday's review, so disagreement happened in private, where it is cheap, not in front of the CEO, where it is expensive. Fifth, she anchored the story on the customer's own screen rather than vault architecture. Sixth, she gave each function a visible piece of the win — Karthik's team the permanent fix, Meera's team the customer save. Seventh, she closed with clarity: one decision, two owners, dated commitments, in writing within the hour — the step that feels like paperwork and is, not coincidentally, the one most often left undone.

The two paths, priced

The review came down to two options, and Ananya had done the arithmetic rather than asserted the conclusion. Of the ₹180 crore in monthly GMV through the affected flows, the 7.2-point jump in failure (4.1% to 11.3%) represented transactions that used to succeed and no longer did — not the whole ₹180 crore, a distinction Rajiv needed spelled out twice. That incremental leakage came to ₹1.30 crore a month, roughly ₹30 lakh a week, concentrated in the top twenty accounts.

Read naively, A looks cheaper and B looks more thorough, and a competent PM often stops there and recommends whichever stakeholder is loudest. Ananya's call was neither: run both in parallel, funding A immediately while B proceeds on its own track — the two were not substitutes, since A bought time and B bought durability, and B's ₹30 lakh cost was trivial next to seven weeks of exposure alone. A second pass, run when Karthik warned failure could climb further first, repriced the table at a hypothetical 16%: leakage rises to roughly ₹2.16 crore a month, about ₹50 lakh a week, justifying two more engineers on A at an extra ₹6 lakh — a spend the first pass would not have supported.

Where the idea gets blurry

Vision is not authorship. The word tempts people into imagining a PM who invents the future alone. In practice it is usually a synthesis of what a dozen conversations already implied, said a week before anyone else said it aloud. Claiming sole authorship, rather than crediting the synthesis, is a reliable way to lose the alignment the vision was meant to build.

Alignment is not consensus. Waiting until everyone agrees is a filibuster with better manners. What Ananya needed from Karthik and Meera was commitment despite disagreement: Karthik still believed the plan under-resourced the long-term fix, said so, and committed anyway. Alignment is measured in what people do after the meeting, not what they say during it.

Data changes minds or it is theatre. The tell is whether a PM can name, in advance, the number that would change their recommendation. Ananya could: below ₹15 lakh a week of leakage the parallel-path spend would not be justified, and she said so before the number came in above it. Data introduced only to defend a conclusion already reached is decoration, not analysis.

Story is not spin. A story that survives scrutiny is falsifiable — someone could check whether the merchant's dashboard really showed what Ananya said. Spin sounds identical and collapses the first time anyone checks.

Bringing people along is not being liked. Some of a great PM's hardest calls stay unpopular for weeks before being vindicated. Karthik disliked seeing his rebuild treated as one of two tracks rather than the only priority; being right later does not require being popular now.

Clarity is expensive, not natural. PMs who seem to produce it effortlessly are usually the ones who spent Wednesday night writing the one-pager nobody saw. Clarity is manufactured before the meeting, not improvised inside it.

What none of this can tell you. It does not say which problem is worth solving — that is strategic taste, a prior judgment — nor fix an organisation whose reporting lines need nine sign-offs per decision. A great PM inside a badly designed structure looks, from outside, indistinguishable from a mediocre one for far longer than seems fair.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and scale

The same five ingredients weigh differently depending on what is built and how large the company already is. In a consumer product, story tends to dominate, since the audience is broad and moved by intuition rather than a return-on-investment calculation. In a B2B product such as Onkar's own infrastructure, alignment and data dominate, because the buyer is a committee whose pitch must survive a finance reviewer never in the room. In a marketplace, bringing people along becomes two jobs rather than one, since supply and demand sides have opposed incentives and a plan that satisfies merchants can alienate shoppers, or the reverse.

Table 2 — Where the emphasis shifts by product type and company stage
ContextWhat dominatesWhy
ConsumerStoryBroad, non-expert audience moved by intuition, not spreadsheets
B2BAlignment + dataBuying committees, finance reviewers absent from the room
MarketplaceBringing along, doubledSupply and demand incentives frequently conflict
Early-stageVision, directFew layers; PM often the only source of direction, close to customers
Large companyClarity, in writingAlignment work multiplies faster than headcount; charisma stops travelling

Stage compounds this further. In an early-stage company the PM is often the only person holding a point of view at all. At Onkar's size — roughly four hundred employees — Ananya's story had to travel through people who would repeat it in rooms she would never attend, which is why the written follow-up mattered as much as the meeting.

How this goes wrong

Table 3 — Common failure patterns and how to catch them cheaply
SymptomUnderlying misunderstandingCheap diagnostic
Team ships fast, org still confused about priorityMistaking velocity for clarityAsk five people the top priority; divergent answers reveal the gap
Decision unwinds once the sponsoring exec is awayAlignment borrowed from authority, not convictionCheck whether stakeholders can state the "why" unprompted
Numbers shown without ranges or counter-casesAdvocacy dressed as analysisAsk "what data would change your mind?" — silence is the tell
Meeting ends warmly, commitments erode within a weekConfusing enthusiasm in the room for alignmentWritten decision doc with owner and date, checked after 48 hours

Each pattern is visible from outside within days, which is why it persists: the symptom looks like a scheduling problem, and only the diagnostic reveals a missing step from the loop above — usually the pre-wiring or the written close, the two steps that feel most dispensable and prove least dispensable afterward.

What the recovery actually looked like

Six weeks later, the same dashboard told a different story. Option A's patch cut failure to 5.8% within twelve days; B's rebuild finished in its seventh week at 2.9%, better than the original 4.1%. The renewal call opened with the ops manager referencing the Friday follow-up email — two owners, two dates — rather than the outage itself. It closed at the same ₹40 crore run rate, with an added clause for a defined incident-response window, already built into Karthik's new architecture. Nothing about the recovery was dramatic; it looked like a plan simply followed, on schedule, by people each given credit in advance.

The call, and what's next

Ananya's decision was to fund both paths at once rather than choose between them, priced against a leakage figure her team could defend line by line, pre-wired through private conversations, told through the customer's own dashboard, and closed with a written commitment that survived the meeting. None of the five ingredients — vision, alignment, data, story, clarity — did the work alone; the renewal was saved by their sequence, run inside one week, under real pressure.

Two questions worth sitting with: which of the five ingredients do you reach for first under pressure, and which do you skip — and can you name, right now, the number that would change your current recommendation?

Four topics extend from here. Influence without authority and telling the customer story were this page's assumed prerequisites, worth revisiting if either felt unfamiliar above. What follows is creating clarity and energy at team scale, resilience and handling failure, how this is tested in PM interviews, and how it compounds into executive presence and credibility. The best programmes teach the alignment half through role-play built around genuine stakeholder conflict; a curriculum skipping real disagreement teaches the vocabulary without testing whether a student can produce it.

What Makes a Great PM: The Diyafa Decision at Ekjut Handloom Exchange

A short decision case for the module on leadership and team, Indian School of Business

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 14 September 2026, Gitanjali Mohapatra stood at the whiteboard in Ekjut Handloom Exchange's office in the Chandrasekharpur tech corridor of Bhubaneswar, looking at a sprint board that would not fit the work in front of it. As Group Product Manager, she owned the roadmap for the company's marketplace and provenance systems. In four days, at Thursday's 6:30 p.m. sprint-planning call — timed so colleagues in Chennai, Toronto, Berlin, Singapore and New Jersey could all join without one of them dialling in at midnight — she had to tell the squad where its next twelve developer-weeks would go. Three proposals sat on her desk, each backed by a capable colleague, each defensible, and no combination fit inside the sprint. Whatever she chose would decide whether a ₹1.8 crore export order shipped on time, whether hundreds of waiting artisans got onto the platform before the festive season, or whether the company's newest idea for selling craft got built at all.

2. Company Background

Ekjut Handloom Exchange was founded in Bhubaneswar in 2019 to do for India's handloom and handicraft clusters what Flipkart and Meesho had done for mass retail, but with a difference: every listing carried a verifiable link back to the artisan and, where applicable, to the product's Geographical Indication registration with the GI Registry in Chennai. The company onboarded weaver and craft clusters directly — training them, photographing their work, handling logistics and export paperwork so a weaver in Kotpad never had to deal with a freight forwarder. By September 2026, Ekjut worked with roughly 340 clusters across nine states and around 12,400 active artisans, competing for attention against Okhai, iTokri, Gaatha and Fabindia, and increasingly meeting the same buyers as Aditya Birla's Jaypore and Tata's Taneira at trade fairs run by the Export Promotion Council for Handicrafts. Exhibit 1 shows the scale and mix of the business that week. Ekjut had also begun listing select clusters on ONDC and opened a small export desk for boutique buyers in the Gulf and Europe who wanted authenticated Indian craft rather than anonymous stock.

3. The Situation

Three pressures had converged on the same sprint. First, Diyafa Home Collections, a Dubai-based home-décor retailer that re-exported to partner stores in Germany and the Netherlands, had placed a ₹1.8 crore order for forty SKUs of Sambalpuri ikat sarees and stoles, conditional on digital, verifiable provenance documentation for each piece — not the scanned paper certificates Ekjut had always couriered. The shipment had to leave for Dubai by 10 October for Diyafa's Diwali floor sets. Second, Aishwarya Subramaniam, Ekjut's Singapore-based customer-success lead, had been escalating for six weeks: 470 artisans, concentrated in the Kotpad natural-dye and Bastar dhokra clusters, sat in a manual onboarding queue averaging nineteen days, and would miss the festive buying window if nothing changed before early October. Third, data from Lukas Brandt's design team in Berlin showed listings built with full artisan storytelling — a short video, process photographs, a written craft narrative — converting at 4.1% among European-linked visitors against 2.9% for standard listings, a segment that was 18% of traffic but 26% of revenue given its larger basket size. Each proposal solved a real problem; none solved all three, and the sprint could not fund all three at once.

4. The People

Debasish Nayak

Engineering Lead · Chennai

Runs the four-engineer pod that would build whichever proposal won. Wants one unambiguous priority, and is wary the provenance pipeline's unfinished data model could slip past estimate.

Priyanka Deshmukh

Data Scientist · Toronto

Has spent four months building the GI-provenance pipeline — linking weaver ID, loom register and GI certificate scans into a tamper-evident ledger, 70% complete. Believes Diyafa is the first of many buyers who will soon demand exactly this.

Lukas Brandt

Design Lead · Berlin

Built the storytelling prototype and holds the conversion data. Argues Ekjut's real advantage over Okhai and iTokri is narrative, not paperwork.

Neil Fernandes

Head of Global Partnerships · New Jersey

Closed the Diyafa deal and has three similar Gulf and European prospects watching how it goes. Wants the documentation requirement met in full and on time, whatever else waits.

Aishwarya's view reached the meeting through Gitanjali and Debasish: every week the queue stayed long, she reported, artisans in Kotpad and Bastar sold festive stock to local traders at lower margins instead of waiting for Ekjut.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — Ekjut Handloom Exchange, scale by craft cluster, FY26

Exhibit 1 shows why no proposal was trivial to reject. Kotpad, hit hardest by the backlog, was small in GMV but held a disproportionate share of the 470 waiting artisans; Sambalpuri ikat, behind the Diyafa order, was already the largest export earner.

Exhibit 2 — Comparing the three proposals

Effect of each option against the sprint's twelve developer-weeks

Exhibit 3 — The decision window

Exhibit 3. The 18 September decision had to produce results before both the 10 October cutoff and the close of the onboarding window.

6. The Options

Option A — Fund the full GI-provenance pipeline

Commit ten of twelve developer-weeks to finishing Priyanka's pipeline platform-wide. This gives Diyafa exactly what it asked for and builds infrastructure future Gulf and European buyers will likely require. Its cost: almost nothing else in the sprint gets built, the onboarding backlog runs into the festive season untouched, and Ekjut risks losing an estimated ₹3.1 crore of GMV that Kotpad and Bastar artisans would otherwise have brought onto the platform.

Option B — Fund self-serve onboarding, cover Diyafa manually

Commit nine developer-weeks to the onboarding app, clearing the 470-artisan queue before early October, and serve Diyafa with the existing paper certificates couriered as before. This protects festive-season supply and artisan goodwill, but risks the Diyafa relationship, and the three prospective deals Neil is nursing behind it, if compliance treats paper certificates as inadequate.

Option C — Fund the storytelling feature

Commit eight developer-weeks to Lukas's storytelling templates, lifting conversion among the highest-value visitor segment and giving Diyafa a richer, if not audit-grade, documentation packet. This leaves both the Diyafa compliance question and the onboarding backlog unresolved, trading a near-term revenue lift for two unaddressed risks.

7. Questions for Discussion

  1. What does each stakeholder's position reveal about what they believe Ekjut's business depends on — and where do those beliefs conflict?
  2. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, which cost — the Diyafa order, the onboarding backlog, or the conversion opportunity — is most reversible if left unaddressed this sprint, and which is least?
  3. A great PM is often described as bringing vision, alignment, data, story and clarity to a decision like this. Where has each already been supplied by someone other than Gitanjali, and what is left for her to add?
  4. Is a three-way choice among Options A, B and C the right way to frame this decision, or could the twelve developer-weeks be split differently?

8. A Note for the Learner

The difference between a competent PM and a great one rarely shows in which option gets picked from a list — it shows in whether the PM accepts the list as given. Debasish, Priyanka, Lukas and Neil have each supplied one ingredient of good judgment: sizing, data, story and market urgency. None has stepped back to ask whether the real requirement behind each proposal is as large as its proposal assumes.

Look again at what Diyafa actually asked for: verifiable digital provenance for forty SKUs, not Ekjut's entire catalogue. Priyanka's pipeline was built to serve all 340 clusters eventually, but nothing requires it to launch that way. The defensible path scopes Option A down to what the Diyafa order needs — provenance records for those forty Sambalpuri ikat SKUs, built on the 70%-complete pipeline — which Priyanka estimates at three developer-weeks, not ten. That leaves nine developer-weeks, the full cost of Option B, to clear the onboarding backlog before the festive window closes. Lukas's templates wait for the next sprint, but nothing about them decays by waiting, and the forty Diyafa listings can carry hand-written artisan narratives from the content team at no engineering cost meanwhile.

This path costs Gitanjali something real: she tells Priyanka the platform-wide vision waits, and tells Lukas his data-backed win waits too. That is the clarity a great PM owes people — not the absence of disappointment, but disappointment delivered with a sound reason and a date when the work resumes. Vision here is not "build the most ambitious version of everything"; it is recognising that trust infrastructure and festive supply are not actually in competition once the first is scoped to the deadline in front of it.
