Building Trust with Teams

A near-expert treatment: what a team’s verification actually costs, why one falsified statement takes fourteen clean ones to undo, and when the advice to build trust is wrong.

1. Two decisions, eleven weeks apart

On 4 March 2025, three days before the quarterly roadmap review at Nirvaah Clinical Systems — a Pune company whose hospital information system runs admissions, billing and pharmacy for 140 facilities across nineteen private chains — Faizan Qureshi sent his principal product manager a spreadsheet. It was not a status report. The engineering manager and two colleagues had spent an evening reconstructing what they believed Rohini Deshmukh’s prioritisation logic to be, so they could guess which of eleven candidate items would survive the review. They had done this, Faizan wrote, “because we could not predict your call, and we did not want to find out in the room.”

Nothing in Rohini’s record suggested dishonesty. She had missed two dates in a year and flagged both early. What she had done, across eighteen prioritisation decisions that quarter, was justify the same decisions differently depending on the listener: clinical-safety risk in the pod, revenue exposure with the chief executive. The week before, Lalita Bhatt, a staff engineer in Hyderabad, had declined the technical lead role on the pharmacy module, saying she would rather not own something whose scope she could not forecast. Faizan’s reading, offered reluctantly, was that Lalita had concluded the scope depended on which conversation happened last.

Eleven weeks later, on 19 May, Harshad Vaz met a version of the same problem at Tasveer Vision Cloud, a Bengaluru and Coimbatore company whose edge cameras and on-premise inference boxes detect surface defects on auto-component lines across 23 plants. Release v4.2 lifted mean precision from 0.91 to 0.94 and dropped recall on one customer’s poorly lit night-shift line from 0.88 to 0.71. That customer’s quality head wanted an accuracy figure in the renewal. Harshad’s field lead in Coimbatore, Bhaskar Nayak, had begun re-testing every release himself — eleven person-days each — because the notes described the average and his plants lived in the tail. Harshad could not honestly promise a number, and the question was what he could promise instead.

2. A precise definition, and four schools that will not merge

Trust, operationally, is a counterpart’s willingness to reduce their own verification of a product manager’s claims and commitments, and to expose their work to that manager’s judgement before the evidence arrives. Its measurable trace is not sentiment but reliance: the share of the manager’s assertions the team acts on without checking. Faizan’s evening spreadsheet and Bhaskar’s eleven person-days are the same object — verification, priced.

The construct arrived from experimental game theory. Morton Deutsch’s 1958 mixed-motive experiments framed trust as a choice under risk rather than a feeling; Dale Zand’s 1972 work tied it to information flow, showing that distrusted managers receive filtered data and then decide badly, which confirms the filtering. The familiar triangle of ability, benevolence and integrity comes from Mayer, Davis and Schoorman in 1995, and its most useful feature is the part usually dropped: they separated trust from trusting behaviour, mediated by perceived risk, so a team can hold a high opinion of a manager and still verify everything because the stakes justify it. McAllister split cognition-based from affect-based trust; Meyerson, Weick and Kramer described “swift trust” in temporary systems; Dirks and Ferrin’s 2002 meta-analysis showed trust in one’s direct leader and in the institution behaving as distinct variables. Edmondson’s psychological-safety work sits one level up: safety is a property of a team, trust of a pair, and the two are routinely conflated.

Four schools disagree about what a manager should therefore do, and the disagreement is substantive rather than terminological.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Calculative (Williamson, agency theory)Reliability is explained by the incentives and monitoring around a manager; trust in commerce is calculated risk renamed.That trust is a personal asset accumulating independently of incentives.
Relational (McAllister, Lewicki)Affect-based trust is a separate factor; teams extend credit beyond the evidence, and that is real, not error.That trust is a running average of kept promises.
Institutional (Zand, Luhmann)Replace the manager and reliance barely moves, provided the operating system is intact.That relationship work is the primary lever.
Signalling (costly signals)Only commitments expensive to keep carry information about future behaviour.That transparency alone builds trust; cheap disclosure is cheap talk.

Rohini’s situation is a live test between them. The calculative school says her incentives rewarded telling each audience what moved it. The institutional school says her criteria were never written down, so the pod had no artefact and built its own. The signalling school says she had never paid a visible price to keep a stated principle, so her principles carried no information. All three are partly right, and their remedies differ enough that she cannot pursue all of them.

3. Mechanics: reliance, the verification tax, asymmetric updating

Expert practitioners instrument reliance rather than sentiment, because the two diverge exactly where it matters. Over six weeks Rohini’s pod logged 64 substantive assertions from her — dates, scope boundaries, claims about what a customer had agreed. Forty-one were acted on directly; 23 were checked first, at about 2.4 engineer-hours each: 55.2 hours per six-week window, a standing 0.23 of an engineer devoted to not believing her. At a fully loaded ₹38 lakh per engineer-year over some 1,800 productive hours, the rate is ₹2,111 an hour, so the tax ran ₹1.17 lakh a window, roughly ₹10.1 lakh a year. It was unevenly spread, too — 71 per cent reliance in co-located Pune against 48 in Hyderabad, where Lalita heard decisions second-hand.

The second piece of machinery is the updating rule, where practitioner advice goes quietly wrong. Treat the team as holding a belief about which kind of manager it has: a reliable one, whose checkable statements hold 99 times in 100, or a convenient one, whose hold 80 times in 100 because they drift toward whatever was comfortable to say. Suppose the pod starts generous, at 80 per cent on the reliable type. One statement is then falsified — likelihood 0.01 under reliable, 0.20 under convenient — so the posterior becomes (0.80 × 0.01) ÷ (0.80 × 0.01 + 0.20 × 0.20) = 0.008 ÷ 0.048 = 16.7 per cent. Four-in-five confidence collapses to one-in-six on one observation.

Recovery runs the same ratio in reverse. Each statement that holds multiplies the odds by 0.99 ÷ 0.80 = 1.2375. Post-breach odds are 0.20; restoring 80 per cent needs odds of 4.0, a twentyfold climb, requiring ln(20) ÷ ln(1.2375) = 14.1 clean statements. One falsification costs roughly fourteen kept ones. At four checkable commitments a fortnight that is seven sprints, and no amount of sincerity shortens it.

Two consequences follow. First, a disclosed slip is not a falsification: “the date has moved to the 14th, I found out on Tuesday, here is the cause” is a true statement about a changed world, equally likely under both types, so it barely moves the posterior. The damage sits entirely in statements the team later finds were wrong when spoken. Second, because repair is paced by observation count, the lever is cadence: a manager who manufactures observations — a short written forecast each Friday, checkable by Monday — converts fourteen statements from a year into a quarter.

The third mechanism is criterion stability, measured rather than asserted. Rohini’s eighteen decisions were coded twice, by the reason given inside the pod and the reason given upward. Concordance was 5 of 18, or 28 per cent — a number that explains Faizan’s spreadsheet better than any account of her character. A published ranked criterion list fixes it, at a cost the literature underplays: once the rank is public the team can predict the call, which binds the manager where she would rather have decided otherwise. That binding is the costly signal.

The fourth mechanism is credit routing, which fails structurally rather than morally. Nirvaah’s origination audit asked eleven pod members separately who first proposed each of twelve shipped items; consensus gave five to engineers, three to design, four to Rohini. The executive update named engineers on two and design on one, calling nine the work of “the product team” — attribution accuracy 3 of 12, from a manager who praised people generously in retrospectives. Credit given where it costs nothing does not register; it must travel in the artefact that goes upward. Backlog ideas fell from 6.2 a sprint to 2.1.

One second-order effect cuts against all of this. Verification is not only a tax but an error-detection mechanism: a pod checking 36 per cent of its manager’s assertions catches some of her mistakes, and driving reliance to 95 per cent removes the catches along with the cost. Experts substitute deliberate challenge — a named person arguing the other side — rather than banking the whole saving.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

Trust is worth building in proportion to five conditions, each checkable rather than assumed.

ClaimNirvaah (Rohini)Tasveer (Harshad)
C1. Trust pays where the team must commit before evidence arrives.Holds: cycles run six to nine months and migrations are irreversible.Holds weakly: model behaviour is visible within days.
C2. Trust pays where verification is expensive.Holds: contract terms live in her conversations, not a shared system.Fails: shared eval dashboards make facts cheap.
C3. Trust needs repeated interaction with the same counterparts.Holds: stable pod, four years’ average tenure.Partly: field engineers rotate, so swift trust does the work.
C4. Trust needs discretion enough for a promise to mean something.Holds: she owns scope inside the release train.Holds for process, not for accuracy he cannot control.
C5. Trust must be earned in the dimension relied on.Fails on credit fairness, holds on factual accuracy.Fails on forecasts, holds on technical judgement.

Where the conditions fail, the standard advice becomes actively misleading. A manager with no real decision rights cannot make costly promises, and coaching them to build trust is cruel: the team’s discount is correct, and the fix is authority. Where the defect is a broken operating system, trust work substitutes for the repair. Where distrust accurately reads a bad incentive, restoring reliance makes the organisation worse. And in controlled environments, reduced verification is a compliance failure rather than an achievement.

5. Hard edges: seams where the mechanism inverts

At Tolmol Bazaar Networks, a Nagpur commodity exchange matching farmer producer organisations to food processors, the product manager’s reliance split by side of the market: 79 per cent on the demand-side team, 44 in supply-side operations, with nothing in her conduct differing. Supply read every buyer-favouring call as capture, because on a two-sided platform the internal teams are partial advocates and the manager’s neutrality is itself the contested claim. What works is publishing the exchange rate between the sides — how much seller liquidity a point of buyer conversion is worth — and applying it visibly against whichever side shouted loudest.

At Nigraani Risk Cloud in Mumbai, which supplies limit-monitoring and audit trails to non-banking financial companies, an internal goal to “reduce dual review by 30 per cent as trust improves” was flagged by the firm’s own auditor. Four-eyes review on some 340 limit changes a month is a control, not a verification tax, and credibility cannot substitute for it. A manager’s word buys speed in framing decisions and nothing in executing controlled ones — and saying so is itself a trust-building act.

Hardware changes the arithmetic of reversibility. Tasveer’s camera enclosures go to tooling eleven weeks before a rollout; a specification change after tooling costs about ₹34 lakh and no hotfix undoes it. A manager who reopens a frozen spec destroys trust in a way no software reversal does, because the team’s exposure was irreversible. Mature hardware organisations publish a cost-of-change calendar, so the freeze is arithmetic rather than authority.

The AI-native seam is sharpest. Harshad cannot promise accuracy, because the model is stochastic and the distribution shifts with every new plant. The expert move migrates the promise from outcome to process: not “precision stays above 0.93” but “every model swap ships with a per-plant eval delta inside 24 hours, including when it is worse, and no silent rollbacks.” Multi-product firms meet a milder version at the platform boundary, where a manager’s customers are other managers: what they say is that shared objectives align everyone, and what holds is a few written, dated, cancellable commitments with a social price for defection. Across all of them sits the matrix seam, where the manager reports to a different chain than the engineers, creating two ledgers and an incentive to spend team trust on manager trust.

6. Nine distinctions that separate the expert

Reliance, not sentiment, is the instrument. The tell is a pulse score above four out of five alongside engineers who still re-derive the manager’s numbers before every review. Surveys measure opinion, and opinion diverges from behaviour where risk is high.

Disclosure is a likelihood ratio, not an apology. The tell is disclosure inflation: weekly notes so long nobody replies. More disclosure is not monotonically better, because undifferentiated noise buries the news that matters.

A costless promise carries no signal. The tell is a manager all of whose commitments were going to happen anyway. Experts make fewer, dearer promises, because the information comes from the price paid, not the words.

A breach revises your class, not your tally. The tell is a manager stacking wins after a lapse and finding they do not land. The team is not subtracting a point; it has moved probability onto a different model of who you are.

Criterion stability beats criterion quality. The tell is that engineers can predict your call before the meeting. A predictable but imperfect rule produces more reliance than an optimal unpredictable one, which offends every instinct about deciding well.

Credit counts only in the travelling artefact. The tell is a retrospective that names the engineer and a board deck that does not. Praise in the room is free, and it reads as free.

In hierarchical settings distrust looks like compliance. The tell is a team doing exactly what was asked and nothing more, and starting to ask for instructions in writing. Sudden procedural politeness is the local analogue of open pushback.

Excess reliance is a defect. The tell is reliance above ninety per cent with falling defect-detection in review. Trust monocultures ship confident mistakes; the expert installs a standing challenger.

Repair is bounded by opportunity, not effort. The tell is a manager on a slow cadence who cannot see why a good quarter changed nothing. The lever is creating more checkable statements.

7. What changes across product types and stages

Two things are invariant. Credit routing into the travelling artefact, and stability of stated criteria, work identically in a consumer app and a turbine-monitoring platform; claims otherwise are usually claims about tooling. What varies is the cost of verification and the length of the blind commitment, which together set how much trust is worth.

Consumer teams verify cheaply, so the trust that matters concerns interpretation — whether a manager’s reading of an inconclusive test bends toward the roadmap already chosen. In business software, commitments travel outward to named customers through sales and implementation, so a soft promise costs someone else’s credibility. Enterprise work adds irreversibility, and teams verify more in proportion. Platforms and marketplaces add partiality, as at Tolmol; hardware adds the cost-of-change calendar; AI products move the promise to disclosure cadence.

Stage changes the mechanism, not the principle. In a twelve-person startup reliance is repaired face to face inside a fortnight and written criteria feel bureaucratic, but every promise is personal, so a founder’s reversals are catastrophic. At a few hundred people, most people extending reliance have never watched the manager work, so consistency must be documented to exist at all. At scale a new manager inherits reliance in the seventies on day one — institutional trust, not theirs, and mistaking it for personal capital is the commonest senior error.

8. Three worked cases, one of them a failure

Nirvaah. Rohini published a ranked criterion list — clinical-safety risk above contractual commitment, above revenue exposure, above engineering cost — and scored every decision against it in the open for ten sprints. Concordance moved from 5 of 18 to 16 of 19. Reliance rose from 64 to 86 per cent, cutting the verification tax from ₹10.1 lakh to roughly ₹3.9 lakh a year, and backlog submissions recovered from 2.1 to 5.8 a sprint. The cost was real: the rank bound her twice into outcomes she judged inferior, including deferring a ₹2.4 crore upsell behind a safety fix. That visible price is what made the list credible.

Tasveer. Harshad refused the accuracy clause and committed to a cadence instead: a per-plant eval delta within 24 hours of every model swap, regressions included, no silent rollbacks. Across the six releases before, three of six regressions reached a plant before his own field team knew; across the eight after, all eight were disclosed within 24 hours. Field reliance on release notes rose from 55 to 89 per cent, and Bhaskar’s re-testing fell from eleven person-days a release to three, about ₹10.8 lakh saved across eight releases. The price was paid outside: one customer, reading an honest regression note, paused a twelve-line rollout at four, deferring some ₹1.4 crore by two quarters.

Taleem Learning Networks — where the playbook failed. At this Noida after-school learning company, Ritika Sondhi ran the same programme — published criteria, weekly written commitments, credit audit — and reliance fell, from 58 to 41 per cent. The cause was structural: of eleven published commitments in a quarter, seven were reversed within days by the founder-chief executive, a hold rate of 4 in 11, barely above the discount the team already applied. Publishing commitments that are then overturned does not build a record; it converts diffuse suspicion into documented evidence. The recovery was a rights negotiation. Ritika agreed a written envelope — pricing experiments under ₹5 lakh of exposure, release scope inside a frozen three-week window — and stopped promising outside it, saying so openly. Inside it the hold rate reached 12 of 13 commitments kept, a separate measure from reliance, which recovered to 72 per cent over five months. Shrink the domain of your promises to the domain of your authority.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Audience-tuned rationaleTwo reasons circulating for one callWould three people give the same reason we deprioritised X?Every decision re-litigated
Credit leakageFalling idea submissionsName the originator of the last five ships — does the update agree?Surfaces as slowed invention two or three quarters later
Promise inflationCommitment count rising, hold rate fallingHow many of my commitments would have happened anyway?Your word stops carrying information
Disclosure inflationLong transparency notes, no repliesCan the team say what changed without re-reading?Real bad news arrives buried
Trust monocultureNo challenge in three reviewsWhen did someone last change my mind in public?A confident wrong decision at scale
Borrowed authority“Leadership wants this” closes debateHow many calls were justified by a person, not a reason?Your judgement never earns standing
Promising outside the envelopeCommitments reversed from aboveWhat share of mine was overturned by someone senior?Documented unreliability, as at Taleem
Distance decayRemote sub-pod below the co-located oneWho hears my decisions second-hand?Silent divergence, then an integration surprise

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The calculative position holds that per-manager variation is an artefact of unmeasured differences in incentives, information access and discretion, and that organisations chasing trust should instead share telemetry and fix what gets rewarded. Its evidence is the jump in reliance when a team gains direct access to data a manager used to relay. It would be wrong if two managers inside an identical system showed persistent large gaps — which Nirvaah’s numbers suggest, since Rohini sat at 64 per cent while her peer on the pharmacy module sat at 81 with the same tooling. The reply is that their discretion was never actually identical.

The institutional position holds that the durable object is the operating system — written decisions, visible criteria, shared instrumentation — which survives personnel change, and cites the day-one inheritance of reliance by new managers. It would be wrong if trust travelled with people across systems, reproducing itself within a quarter at a differently run company; that study has not been done. The relational position insists affect-based trust is separable and lets teams ride out bad patches no record would justify, and would be wrong if warmth added nothing once record is controlled. The signalling position insists only costly commitments inform.

The live practitioner disagreement is narrower: should a manager absorb blame publicly for a team’s miss? The sponsorship view says yes, always, because shielding is the reciprocal of credit-sharing. The accuracy view says no — attributing a miss to yourself when it was not yours is itself a false statement, and teaches the team that the record is negotiable. It turns on whether teams read shielding as generosity or as accounts shaped for effect.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves in ways that look faintly odd from outside. They measure reliance instead of running engagement surveys. They make strikingly few promises, and the ones they make are expensive. They publish decision criteria knowing the list will bind them against their own preference, and accept the two bad outcomes a year that proves. They route attribution into documents that leave the room, and treat verbal praise as pleasant but inert. They can say “I do not have the standing to promise that” without embarrassment, and treat inherited reliance as a loan from the institution. They install someone whose job is to disagree.

12. What the protagonists decided

Rohini published the ranked criteria on 14 March and stopped giving the executive team a different reason than she gave the pod — which meant telling her chief executive, in a recorded review, that a ₹2.4 crore upsell was going behind a safety fix. She also declined his request for a date on the pharmacy module, because the sequencing sat with the implementation organisation in Chennai. Her reasoning was that concordance at 28 per cent, not any missed date, had made her unpredictable. Harshad refused the accuracy clause, committed to the 24-hour eval-delta disclosure, and accepted the paused rollout as the price: without the field team he would not learn about the tail cases at all.

Discussion questions. (1) Rohini’s criterion list cost a ₹2.4 crore upsell deferral to buy 22 points of reliance worth about ₹6 lakh a year. On what basis other than the arithmetic would you defend that trade?

(2) Harshad raised internal reliance and deferred ₹1.4 crore of external revenue — right problem, or was the answer a contractual accuracy floor with a remediation clause?

(3) Ritika’s programme made things worse before the envelope made them better. A mistake, or the only way to make the authority deficit negotiable?

13. Going deeper

  1. Influence without authority — reliance is what lets a suggestion function as a decision.
  2. Psychological safety and team health — the team-level construct dyadic trust enables, and the candour the diagnostics depend on.
  3. Coaching and feedback — feedback lands only where the receiver believes the giver acts in their interest.
  4. Partnering with engineering and design leaders — peer trust runs on written cancellable commitments, not warmth.
  5. What makes a great PM — places reliance among the other competences, and shows what it cannot substitute for.
  6. Conflict and disagreement — the standing challenger works only if disagreement is survivable in public.
  7. Negotiation for PMs — the skill that made Ritika’s envelope, and her recovery, possible.
  8. Working in diverse and global teams — why distance decays reliance, as Pune to Hyderabad showed.
  9. Creating clarity and energy — published criteria are a clarity instrument first.
  10. Leading through a crisis — where the repair curve is compressed, and borrowed authority most tempting.

Nishtha Analytics: The Credit Line

A teaching case on building trust with teams · Mumbai, Pune, Bengaluru, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore, New Jersey

On the morning of 14 October 2025, Ishaan Vora stood outside Conference Room 4B at Nishtha Analytics' Lower Parel office, holding a cold cup of filter coffee and a decision he had put off for six days. In six days, on 20 October, two days before Diwali, he would present the shelf-intelligence pod's quarter to Rehan Kapadia, the company's Chief Product Officer, and to the pod itself — engineers in Bengaluru and Pune, a designer in Berlin, a data scientist in Toronto, a customer-success lead in Singapore. Before that Monday, Ishaan had to decide not what to say about the product, but what to say about who had built it.

1. The company

Nishtha Analytics was a nine-year-old Mumbai product company selling demand-forecasting and shelf-intelligence software to organised retail chains — the layer of prediction that told a store planner how many packets of ghee to stock before a festival weekend. Clients included regional arms of Reliance Retail and Spencer's Retail; competitors were Fractal Analytics, Mu Sigma and Tredence. Nishtha's pitch was accuracy that held during Diwali, Onam and the IPL season, when Indian retail lived or died on inventory calls. Revenue had grown to ₹146 crore, of which Ishaan's pod contributed close to ₹41 crore across fourteen accounts.

Ishaan had joined eighteen months earlier and led the pod for five months, taking over from a PM who left for a Bengaluru unicorn. The pod itself was older: Omkar Jadhav, a senior engineer in Pune, had built, largely on his own initiative, the forecasting-correction algorithm that held accuracy during festival spikes — the feature clients cited most in renewal calls.

2. The situation

On 30 September, Ishaan had presented the shelf-intelligence roadmap at Nishtha's leadership offsite in Goa, a slot Rehan had given him as a vote of confidence. The deck's strongest slide showed the festival-accuracy improvement — the algorithm Omkar had built — with a chart, client quotes, and a line reading "built by the shelf-intelligence team." When Rehan asked who had led the work, Ishaan said "the whole team, but especially the Pune engineering group," and moved on. He did not say Omkar's name. He had done something similar twice before that quarter, in a client case study and a Slack update, each time folding individual contribution into "the pod" language he considered humble.

Omkar, watching the recording later, mentioned it in passing to Prateek Nair, the Bengaluru engineer he partnered with, who mentioned it to Lukas Weber, the Berlin designer. By the time Ishaan heard of it, from HR, who had seen it surface in the pod's anonymous pulse survey, the story was no longer about one slide. It had become "Ishaan takes the story upward and leaves the specifics behind," and three earlier incidents were now cited: a headcount promise to Daniel Cho, the Toronto data scientist, that had quietly slipped two months; a promise to Mei-Lin Tan, the Singapore customer-success lead, to loop her into an escalation call Ishaan took alone; and a roadmap date given to Marcus Feldman, the New Jersey sales head, for a feature that shipped six weeks late unflagged.

Individually, Ishaan could explain each one — a scheduling clash, a call that ran long, a freeze he had not caused. Together, read by a team spread across five time zones who mostly saw him through Slack and quarterly calls, they read as a pattern: politeness, but inconsistent follow-through, and credit running toward Mumbai and Goa rather than Pune. The trust index in Exhibit 1 had fallen for the second straight quarter, furthest among members outside Mumbai — least able to correct a record they had not been in the room for.

Exhibit 1 — Pod pulse-survey trust index, by location (0–100 scale, anonymous, quarterly)
Location & roleQ1 FY26Q2 FY26Change
Mumbai – PM & adjacent roles7874−4

Source: Nishtha Analytics internal pulse tool, anonymised by location; Q2 survey closed 8 October 2025, six days before the case opens.

The drop was steepest where credit had been missed and commitments had slipped, shallowest in Mumbai, where people watched Ishaan up close. Exhibit 2 lays the four incidents against the calendar; together they show not one lapse but a rhythm of small, unrepaired breaks.

Exhibit 2 — Timeline of the four incidents cited in the pod's pulse-survey comments, July–October 2025.

3. The people

Omkar Jadhav — Senior Software Engineer, Pune. Built the festival-accuracy algorithm largely unsupervised; wants his name attached where it was left off, not just acknowledged privately.
Rehan Kapadia — Chief Product Officer, Mumbai. Sponsored Ishaan's Goa slot personally; wants the review to show a pod executing cleanly, and does not yet know how far the survey numbers have fallen.
Mei-Lin Tan — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Manages the Reliance Retail and Spencer's relationships; wants to be looped into client-facing moves before they happen, not after.
Daniel Cho — Data Scientist, Toronto. Was promised a second data scientist in April; wants either the hire or an honest, early word that it isn't coming.

Each was watching for something different: Rehan for the numbers to hold, Omkar for a specific correction, not a general "great job, everyone," and Mei-Lin and Daniel, further from Ishaan's day-to-day, for whether the next promise would be kept — the pattern mattering more to them than any apology.

4. Options before the review

Option A — Correct the record publicly, at the review

Ishaan opens by naming Omkar's algorithm explicitly, in front of Rehan and the full pod, and states plainly that the Goa slide should have said so. Upside: it repairs the exact wound the survey shows, quickly and visibly. Cost: it draws Rehan's attention to a mistake he had not noticed, and without anything structural to follow, the team may read it as a gesture made because Ishaan was caught, not because he changed.

Option B — Repair privately, one relationship at a time

Ishaan calls Omkar, then Mei-Lin, then Daniel, individually over the following week, and quietly redirects future credit and communication. Upside: lower risk with Rehan, tailored to each person. Cost: a deficit created partly by peer-to-peer comments is unlikely to be repaired only by conversations no one else can see, and the review passes with the pod's shared story unchanged.

Option C — Build a standing contribution-and-commitment ledger

Ishaan proposes, at the review, a shared log — who owns what, promised by when, credited by name at each release note and case study, visible to the pod and Rehan. Upside: it addresses the pattern, not just the incident, and lets distant members verify follow-through without depending on Ishaan's goodwill. Cost: it takes a quarter to show results, can feel like process dodging an apology, and does nothing for Omkar's feelings on 20 October itself.

Exhibit 3 — What the pod's engagement is worth to hold

Exhibit 3 made the choice feel urgent, not merely awkward: fourteen crore rupees of at-risk revenue sat behind a twenty-one lakh replacement cost and a four-month knowledge gap — figures showing the pod's trust in Ishaan was a fairly direct input into the business, not a soft concern beside it.

5. Questions for discussion

  1. What, specifically, broke the pod's trust — the missed credit in Goa, the pattern of four incidents, or the distance between Mumbai and the rest of the team?
  2. Exhibit 1 shows the steepest decline in Pune, Toronto and Bengaluru, not Mumbai. Why might distance from a PM make consistency and credit-sharing matter more, not less?
  3. Weigh Options A, B and C. Which repairs the wound fastest, and which holds up over the next two quarters? Can more than one be done together, and in what order?
  4. What should Ishaan tell Rehan about the survey numbers, and does that disclosure choice itself say something about the trust question at the heart of this case?

6. A note for the learner

This case is built to make one idea concrete: teams do not trust PMs for vision or charisma; they trust PMs who are consistent, who share credit accurately, and who follow through — or who say clearly, early, when they cannot. Influence without authority, the topic this one builds on, only works once that trust exists; a PM who has not earned it can get compliance through a manager's authority, but not the discretionary effort a distributed pod gives willingly. The four incidents in Exhibit 2 are not separate mistakes to weigh individually — they are one pattern, which is what Exhibit 1's survey is actually measuring.

A well-reasoned answer notices Options A, B and C are not mutually exclusive, but that order matters. Private repair alone (Option B) is too slow and invisible for a harm that happened in a public room, and leaves Toronto and Singapore untouched. A structural fix alone (Option C), without the specific correction, risks reading as bureaucracy dodging an apology, especially to Omkar, who wants his name said aloud, not filed into a system.

The defensible path sequences them: open the review with the named correction — Option A, brief, aimed at Omkar, witnessed by Rehan and the pod together — then propose the Option C ledger in the same session, framed as the mechanism that makes the next four quarters different, not as apology. Option B's one-on-ones follow the next week, as proof the public words were not only for Rehan's benefit. This is defensible, not merely comfortable, because it treats trust as Exhibit 1 does — rebuilt by particular, verifiable acts over time, not one sentence.

People, Leadership & Organisation · Leadership & Team

Dastak Lending Cloud: The Pune Earn-Out

A teaching case · Hyderabad, Pune, Bengaluru, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore, New Jersey, Dubai

1. The night before

At half past eleven on the night of Sunday, 1 March 2026, Meghana Pai was still at the dining table of her flat in Kondapur, Hyderabad, two laptops open and the board pre-read unfinished. The windows were shut against the smell of the first Holi bonfires stacked in the lane; the festival fell on Wednesday, and half of Dastak Lending Cloud would be away from Tuesday evening.

On her left screen was a slide she had rewritten four times, titled Collections: one platform, one roadmap. It committed the company to retiring the Dhaarna collections product — the product twenty-two engineers in Pune had built, been acquired for, and were still being paid an earn-out against — into Dastak's unified platform by the end of June. On her right screen sat an unanswered 9:14 p.m. message from Devansh Chitale, VP of Engineering in Pune: “Before you send that deck. Do you remember what Anuj said to my team in the Baner office in October 2022? Because they do. Word for word.”

The board call was at eleven on Monday. Meghana, thirty-four, promoted nine months earlier to own the collections line, had to decide what to put in front of six directors and then what to say to ninety people in seven cities who would read the decision in the release notes whether or not she explained it. She had spent those nine months believing her problem was a roadmap problem.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Dastak Lending Cloud was founded in Hyderabad in 2016 by Anuj Sarin and two colleagues from a core-banking practice. Its first product was a loan-origination system for non-banking financial companies — the software that takes a borrower from a form on a phone to a disbursed two-wheeler loan. By 2026 it served eighty-one lenders and booked ₹238 crore of recurring revenue.

Collections — the part that runs when a borrower misses the fourth EMI — Dastak did not build. In September 2022 it bought it. Dhaarna Collections Systems, a twenty-six-person Pune company with a field-agent app and a dialler engine that mid-sized NBFCs liked because it worked on cheap Android handsets in patchy networks, was acquired for ₹64 crore: ₹31 crore upfront and ₹33 crore as an earn-out in three annual tranches, each tied to collections-module ARR crossing a threshold. The third and largest, ₹16 crore, fell due on 30 June 2026.

Two things were said in the Baner office the day the deal closed, by Anuj himself. First, that the earn-out was structured so that “the people who built it keep the upside.” Second — the one Devansh's message meant — that the Dhaarna name would stay on the product and release notes would keep carrying the names of the engineers who shipped each module, a practice kept since Dhaarna's first customer. Neither promise was in the share purchase agreement; both were made before the whole team and repeated at two later all-hands.

Dastak's own culture had no such practice. Release notes credited pods; case studies credited “the Dastak team”; two patents filed in 2024 listed the Hyderabad architecture group and the CTO. Nobody had decided this; it was how a company grown out of services wrote things down.

3. The industry

Indian lending software in 2026 was being reshaped from two directions. From above, the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework and the expanding Unified Lending Interface pilots had turned compliance from a differentiator into a floor: every lender's board now asked its vendor for audit trails, data-localisation attestations and consent artefacts under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. From below, the Account Aggregator rails and UPI Autopay had changed what collections meant — a mandate debited automatically is a different product from a field agent knocking on a door in Nagpur.

The competitive set reflected the churn. Lentra and Perfios had pushed into origination; Yubi had built a different market shape; Signzy and others owned pieces of onboarding. Indian SaaS at large — Zoho, Freshworks, Postman — had made it normal for a Hyderabad team to sell to New Jersey and Dubai without an American parent. Lenders were consolidating vendors: three platforms, not eleven.

That consolidation was the argument for retiring Dhaarna: Dastak could not credibly sell “one platform” while shipping two codebases, two data models, two audit-log formats and two consent implementations. The argument had a number attached. Durrah Financial Services LLC, a Dubai consumer lender expanding into two further Gulf markets, had signed a letter of intent in January 2026 for a ₹27 crore three-year contract, conditional on one unified audit trail certified against Indian and DFSA-facing requirements by 31 July 2026. Gregory Marsden in New Jersey had built the pipeline; Wei Ling Chua in Singapore would run it.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Meghana took the collections line in June 2025 and inherited an organisation that looked, from Hyderabad, healthy: Pune shipped predictably, attrition was in line with the company, and the pulse survey put Pune's “I trust the leadership of my product area” at 71.

Her first act was a listening tour: twenty-six one-to-one calls across six cities in five weeks, at hours that suited everyone but her. She logged every commitment into a shared sheet she called the ledger — owner, promise, date, status — and closed 82 per cent on time. This, she believed, was what would make a distributed team trust a leader they saw only on video.

In August 2025 the unification proposal surfaced. In September, Meghana asked Devansh what it would cost to port Dhaarna's dialler engine into the platform, framing the question as hypothetical. He returned fourteen engineer-months and asked, in the same message, whether the earn-out threshold would be recomputed if the module stopped being a separately reported revenue line. Meghana replied that no decision had been taken. This was true, and it was the first of several moments in which a true statement functioned as an evasion.

In October 2025 the release-note template was changed in Hyderabad as part of a tooling migration. It dropped per-module contributor names. Nobody consulted Pune; nobody in Hyderabad knew the field was load-bearing. Kavya Ramanathan, a staff engineer in Bengaluru, flagged it in a channel Meghana was in. Meghana read the message, thought we should fix that, and did not put it in the ledger, because it was not a promise she had made.

In November, marketing published a case study on a gold-loan NBFC's recovery-rate improvement — largely produced by the Dhaarna app's offline queueing — and credited “Dastak's collections platform.” In December two Dhaarna-origin engineers left; both exit interviews recorded “career growth.”

In January 2026 the Durrah letter of intent arrived and the timeline hardened. That month the Q4 pulse survey went out and Pune scored 74 — up three points, a number Meghana cited in her business review as evidence the transition was going well. Three weeks later the people team sent her a report she had not asked for: internal-transfer requests out of the Pune group had gone from one in twelve months to seven in a quarter, six from Dhaarna-origin engineers. The survey closed on 16 January. The retention bonus for the second earn-out tranche was paid on 9 January.

Figure A — The sequence as Meghana reconstructed it on 28 February 2026, working backwards from the transfer-request report.

5. The people

Anuj Sarin — Co-founder and CEO, Hyderabad. Made both Baner promises; remembers one. Position: unify before the Durrah window closes; “branding is not a promise, people are.” Incentive: a Series D conversation that needs a clean single-platform story. Not saying: his recollection of October 2022 is thinner than Pune's, and he has not rewatched the recording.
Devansh Chitale — VP Engineering, Pune; formerly Dhaarna's co-founder. Position: the port is sound, the sequencing wrong, and the third tranche must be protected. Incentive: his own tranche is the largest single payment, and twenty-two people read his face before any deck. Not saying: two of his strongest engineers have told him they will leave if the name goes; passing that on would look like a threat.
Kavya Ramanathan — Staff engineer, Bengaluru. Position: two codebases are a compliance liability, said in writing three times. Incentive: she is up for a principal role scoped to the unified platform. Not saying: she flagged the release-note change in October, nothing happened, and she has quietly stopped raising process issues.
Ingrid Halvorsen — Design lead, Berlin. Position: the app's offline patterns are the best design work in the company and should survive as a named system, not be absorbed. Incentive: her design-system charter is her promotion case. Not saying: she speaks to the Pune designers weekly and has a better picture of morale than anyone in Hyderabad, unasked for and so unoffered.
Rohan Chatterjee — Senior data scientist, Toronto. Position: the November uplift splits roughly 60/40 between Dhaarna's queueing and Dastak's propensity model, but the interval is wide. Incentive: his team's budget rests on the model's contribution. Not saying: the split came from one back-test on eleven months of a single client's data, and he thinks it too fragile to cite.
Wei Ling Chua — Customer success lead, Singapore. Position: Durrah's procurement will not accept a dual-codebase answer, and it is her largest account. Incentive: her variable pay is tied to the go-live. Not saying: their technical lead told her informally that a documented plan, not a finished migration, would likely satisfy the July gate — repeating it would cost her the urgency that buys engineering attention.
Gregory Marsden — Head of Sales, New Jersey. Position: one platform, one price book, by June. Incentive: Durrah is a third of his quota. Not saying: he has already described Dastak to two further Gulf prospects as single-platform.
Sneha Iyengar — Director, People Operations, Hyderabad. Position: the pulse data does not support a trust crisis, and she distrusts a narrative built on seven transfer requests. Incentive: engagement scores are hers to report to the board. Not saying: she knows the January survey closed a week after the retention-bonus payout, and did not flag it.

6. Exhibits

Meghana assembled five exhibits in the last week of February. Two of them, side by side, describe different companies.

Exhibit 1 — Quarterly pulse survey: “I trust the leadership of my product area” (0–100)

Exhibit 1 says Pune's trust in its leadership rose. Exhibit 2 says a third of the group has asked to be elsewhere, almost all of it since the release notes changed. Sneha Iyengar reads the first as data and the second as noise; Devansh reads it the other way.

Exhibit 3 — Meghana's commitment ledger, June 2025 – February 2026

Exhibit 5 held the sentence that kept Meghana at the table. If the module stops being reported separately before 30 June, nobody can say how the tranche is computed — and the people whose money it is are not being asked.

7. Voices

Devansh Chitale, direct message, 9:14 p.m., 1 MarchNobody here will fight you on the architecture. Kavya is right about the audit trail and everyone knows it. What they will not forgive is finding out from a release note. Twice.
Kavya Ramanathan, #eng-platform, 14 October 2025Heads up — the new release-note template drops the contributors field. Intentional? Pune uses it. (No replies.)
Anuj Sarin, leadership call, 19 February 2026I am not running two products so a brand name survives. If somebody feels the name was a promise, talk to them about what we can actually give. Scope, title, money. Not a logo.
Ingrid Halvorsen, design review, 23 February 2026Three of the Pune designers have asked me, separately, whether the offline flows will keep their names on them. None of them has asked Meghana. Not because they trust her less — because they think she can't change it.
Gregory Marsden, email, 25 February 2026I need a date I can put in writing. I have told Durrah and two others that we are one platform. If that is not true in July, that is not a roadmap issue. That is me having misrepresented us.
Wei Ling Chua, call notes, 26 February 2026Their head of technology asked for the migration plan, the certification scope and the rollback path. He did not ask for the migration to be finished.
Anonymous free text, Q4 pulse survey, January 2026Nothing promised to us was broken. Things were just not said. That is different, and somehow worse.

8. The options as Meghana currently sees them

Option A — Commit on Monday, and buy the relationship back. Announce the June retirement to the board and the company in the same week, pair it with an earn-out floor negotiated with the CFO, restore the contributor field, and give the Pune leads named ownership of the migrated components. Fast, honest about direction, and it answers Gregory and Wei Ling. It also confirms, to twenty-two people, what a promise is worth when it is not in the agreement.
Option B — Sequence the port after 30 June. Keep both codebases until the earn-out is assessed, ship a documented migration plan for the July gate, and start on 1 July. Protects ₹9.4 crore of other people's money, and a promise. Costs four months of double maintenance, leaves Kavya's objection unanswered, and asks Gregory to walk something back with a client he has already told.
Option C — Give Pune the decision. Put the constraints in front of Devansh's group — the gate, the earn-out ambiguity, the compliance exposure — and ask them to choose the sequencing, backing their choice at the board. Highest chance of real buy-in; also a delegation she may not be able to honour if the board overrules it, which would be the third and largest break.
Option D — Escalate the promise itself. Ask Anuj to stand up in Pune, before Holi, and address the 2022 commitments: what he said, what has changed, what he will do instead. Meghana handles the roadmap; the founder handles the word he gave. It also means telling the CEO he has a debt he does not fully remember incurring, a day before a board meeting, and leaves open whether a repaired founder promise does anything for a team whose daily experience is of Meghana.

Every option is framed as a choice about roadmap and money. Writing them out, Meghana noticed that not one is a choice about whether Pune hears anything before the board does — and that in the three incidents that did the damage, the template change, the case study and the unanswered earn-out question, no promise was broken at all.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board call is at eleven on Monday, 2 March. Holi falls on Wednesday; Pune and Hyderabad thin out from Tuesday evening and return Friday, removing three working days from any communication plan. The Durrah gate is 31 July, with the audit scope due by 30 April. The earn-out is assessed on 30 June against a threshold counsel calls ambiguous. The port is fourteen engineer-months against a Pune group of twenty-two from which four senior people are plausibly leaving, and Exhibit 5 does not price the months of context that go with them.

Meghana can commit ₹18 lakh without sign-off. She cannot change the earn-out terms, the release-note tooling roadmap, or Gregory's pipeline commitments. She can change what she says, when, and to whom first — and the order in which ninety people in seven cities learn what she has decided.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, has been damaged at Dastak? Distinguish the 2022 promises, the autumn omissions, and the pattern of true-but-evasive answers. Which would a Pune engineer name first, and which Meghana?
  2. Exhibits 1 and 2 cannot both be a fair picture of Pune. Reconstruct how each was produced, and say what you would need before citing either to a board.
  3. Exhibit 3 shows an 82 per cent on-time record on logged commitments; Exhibit 4 shows no Pune engineer named in a case study, talk or patent since 2024. What does it mean to be reliable on the ledger you keep and unreliable on the one your team keeps?
  4. Devansh, Wei Ling, Rohan and Sneha each withhold something material. Is that a trust problem between Meghana and her team, one inside the leadership group, or both — and does it change what she should do?
  5. Options A to D all treat this as a decision about sequencing and money. Propose a fifth framing the evidence supports better, and price it.
  6. It is 7 a.m. on Monday, 2 March. What does Meghana do before the eleven o'clock call, what does she say to the board, and what does she say to Pune afterwards — in what order, and why?

At ten past midnight Meghana closed the deck without saving the last change and opened the recording of the October 2022 all-hands, which someone in Pune had kept. Anuj was thirty seconds from the end, in a half-empty Baner room, and the audio was poor. She could hear him say the word “names.” She could not hear what came after it, and the person holding the camera had turned towards the door.

Building Trust with Teams

Why do teams trust some product managers and not others — and what, exactly, does a PM do differently to earn it?

1. A ledger with no name on it

On the morning of 11 February 2025, Meera Iyer, Group Product Manager at Waapsi Logistics Cloud, a Bengaluru-based reverse-logistics platform helping D2C brands manage product returns, walked into the weekly engineering sync and noticed something she hadn't seen in eight months: nobody had an update ready for her. Not because there was nothing to report — the returns-triage service the team had committed to shipping by 31 January was three weeks late — but because, as engineering lead Arvind Pillai told her over coffee afterward, "nobody wanted to be the one who told you first." Waapsi served 340 D2C sellers, processing roughly 46,000 returns a month, and the service was meant to cut manual sorting time by 60%. It was still in staging.

Over the previous two sprints, Meera had told the seven-person pod the feature was "basically done" in three stakeholder updates, each based on the most optimistic status she'd heard in standup rather than what she'd verified herself. When a pipeline bug pushed the date out again, she absorbed the blame publicly — good sponsorship, on its face. But inside the team, two engineers had begun routing around her, raising blockers straight to the VP of Engineering and telling her in standup only what couldn't be checked. Arvind put it plainly: "We don't think you're dishonest. We think you tell people what you wish were true, and then we have to clean it up." Meera had four months before Waapsi's board review, a roadmap riding on this pod's goodwill, and a growing sense that the real problem wasn't the missed date. It was that her word had stopped being reliable.

2. What trust actually is

Trust, in the sense a PM needs it, is a team's willingness to act on the PM's word without first verifying it — to ship on the strength of "we've agreed on the plan," to raise a hard truth early rather than manage around it, and to give the benefit of the doubt when something is ambiguous. It is not affection and not authority. A PM can be well liked and still not trusted with bad news; a PM can hold a title and still be quietly bypassed, as Arvind's team was doing to Meera.

The most durable account of what trust is built from comes from Roger Mayer, James Davis and F. David Schoorman, who in a 1995 paper in the Academy of Management Review proposed that willingness to be vulnerable to another party rests on three judgments: ability (is this person competent here?), benevolence (do they want good things for me, not just themselves?), and integrity (do their words match their actions?). A PM can score high on ability and still be distrusted if the team doubts benevolence or integrity — exactly Meera's problem: nobody doubted her competence, but her habit of repeating the rosiest version of events had damaged the integrity leg.

The sentence Meera needed — one she could say without sounding glib — is this: my team trusts me to the exact extent that what I tell them turns out to be true, what I promise turns out to happen, and credit lands on whoever earned it. Trust is not a feeling she needs to inspire. It is a track record her team is silently keeping, whether she asks them to or not.

3. The mechanics: three behaviours, repeated in view

Working knowledge of trust-building comes down to three disciplines the learning objective names directly: consistency, credit-sharing, and follow-through. None is a personality trait; all three are behaviours a PM chooses, sprint over sprint, in view of the people whose cooperation depends on them.

Consistency means stated priorities and the criteria used for trade-off calls stay stable across contexts — the same in a one-on-one as in a leadership review. What practitioners leave implicit is that consistency is judged against the PM's own past statements: if Meera says "quality gates aren't negotiable" in January and waives one under deadline pressure in February without explaining why, the team doesn't file that as a reasonable trade-off. They file it as evidence her principles are decorative.

Credit-sharing means that when the triage service ships, the engineer who found the root cause is named — to the VP, in the update, in the retro — before Meera describes her own role. The implicit step is timing: credit given only after someone else points out their own contribution reads as begrudging, not generous. It has to be volunteered first, or it doesn't register as benevolence at all.

Follow-through means commitments, even small ones like "I'll find out by Thursday whether legal has signed off," are closed out explicitly, even when the answer is "still waiting." What practitioners forget to name is that a disclosed miss and a silent miss are not the same event to a team, even when the underlying failure is identical. Saying "I told the board it was basically done, that was wrong, here's what happened" withdraws from the ability account but deposits into the integrity account. Letting the team discover the gap on its own withdraws from both.

4. A worked ledger: two quarters at Waapsi

Trust is easiest to see as a running ledger. Below is Meera's record across six sprints in Q4, alongside the pod's fortnightly pulse score on "I trust Meera's updates," rated 1–5.

SprintCommitments madeDelivered on timeMisses disclosed earlyMisses discovered by teamPulse score (1–5)
Sprint 1954104.1
Sprint 2065104.0
Sprint 2153023.1
Sprint 2264022.6
Sprint 2354103.0
Sprint 2465103.6

A simple index makes the pattern legible: Trust Index = 0.4 × (delivered ÷ committed) + 0.6 × (misses disclosed early ÷ total misses), weighting disclosure higher because integrity was the leg that failed. In Sprint 19, delivery was 4/5 = 0.80 and disclosure 1/1 = 1.00: 0.4(0.80) + 0.6(1.00) = 0.92. By Sprint 21, delivery had dropped only slightly, to 3/5 = 0.60, but both misses that sprint were discovered by the team, not disclosed, so disclosure was 0/2 = 0.00: 0.4(0.60) + 0.6(0.00) = 0.24. The pulse score tracked the index, not the delivery rate.

Run the second pass: hold delivery constant at 0.60, but change the one input Meera controlled — whether she disclosed the slip before the team found it. If both misses had been disclosed early, the index becomes 0.4(0.60) + 0.6(1.00) = 0.84, nearly back to Sprint 19's level on identical delivery. A 20-point drop in what she delivered cost far less trust than a 100-point drop in what she disclosed. Teams forgive missed dates; they do not forgive finding out about them last.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Trust is not likability

A PM can run warm, well-attended one-on-ones and still be the person engineers route around on hard calls, because likability answers "do I enjoy this person" while trust answers "can I be vulnerable to this person's decisions." Meera was well liked throughout the slip. She was not, for those eight weeks, trusted.

Trust is directional, not a single number

Different stakeholders extend different kinds of trust: engineers trust a PM's technical judgment, sales trusts (or doesn't) the delivery dates, design trusts (or doesn't) that its rationale survives a trade-off. A PM can be strong on one axis and nearly bankrupt on another, and treating trust as one score misses where repair is actually needed.

Swift trust is not deep trust

Cross-functional squads on a short project often extend "swift trust" — a provisional, role-based assumption of competence letting people move before anyone has a track record. It is real but thin: it evaporates at the first unexplained miss, unlike deep trust, which survives a bad sprint.

The ledger is asymmetric

One undisclosed miss typically costs more than several kept commitments earn back, because a single breach forces the team to re-audit everything the PM has said. Rebuilding trust is rarely a grand gesture; it is a long run of small, disclosed commitments.

What trust cannot tell you

A highly trusted PM can still make the wrong call. Trust governs whether the team acts on a decision without re-litigating it, not whether the decision was correct. Trusted PMs occasionally walk a team confidently into a bad roadmap precisely because nobody felt the need to push back.

Hierarchy changes how distrust is signalled

In flatter teams, distrust surfaces as direct pushback. In many Indian corporate settings it more often surfaces as quiet non-escalation — exactly what Arvind's team did, routing around Meera rather than confronting her. A PM watching only for verbal pushback will miss the signal.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and startup versus scale

In a consumer team, trust rests on data discipline: does the PM's read of an A/B test match what happened, or do they favour the interpretation that supports the roadmap they already wanted? In a B2B team, trust extends to sales and support, who must believe the PM's commitments to a named client will hold, since their own credibility rides on it. In a marketplace team, trust is two-sided: a decision that helps sellers can cost buyers, and credibility depends on being seen to weigh both honestly rather than defaulting to whichever side shouts louder that week.

Stage changes the mechanics more than the principle. In an early-stage team of eight, trust is built and repaired face to face within days. At a larger company, it is mediated by artifacts the PM doesn't fully control — a slide forwarded three levels up without context, a thread read by someone who never met the PM. At scale, consistency has to be documented, not just felt, because most people extending trust have never seen the PM operate directly.

7. Common mistakes

Over-promising to seem helpful. Symptom: a PM who says yes to nearly every ask, then quietly triages later. Misunderstanding: an enthusiastic yes builds goodwill, when it just delays the moment the team learns the yes was unreliable. Diagnostic: last quarter's delivered-to-committed ratio; under 70% with no early disclosure is the tell.

Hoarding credit in upward updates. Symptom: engineers who stop volunteering ideas in front of leadership. Misunderstanding: treating visibility as a zero-sum resource to protect. Diagnostic: ask two engineers, separately, who proposed the last three shipped features, and compare answers with what leadership was told.

Recovering from misses silently. Symptom, as at Waapsi: a team consistently surprised by slips it should have seen coming. Misunderstanding: quietly fixing a problem looks more competent than flagging it early. Diagnostic: in the last five misses, did the PM surface the problem first, or did someone else?

Mistaking endless alignment for trust-building. Symptom: a PM who pre-sells every decision in a round of one-on-ones before the room ever sees it. Misunderstanding: treating consensus as a proxy for trust, when a team that trusts the PM's judgment doesn't need pre-selling — only to be informed and given room to object.

8. What good looks like

Six months later, Waapsi's next major feature — automated refund routing — hit the same kind of pipeline snag the triage service had. This time Meera flagged it the day she learned of it: "The refund-matching logic breaks on split shipments, I found this Tuesday, new date is the 14th." She named the engineer who'd caught the edge case in the same message, before the VP asked. Arvind's team didn't route around her that quarter; the pulse score held at 4.3 through the slip. The engineering difficulty was no smaller; only the discipline with which the truth reached the team had changed.

9. What Meera decided, and what to read next

Meera's decision, once Arvind named the problem plainly, was not a rousing speech. She rebuilt a visible ledger: a shared document where every commitment carried a date, and every miss was logged by her, in writing, before anyone else raised it. Six sprints of disclosed misses outweighed eight months of optimistic updates, because the team was never grading her on whether she was ever wrong — only on whether she said so first.

This topic is what makes the next two useful rather than performative: psychological safety depends on trust already existing in the room, and coaching or feedback lands only when the receiver believes the feedback-giver acts in their interest, not just their own. Building either on a trust deficit is building on sand.

Two questions to sit with: If your team kept the ledger from Section 4 on you this quarter, what would the Trust Index show? And think of the last commitment you missed — did your team learn about it from you, or from someone else?

Resilience and Handling Failure

Surviving a failure and rebuilding the trust it consumed are two different problems, with different arithmetic — and the second has schools of thought that contradict each other.

1. Two decisions, eleven days apart

On 4 June 2026, in Baner, Pune, Devika Kulkarni was looking at a number that had grown sixfold in three weeks. Devika was Director of Product at Chaupaal Commerce Network, a platform connecting 62,000 monthly-transacting kirana retailers in small-town India to FMCG distributors — Udaan and ElasticRun territory. Four months earlier her team had launched Bharosa Stock, under which Chaupaal guaranteed to buy back unsold inventory on a curated list of slow-moving SKUs.

It worked: 11,400 retailers enrolled and private-label attachment climbed. It also worked in a way nobody had modelled. The rules let a retailer enrol a SKU after ordering it, so the programme selected for exactly the stock that had already failed to sell. Suhas Bhatt, who ran category management from Indore, flagged the pattern in April. By 4 June the controller in Kochi, Kavita Menon, had a figure: ₹34.2 crore of accrued liability against a ₹6 crore budget.

Nothing was broken. Devika had designed a promise the company could not afford to keep, and had eleven days before the quarterly review. Honour it and the year's contribution margin disappeared. Withdraw it and she became the person who taught 11,400 shopkeepers that Chaupaal's word had a ceiling.

Eleven days later, Vikram Sundaram faced the opposite kind of failure. Vikram was VP Product at Laalten Energy Systems, a Coimbatore maker of commercial solar inverters sold through some 140 rooftop installers. On 15 June, firmware 4.2.0 went over the air to 22,400 units with a corrected coefficient for battery state-of-charge estimation. On about 2,100 — those paired with one particular battery-management module — it pushed the estimate below a protective threshold and the inverters shut down.

Aditi Pandit, the firmware lead in Ahmedabad, had a rollback in four hours. It reached 1,760 units. The other 340 had lost their cellular radio mid-downgrade and needed a person with a laptop in front of them, at ₹4,200 a visit by the reckoning of Joel Mathai, who ran service from Kochi. Sneha Barman, quality head in Kolkata, noted that eighteen installers carried 61% of the forward order book.

2. The idea: three literatures that disagree

Define the term precisely, because the everyday meaning causes most bad practice. Colloquially, resilience is a property of a person: toughness. In the technical literature product organisations have quietly inherited, it is a property of a system — its capacity to detect a disturbance, adapt while it is still unfolding, and restore the confidence of dependent parties faster than the disturbance erodes it. Erik Hollnagel and David Woods (2006) called stretching at the edge of designed competence, rather than snapping at it, graceful extensibility.

Organisational learning arrives by another door. Chris Argyris separated single-loop learning, fixing the error, from double-loop learning, which questions the goal that made the error possible. Amy Edmondson's 1999 work on psychological safety produced the finding that made the field usable: teams reporting more errors were often the better teams, because reporting is a behaviour, not a defect count. Her 2011 taxonomy — preventable, complexity-related, intelligent — forces a classification step.

A third literature, trust repair, is the one practitioners never read and most need. Peter Kim, Donald Ferrin, Cecily Cooper and Kurt Dirks showed experimentally (2004, 2006) that the right response depends on violation type. For a competence violation — we tried and got it wrong — apology repairs better than denial. For an integrity violation — we knew and did it anyway — apology is worse, because it confirms the attribution. Maximal transparency is therefore a strategy with a boundary, not a law.

Table 1 — Five positions, and the sentence each would and would not sign.
SchoolWould signWould not sign
Resilience engineering
Hollnagel, Woods, Dekker		"The system produced this and will again.""Some failures need a named individual held accountable first."
Organisational learning
Argyris, Edmondson		"Classify failures first; few are intelligent failures.""All failure is blameless." Blame is reserved for deviance.
Trust repair
Kim, Dirks, Ferrin		"The wrong apology destroys more trust than silence.""Disclosure dominates whatever it implies about motive."
