Reflective Practice

What did I believe, what changed, and why? — and the harder question underneath it: is the procedure that produced the belief any good?

1. Two Ledgers, Opened in the Same Month

On 12 August 2026, Rukmini Deshpande spread six printed pages across a table in Bhaav Pricing Cloud's Pune office. Bhaav sold margin-management and repricing software to mid-market Indian grocery chains — the 150-to-400-store operators competing with DMart and Reliance Smart — and closed FY26 at ₹58 crore of ARR across 41 accounts. In three weeks she had to recommend whether autonomous repricing — the engine changing shelf prices without a category manager's approval — should become every account's default rather than an opt-in. They were the predictions she had written and dated before each of her last six decisions, with what happened beside them.

Eight hundred kilometres north-west, on 3 September 2026, Ibrahim Qureshi was doing an uglier version of the same exercise at Dinkar Energy Devices in Ahmedabad. Dinkar built hybrid rooftop-solar inverters and battery packs, sold through about 900 installer partners, and booked ₹412 crore on 63,000 units in FY26 as the PM Surya Ghar scheme pulled demand forward. He had to freeze the next-generation bill of materials that month, and lead time on the cellular module ran fourteen months. In February 2024 he had made the opposite call — Wi-Fi only, plus an optional ₹1,100 dongle — on a belief he never wrote as a number: that homeowners' Wi-Fi reached the inverter and installers would upsell the dongle. Attach came in at 6.2 per cent against a forecast of 25.

Both decisions rhymed with an earlier one, and neither record said what to do next. Each said how its owner generates beliefs, which is this page's argument: the output of mature reflective practice is a corrected belief-generating procedure, and the evidence lives in the pattern across a portfolio of scored predictions, not in the autopsy of one decision.

2. The Idea, and Who Disagrees About It

Reflective practice is the disciplined examination, after an outcome is known, of the belief that made a decision feel right before it was known. Three parts are load-bearing: it is retrospective on a specific prior belief, not on events; comparative, an expectation set against a result; and generative, terminating in a claim a future decision could test.

It was invented to explain why professionals improve at a rate out of all proportion to their hours. Dewey's How We Think (1933) located the mechanism in interruption: learning begins when activity breaks and assumptions must be inspected. Schön's The Reflective Practitioner (1983) made this a theory of expertise — practitioners hold a running conversation with a situation that keeps surprising them — and with Chris Argyris he drew the distinction that does most of the organisational work: espoused theory, what a person says they believe, against theory-in-use, what their behaviour implies. Mezirow added that reflection's real object is not the belief but the frame behind it.

Four schools now disagree substantively. The professional-artistry school, after Schön, would sign: a practitioner can recover and improve reasoning they could not articulate while using it; it would not sign that unscored reflection is worthless. The calibration school, after Tetlock (2005), would sign: a belief never stated as a probability on a resolvable question cannot be honestly reviewed; it would not sign that narrative reflection teaches anything reliable.

The introspection-sceptic school is the most corrosive and least discussed. Nisbett and Wilson's "Telling More Than We Can Know" (1977) showed people confidently report causes of their judgements that demonstrably did not operate; Eraut argued reflection-in-action is largely myth, since under time pressure practitioners pattern-match and construct the reasoning later. It would sign: a recalled prior belief is generated, not retrieved, and reflection improves the story's coherence more reliably than the model's accuracy. It would not sign that reflection is useless: it accepts a belief read off a dated document rather than out of a memory.

The learning-environment school — Hogarth's Educating Intuition (2001), and the 2009 paper in which Kahneman and Klein agreed about when intuition works — makes this depend on feedback structure: kind environments give fast unconfounded feedback, wicked ones slow and contaminated feedback that installs false beliefs. It would sign: in a wicked environment, outcome-based reflection degrades a model; it would not sign that reflection is good practice regardless of setting.

The best field evidence is Indian: Di Stefano, Gino, Pisano and Staats found that agents at a Bengaluru business-process operation of Wipro's who wrote up what they had learned for fifteen minutes each evening outperformed controls by roughly 23 per cent in a month — on a task with same-day unconfounded feedback, the kindest environment a PM will see.

3. Mechanics: What a Scored Ledger Actually Says

Expert practice has a shape the ordinary retrospective lacks. Before deciding, the practitioner writes five things: the belief in a sentence; the mechanism producing the result; a prediction with a probability and a resolution date; the falsifier; the reference class. Afterwards they score it — the step almost everyone skips.

A negative skill score is humbling: across eighteen months of consequential judgements, Rukmini would have scored better by refusing to have opinions and writing 0.50 on every line. Most stop there, which is the wrong lesson. Allan Murphy's 1973 identity splits a Brier score into reliability (distance from realised frequencies), resolution (discrimination between what happens and what does not) and uncertainty (the base rate's variance, 0.25 here). Her reliability is 0.052, her resolution 0.002: average confidence on her three false claims was 0.717, on her three true claims 0.733. She was not merely overconfident — she could not tell her good beliefs from her bad ones.

Splitting the ledger by subject makes it actionable. Forecasts 2, 4 and 6 concern Bhaav's own machine — override rates, retention, implementation time — and score a mean Brier of 0.078. Forecasts 1, 3 and 5 concern what somebody outside the building wants, and score 0.521. Same person, same period, same confidence range, two different competences.

The split had one cause, which Suhasini Rao identified from Hyderabad: every motive belief rested on self-selected evidence — the managers who answered the survey, the chains that volunteered, the merchants who joined the advisory council. Her procedure was sound about systems she could instrument and unsound about people she heard from only when they chose to speak. That is not a belief to revise but a rule to install.

Scoring changes what gets forecast: once probabilities are visible, the cheapest way to improve a score is to stop making sharp claims.

4. When It Applies, Stated as Testable Claims

Reflective practice is not universally available. Five conditions decide whether it produces knowledge or noise, each checkable in advance — besides the obvious one, a contemporaneous record.

C2 deserves arithmetic, because enterprise PMs assume it away. Rukmini wanted to know whether autonomous repricing would hurt gross retention, now 92 per cent. With 41 accounts in arms of about 20, a two-proportion test at 5 per cent significance and 80 per cent power detects only enormous effects.

So in a low-power environment reflection must attach to mechanism, not outcome. She can honestly review whether category managers behaved as her model said; she can never review whether retention moved. Practitioners who ignore this reflect on noise and install beliefs drawn from two churned accounts.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. Where outcome feedback is confounded, reflecting on results is worse than not reflecting: it produces confident wrong beliefs that are hard to dislodge. Where the belief was correct and the regime changed — merchant resistance to algorithmic pricing may have been real in 2022 and gone by 2026 — expiry is not error. And wherever reflection grades a decision by its outcome: a decision taken at 0.75 that fails is usually a good decision with a bad result, and punishing it rewards what is easy to defend.

5. Hard Edges: Where the Practice Strains

In a multi-product company, beliefs held by different people rest on one invisible shared assumption. Bhaav's repricing, assortment and promotions modules each had a PM; all three had assumed a category manager's stated preference matched their operative one. Nobody owned it, so nobody reviewed it. The fix is a register of cross-product assumptions with a named owner and a review date.

In regulated settings the state often takes the counterfactual away. Dastak Care Systems, a Mumbai company selling teleconsultation, e-pharmacy and claims pre-authorisation software to hospital groups, shipped OCR auto-fill in January 2026 believing document friction delayed pre-authorisation; median turnaround fell from 31 hours to 19. In the same window the move towards IRDAI's health-claims exchange changed one large insurer's API. Sharmila Pathak, the product lead, split the 109 hospitals: the 41 on the new API improved by 22.1 hours, the 68 not on it by 5.9. The weighted average reproduces the headline 12, but Dastak's own contribution is 5.9 — under half what the launch note claimed, and the honest basis for ₹2.4 crore of build. The regime co-authors your results, and a reflection that does not name it is credit-taking.

In hardware the belief is frozen into tooling. Ibrahim's 2024 call could not be revised for two years, and by then two of the four people who held the belief had left. Mature hardware organisations write beliefs into the design review record rather than a person's memory, and define a proxy resolving inside the design cycle: dongle attach at 90 days, not service cost at three years.

In AI-native products the artefact you reflect on may no longer exist. Bodhini Tutor Cloud, a Bengaluru company building an AI tutor for JEE and NEET aspirants, changed its prompt 31 times and its base model three times in nine months, and 140 of its 480 evaluation items were rewritten over the same period. The record must be versioned as strictly as the model, or the ledger becomes fiction.

What mature companies do, as against what they say, is worth stating plainly. Most keep a write-only decision log: entries go in, nobody reads them, and the ritual survives because it is cheap and looks disciplined. The ones that extract value separate the belief-review calendar from the performance-review calendar, so admitting a wrong prior is not a compensation event, and give someone the job of reading the log backwards for the repeated rung-5 sentence.

6. Eight Distinctions That Separate Expert From Competent

Separate the forecast from the decision

A competent practitioner asks whether a call was right; an expert asks what probability was on it, because a decision taken at 0.60 that failed was probably still correct. Tell-tale: their first question is "what did you think the odds were?" Examining failures but not successes grades process by luck.

Reflect hardest on wins that beat forecast

A result far above expectation is as much a model error as one far below, and more dangerous because nobody investigates it. Tell-tale: they open a review of an over-plan launch by asking which belief was wrong in the flattering direction. You learn from surprise, and half of it is pleasant.

The repeated sentence is the finding

One wrong belief is data; the same wrong frame under four unrelated beliefs is the output. Tell-tale: they keep revisions in one place and read them in sequence, hunting the recurring clause — treating each decision as its own lesson changes nothing.

Beliefs have shelf lives, and expiry is not error

A belief can be true when held and false when reviewed, and calling that a mistake trains people towards timeless, useless generalities. Tell-tale: they date the belief and name the regime it assumes — GST rates, UPI interchange, device price points, model capability. The naive reading is that a belief now false was always so.

Distrust your own recalled reason

Nisbett and Wilson apply to product managers: the reason you recall is generated at recall time and feels identical to a memory. Tell-tale: they refuse to answer "what were you thinking?" from memory, going to the artefact even when certain, because the naive reading confuses honesty with access.

Calibration, resolution and accuracy are three things

Being right on average, telling true from false, and being right on a given call are independent virtues. Tell-tale: they report both terms, and notice when a colleague's improving score was bought with hedging — Durbeen's error below.

Ask whether you could have told, before what you learned

Power comes first: if the design could not have detected the effect, the review has nothing to say and should say so. Tell-tale: their first move on an enterprise result is a detectability calculation, whose answer is often "unresolvable." Believing any data beats none is how small samples become doctrine.

Reflection is a social act, and it is priced

Whoever revises a belief in public pays in perceived conviction, which is why senior people reflect privately and juniors not at all. Tell-tale: they revise their own belief first, out loud, and name what it cost; their cadence follows resolution dates, not the quarter. Reflection is not an individual habit: Argyris found defensive routines, not cognition, bind.

7. Differences by Product Type and Stage

In consumer products the loop is fast and the environment kind, so outcome-based reflection works and the constraint is attribution. In B2B and enterprise the loop is slow and the sample tiny, so honest practice is mechanism reflection that admits outcomes are unresolvable — Bhaav's table is the general case, not a quirk. In platforms and marketplaces the distinctive failure is measuring a belief about one side with the other side's metric; the fix is to make every belief name its side. In hardware the belief outlives the believer and must be recorded institutionally; in AI products the referent moves, so the ledger must pin versions. Otherwise the core sequence is identical across all five, and only the resolution horizon, the statistical power and how much of the record lives outside a human head change.

Stage changes the failure mode, not the method. At seed, reflection is cheap and high-leverage, and the failure is that nothing is written, so the third pivot repeats the first's frame. At growth stage it becomes a ritual attached to launches and stops reaching frames. At scale it is professionalised, and the written belief becomes the one safe to be wrong about — espoused theory, filed where theory-in-use should be.

8. Three Worked Cases, Including One Failure

Dinkar, and the twist in the recovery. The belief error was clean: monitoring activation within 30 days ran at 41 per cent (25,830 of 63,000 units) against an assumption of near-universal connectivity, and dongle attach at 6.2 against 25. The obvious correction — a modem in every unit at ₹840 — fails on service economics alone: monitored units generated 11.4 service visits per 100 units a year against 19.8 unmonitored, so universal monitoring avoids about 3,122 visits across the 37,170 unmonitored units, ₹45.3 lakh a year at ₹1,450 a truck roll against ₹3.12 crore of modem cost. The case closes only on subscription attach: the ₹249-a-month Dinkar Assure plan converts 14.8 per cent of monitored owners and 0.9 per cent of unmonitored ones, implying 5,501 incremental subscribers and ₹1.15 crore of gross profit — about ₹1.38 crore a year with the service saving, and a 2.3-year payback. There Ibrahim stopped: 14.8 per cent was measured on owners who chose to connect, the identical self-selection error as his 2024 belief. At 5 per cent, payback passes five years.

Bodhini, and the wrong ruler. Aftab Rizvi's November 2025 belief was that students abandoned a session when the tutor produced a wrong step. Abandonment fell from 34 to 22 per cent while eval accuracy rose from 71 to 88, which looked like confirmation. Renuka Sathe's version-pinned re-run showed the true gain was 76 to 87 on the constant 340-item core; and among the 1,240 students in an 8 per cent holdout who never saw the March 2026 step-by-step reveal, abandonment moved only from 34 to 31. Accuracy was not the mechanism; legibility was.

Durbeen, where the practice itself failed. Durbeen Insight Systems, a Gurugram B2B analytics company, logged 144 forecasts over four quarters under its CPO Gaurav Thakral; 61 per cent resolved true. The headline Brier score improved from 0.249 to 0.240 and the ritual was declared a success. The decomposition tells the real story: with uncertainty fixed at 0.238, reliability fell from 0.052 to 0.008 and resolution collapsed from 0.041 to 0.006. The improvement was bought with hedging — forecasts between 0.45 and 0.55 rose from 12 per cent of the log to 58 — because the log was read in performance reviews, making it rational to stop having opinions. Recovery took three changes: resolution scored alongside reliability; a falsifier on every forecast; and the log moved out of the review cycle, with an "unresolvable" option so abstention need not pose as a 0.50.

9. Failure Modes and Their Early Diagnostics

Ritual without frames. Sign: every revised belief is one clause narrower than the original, and none carries a date or an external condition. Diagnostic: read the last six revisions and ask whether any names a frame. Cost late: years re-testing variants of one wrong idea, as at Bhaav.

Hedging under observation. Sign: the modal probability drifts towards 0.50. Diagnostic: report resolution, not just the score. Cost late: the log survives; the judgement atrophies.

Unresolvable outcomes. Sign: conclusions resting on three or four accounts. Diagnostic: compute the detectable effect first. Cost late: a baseless belief defended for years because it is written down.

Confabulated priors. Sign: "I always had doubts about that." Diagnostic: ask for the timestamp. Cost late: the review installs the reviewer's current preference as a historical lesson.

Reflection as accountability. Sign: the belief review shares a meeting with the performance conversation. Diagnostic: ask who present revised a belief in public this quarter. Cost late: Durbeen's outcome, a healthy-looking process producing worse decisions.

10. Where Experts Genuinely Disagree

The live disagreement is whether the calibration apparatus is necessary or corrosive.

The calibration position rests on tournament evidence: when beliefs are stated as probabilities on resolvable questions and scored, accuracy improves and transfers across domains. Its steelman is that every alternative lets the practitioner grade their own homework, generously. For it to be wrong, scorable questions would have to exclude the beliefs that matter most.

The artistry position holds that the most consequential product beliefs are not resolvable propositions — "this category will reward vertical depth over breadth" has no resolution date — so forcing them into that shape selects for the small and measurable. Its steelman is Durbeen: the apparatus, applied honestly, produced worse thinking. For it to be wrong, unscored reflection would have to correct beliefs rather than reorganise them, which the introspection literature makes doubtful.

A third, environmental position holds that both sides generalise from their own domains: score where feedback is kind, reflect on mechanism where it is wicked, and do not pretend one practice serves both. Its weakness is that it gives no guidance in the mixed case, which is most cases — Dinkar's telemetry is kind and its installer behaviour wicked inside one decision. Anyone claiming this is resolved is selling a method.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has merely studied reflective practice runs good retrospectives. Someone who has internalised it differs in three ways. They write the falsifier before the launch, in one line with a number, because their future self will otherwise reconstruct a belief rather than recall it. They read their revisions in sequence, because the pattern is the finding. And they revise in public and name the cost, because the constraint is not their cognition but whether anyone else believes changing your mind here is survivable.

12. What They Decided

Rukmini neither recommended autonomous repricing as a default nor rejected it. She made it the default for the eleven accounts where Bhaav had instrumented override behaviour directly — where a motive belief could be replaced by a measurement — and opt-in elsewhere, noting in writing that retention effects were unresolvable at this scale. She added a standing rule: no belief about what a customer wants may rest on a self-selected sample; where only such a sample exists, the forecast is marked unresolvable.

Ibrahim committed the modem, but bought the missing number first: a four-week trial of 1,500 units with monitoring pre-activated, to measure Assure conversion on a non-self-selected population. Above 9 per cent the BOM change cleared its hurdle rate; below, it did not. He wrote the threshold down, dated it, and sent it to Meenal Joshi in firmware and Prakash Sahoo in field operations in Bhubaneswar before the data existed — so nobody, himself included, could later remember another number.

  1. Rukmini forecasts her own system well and other people's motives badly. Should she improve her motive forecasting, or stop forecasting motive and buy measurements instead — and what does each cost?
  2. Durbeen's score improved while its judgement deteriorated. Design a reflection process for a 60-person product organisation that cannot be gamed this way, and name what it costs.
  3. Ibrahim must decide before evidence arrives; Dastak cannot obtain a counterfactual at all. When outcome feedback is unavailable, what is left of reflective practice that is more than storytelling?

13. Going Deeper

Influence without authority — the constraint is rarely cognitive; revising a belief in front of stakeholders costs conviction, and this topic is how that cost is managed. Conflict and disagreement — a belief review is a structured disagreement with your past self. Negotiation for PMs — a pre-registered falsifier is a commitment device. Building trust with teams — nobody states a real prior to someone who will use it against them. Psychological safety and team health — the condition for Durbeen's recovery, and why the hedging appeared. What makes a great PM — the portfolio view of judgement a scored ledger makes visible.

Reflective Practice

What did I believe, what changed, and why? — the discipline of examining your own reasoning after a decision, not just the decision's result.

A Verification Badge, Eighteen Months Later

On a Tuesday morning in March 2025, Kavya Iyer sat in a glass-walled conference room on the fourth floor of Sahyog Freight Systems' Bengaluru office, looking at a funnel chart she had built eighteen months earlier and never quite looked at squarely again. Sahyog matched independent truck owner-operators with shippers moving cement, textiles and FMCG cargo across the Bengaluru–Chennai–Hyderabad–Pune quadrilateral, clearing close to ₹340 crore of freight a year by 2025 with roughly 38,000 active drivers on its supply side. Kavya, the senior product manager for driver supply, was two weeks from a decision that rhymed uncomfortably with one she had made in December 2023: whether Sahyog's new payments wallet, built to settle freight fares instantly, should require a fresh round of mandatory video KYC before a driver could receive a payout.

She had pushed hard for a similar mandatory step once before — a GPS-linked "verified device" badge meant to close a trust gap shippers had raised in feedback — and it had cost the company close to a thousand driver signups a month for most of a quarter before anyone understood why. Before making the KYC call, Kavya wanted to understand what had actually happened: not what she now believed, with fifteen months of hindsight, but what she had believed before the outcome was known, and where that belief had gone wrong.

What Reflective Practice Actually Means

Reflective practice is the disciplined habit of examining, after a decision has produced a result, what you believed before the result was known, what evidence exists for and against that belief today, and how it should change in response. It is not the same as simply noting what happened, and it is not assigning blame; its subject is the practitioner's own model of the world, not the sequence of events.

The term comes from Donald Schön, whose 1983 book The Reflective Practitioner: How Professionals Think in Action studied how architects, engineers and managers actually reasoned on the job. Schön argued that expertise shows up less as applying textbook rules and more as a continuous, often unspoken conversation between a practitioner's assumptions and the surprises a real situation produces. He built on the philosopher John Dewey, who had argued in How We Think (1933) that genuine learning begins only when the smooth flow of experience is interrupted by a problem, forcing a person to reconsider what they had taken for granted. David Kolb gave the habit a repeatable shape in 1984 with his experiential learning cycle — concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation.

Reflective practice does not ask what went wrong; it asks what belief made the decision feel obviously right at the time, and whether that belief survives contact with what actually happened.

How It Works, Step by Step

Reflective practice has a sequence, and most of what separates people who do it well from people who merely hold a "retro" is that the first two steps below are the ones everyone is tempted to skip.

First, reconstruct the belief exactly as it stood before the outcome was known — not the belief a person would state now, having seen how things turned out, but the one operative at the time. This is harder than it sounds, because the mind quietly edits the past once it knows the ending; psychologists call this hindsight bias, and it is the biggest saboteur of honest reflection. The only reliable defence is a contemporaneous record — a decision memo, a dated message, a one-line prediction — because without one, "what I believed" and "what I now wish I had believed" become indistinguishable.

Second, state the evidence the belief rested on. Third, lay the actual outcome next to the predicted one, without editorialising. Fourth, the diagnostic heart of the exercise, locate the gap: the belief itself may have been wrong, execution may have failed to deliver a sound belief, or some variable outside the original picture was doing most of the work — a distinction people blur, because blaming execution feels safer than admitting the model of the world was incomplete. Fifth, write the revised belief as a testable claim. Sixth — the step teams skip most often — pre-register what would need to be true before a decision of that kind is trusted again.

Kavya's Ledger: the Belief, the Evidence, the Gap

Kavya's December 2023 decision concerned the "verified device" badge. Shipper feedback in Sahyog's quarterly survey had repeatedly used the word "trust": shippers said they could not tell whether a driver profile represented a real, available truck. Kavya's belief, reasonable enough at the time, was that this distrust was suppressing completed bookings, which was in turn depressing driver retention, because drivers who won fewer loads simply stopped opening the app. The fix she championed required every new driver to complete a GPS-linked device verification before the profile could go live for shippers to see.

Kavya's first read, in early 2024, was that her belief had been broadly right but the execution too blunt — perhaps the flow asked for too many taps. That read led to a modest redesign and a shrug. The more useful pass came in 2025, when her colleague Arjun Nair, based in Coimbatore, interviewed 42 drivers who had abandoned the flow, across Coimbatore, Nashik and Belagavi. Only a handful mentioned distrust of the badge; the dominant complaint was that the verification module would not run on their phones. It required Android 10 or newer, and 34% of the drivers Arjun spoke to were using budget Android 8 or 9 devices bought for under ₹6,000.

When Sahyog's data team segmented the 991 lost completions by pincode tier, the picture sharpened: 704, or 71%, sat in tier-3 and tier-4 towns, where budget-device ownership ran highest; only 287, or 29%, were in metro pincodes. The belief that explained the headline number — "shippers don't trust unverified profiles, so drivers churn" — accounted for, at most, the smaller share of the loss. A belief Kavya had never examined — "our verification technology assumes a phone most of our drivers don't own" — explained most of it.

Seven Distinctions Worth Holding Onto

Reflection is not rumination

Turning a decision over repeatedly is not reflective practice unless it produces a written belief-evidence-gap triple. Without that structure, revisiting a setback becomes anxious replaying that never updates anything — the feeling of reflecting, without its product.

Single-loop learning is not double-loop learning

Argyris and Schön distinguished fixing the action from fixing the belief behind it. Rolling back the GPS badge is single-loop learning. Deciding that onboarding changes must be checked against device-tier data before every future launch is double-loop learning — only the second kind compounds.

Reflection-in-action is not reflection-on-action

Adjusting your read of a situation while still inside it — noticing mid-meeting that a stakeholder's objection doesn't fit your model — is reflection-in-action. Kavya's structured review, fifteen months later, is reflection-on-action. Most teams only practise the second, and lose the cheaper corrections the first offers.

Hindsight quietly rewrites the belief

Ask what someone believed before a launch, after it has already failed, and the answer is usually contaminated by what they now know. Reflective practice is only as honest as the record it works from; without a dated memo, the "before" belief is being reconstructed, not recalled.

It is not a post-mortem, and it is not feedback

A post-mortem typically asks what should change procedurally — more testing, a rollback plan; reflective practice asks a narrower question: what did I believe about the world, and was it correct. Feedback — an NPS comment, a churn number — is data from outside; reflective practice is updating your model in light of it. A person can receive excellent feedback and still fail to reflect, by never examining the prior belief it contradicted.

It cannot manufacture a correct new belief

Reflective practice disciplines updating; it does not guarantee truth. Forty-two interviews are suggestive, not proof, and a belief drawn from a small sample can still be wrong — it deserves the same scrutiny before it is trusted at scale.

Consumer, B2B, Marketplace, and Company Age

In a high-volume consumer product, the loop is fast but the signal is noisy, since many things change at once; a team often needs a segmentation exercise like Arjun's before a belief about "why" can be trusted. In B2B products the loop is slower and each account carries disproportionate weight: one lost enterprise renewal can quietly stand in for "the market." Two-sided marketplaces like Sahyog complicate things further, because a single funnel number conflates two audiences with different beliefs operating on them; Kavya's mistake was looking at a driver-side metric through a shipper-side belief.

Company age matters too. Early-stage reflection tends to be personal and informal, but the stakes are high because each decision is load-bearing for the whole roadmap. At a large company, reflective practice gets institutionalised — quarterly reviews, decision logs, formal pre-mortems — an improvement in principle, but one with its own risk: those rituals can calcify into performance, where the "belief" written down is the one safe to have been wrong about, not the one actually held.

Where Reflection Goes Wrong

Symptom: a retrospective lists only actions — "add monitoring," "simplify the flow" — with no sentence on what anyone believed beforehand. Misread: the team confused a process fix with a belief update. Cheap check: ask the room to state, in one sentence, what they thought was true before the event; if no one can, no real reflection has occurred.

Symptom: the review assigns responsibility by name. Misread: reflection has become an accountability exercise, so people are reluctant to admit a prior belief that turned out wrong and retroactively claim they "always had doubts." Cheap check: look for a timestamp from before the event; a stated belief with no earlier trace is suspect.

Symptom: teams reflect energetically after failures and never after successes. Misread: a belief that happened to work can still be wrong, or right for the wrong reason, and is the seed of a bigger future failure. Cheap check: reflect on a recent win and ask what would have had to differ for it to fail despite doing everything the same way.

Symptom: a reflection meeting runs long, covers six topics, and produces no written decision. Misread: rumination without structure. Cheap check: cap each topic and require one written belief-evidence-revised-belief triple before moving on.

What Good Looks Like

By the time Kavya finished reviewing the GPS badge, she had written three lines she could defend in front of anyone: the old belief, stated plainly; the evidence that overturned it, with the interview count and tier split attached; and a new belief phrased as something a future decision could test — "any mandatory onboarding step must be checked for device-tier impact before an attitudinal explanation is accepted." She dated the note and filed it beside the December 2023 launch memo, so the next reviewer would not have to reconstruct her earlier belief from memory either.

The Second Decision

Kavya did not simply revert the GPS badge, nor wave the new KYC requirement through unexamined. She kept device verification but built a fallback: drivers whose phones could not run the GPS module could complete a short manual video check through Sahyog's regional support desk instead. Before the wallet's KYC step shipped, she wrote down and dated exactly what she expected, broken out by device tier — and asked her team to do the same before their next three launches, whether or not this one went well. What she wants to learn next is the sibling discipline this topic sets up: holding that same honesty about your own beliefs inside a room full of stakeholders who have reasons, some good and some political, to prefer you not revise your view in public.

Two questions worth sitting with: think of a recent decision of yours that worked out — could you write down, today, the belief that made it feel right before you knew the outcome? And is there a change you are resisting reversing right now, not because the evidence says to keep it, but because reversing it would mean admitting the belief behind it was wrong?

The Second Reading: Upvan Fresh Networks and the Cost of Looking Back

Pune, Sunday 27 September 2026

The pack-house floodlights at Ambad were still on when Sharvari Gokhale hung up on Nashik at a quarter past ten. Nine hours from now, off Baner Road, she would open the Second Reading of Project Tarazu — the practice she had invented three years earlier at Upvan Fresh Networks, in which the people who made a large decision sit down eighteen months later, read aloud what they wrote, and say what they believed, what changed, and why.

She had the March 2025 belief note open on one screen. On the other sat a term sheet from Udyat Quick Retail, Upvan's largest customer, asking for a nine per cent price cut and category exclusivity in three cities, signature required by 16 October. Beside it lay an email from Neelima Chowdary, the investor on Upvan's board, asking that Monday's minutes go into the October board pack. And in her inbox, unanswered since Friday, sat a message from Mihir Bhagwat, the co-founder and chief executive, with a subject line that read: Push Monday?

She had built it believing that an organisation which could not say out loud what it used to think would pay twice for the same misjudgement. She was no longer sure the practice did that, and quite sure that whatever happened at nine o'clock would be read by four constituencies as something other than reflection.

2. Upvan Fresh Networks

Upvan was founded in 2019 by Mihir Bhagwat, an ex-ITC agri-business manager, and two Pune colleagues, on the observation that India loses a punishing share of its fruit and vegetable output between field and shelf, and that the loss is not mainly a refrigeration problem but a forecasting one. Upvan aggregated produce from farmer producer organisations in Nashik, Sangli, Kolar and Anantapur, graded and pre-cooled it, and moved it to buyers same-day. Its differentiator was not the trucks, which it leased, but Aavak — the demand-and-indent platform that told each pack-house what to pack, at what grade, for whom, by when.

The decision that most constrains Upvan today was taken in 2023. After an aborted cold-chain expansion at Chakan was written off at ₹19 crore, the company recapitalised its pack-houses with a ₹40 crore term loan under an Agriculture Infrastructure Fund-linked facility. The covenants were unremarkable then and are not now: throughput of at least 1.5 lakh tonnes a year, and a debt-service coverage ratio above 1.25. Tonnage, not margin, became the number the balance sheet required, and every channel argument since has had that fact underneath it.

The write-off left a second, stranger legacy. In October 2023 Sharvari, then VP Product, proposed that every decision above ₹5 crore or three months of engineering carry a one-page note: what we believe, what would have to be true, what would tell us early that we are wrong, and the date we re-read this. The re-reading was the point. She called it the Second Reading, and for a year it was the best thing about Upvan.

3. The industry

By 2026 the Indian fresh-produce chain had three buyers that mattered and they wanted incompatible things. Quick commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart and the regional challengers — wanted small, frequent, unpredictable replenishment into dark stores, three indents a day, and a price that assumed the supplier absorbed the variance. Modern trade — Reliance Retail, DMart, and chains such as the Hyderabad-based Ushas Retail Group — wanted planned weekly volumes and ninety-day negotiations. Exports, governed by APEDA registration and the residue limits of the destination market, wanted traceability and documentation, and paid materially better for it.

Upvan served all three. Ulwan Retail Group LLC in Dubai took grapes, pomegranates and okra for its Emirates stores and had become Upvan's most profitable account per tonne; an ethnic-retail business in New Jersey took speciality lines, and the rupee's drift made both look better on paper. Against that sat the fact that quick commerce was the fastest-growing shelf in urban India, that Ninjacart, WayCool and a dozen funded rivals were chasing it, and that the platforms had begun to build sourcing teams of their own. Regulation touched Upvan at the edges: FSSAI licensing, APMC and eNAM formalities, GST on packaged lines. Nothing in the regulatory environment forced Monday's decision. Everything in the commercial environment did.

4. What was believed, and what has since happened

Project Tarazu was approved on 18 March 2025. Its belief note, drafted by Sharvari and countersigned by Mihir and by Saurabh Pendse, then director of product, committed Upvan to ₹64 crore of capex: rebuilt pack-house lines at Nashik and Kolar, and cross-docks in Pune, Bengaluru and Hyderabad sized for three-times-daily replenishment. It committed product to rewriting Aavak around dark-store signals, and the company, by three-year agreement, to Udyat Quick Retail.

The note stated four beliefs: that quick commerce would take roughly eighteen per cent of urban fresh by 2027; that Upvan's forecasting would drive wastage below six per cent within a year; that scale would protect contribution below modern-trade prices; and — in a line since read aloud more than the other three combined — that “platform verticalisation into direct sourcing is a 2028 risk, not a 2026 one.”

Exhibit 1 lays out what happened, and it is no simple story of error. The market belief was right, possibly conservative. The wastage belief was nearly right: wastage fell from 11.2 to 7.4 per cent, an achievement that missed its number. The unit-cost belief is contested, and Exhibits 2 and 3 disagree so completely that they cannot both describe the same business. The verticalisation belief was wrong by eighteen months: Udyat began an FPO-direct pilot in Kolar in November 2025 and extended it to Nashik in June 2026.

Two things happened alongside. In February 2026, after consignments from a competing origin were rejected on residue limits in the Gulf, Ulwan tripled its indent — and Upvan could serve barely half, its Nashik pre-cooling capacity being committed to the Udyat cycle. In April the data team moved the forecast-error denominator from units ordered to units delivered. The change was defensible and was announced in a Slack thread; it also makes Exhibit 4 discontinuous at the point where it looks most encouraging.

The last development is what has made Monday difficult. In June 2026 Saurabh Pendse left after a disputed performance review in which his own belief note on an abandoned project was quoted back to him. The dispute is unresolved, and since June, as Exhibit 5 shows, notes have grown longer, more numerous and less falsifiable.

5. The people

Sharvari Gokhale — Chief Product Officer, Pune. Author of the Second Reading and of the Tarazu note. Position: Monday proceeds in full. Incentive: the practice is the most visible thing she has built. Unsaid: her own 2023 note set the test “we will know this works if one major decision is reversed earlier than it otherwise would have been,” and she cannot name one that meets it.
Mihir Bhagwat — co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Wants Monday deferred three weeks: a minuted record of what leadership believed about verticalisation is a liability while the term sheet lives. Incentive: a Series C conversation he hopes to open in January. Unsaid: he countersigned that line and has never called it optimistic.
Neelima Chowdary — partner at Uttung Capital Partners and board member, Mumbai. Wants the minutes in the board pack, and cites the practice to investors as evidence of discipline. Incentive: a fund narrative in which Upvan is the rare supply-chain company that learns. Unsaid: her investment committee has asked why Upvan's capital sits in its worst-contributing channel, and a document naming the risk in advance suits her better than one that missed it.
Harish Mudaliar — President, International, New Jersey. Argues Tarazu was a strategic error and Monday should say so. Incentive: the export lane he runs is capacity-starved and, on his team's numbers in Exhibit 2, Upvan's most profitable business. Unsaid: Ulwan's February surge followed a competitor's regulatory misfortune, and his 2027 plan assumes it repeats.
Keerthana Raghunath — Head of Data Science, Toronto. Position: the reflection should stay within what the data supports, which cannot settle unit economics either way. Incentive: her team authorised the April metric change and she does not want a referendum on it. Unsaid: she flagged the discontinuity in May and was told it could wait.
Lukas Brandt — Design Director, Berlin. The practice's loudest defender, and author of the 2024 template. Position: hold the session, publish the minutes, name misjudgements by author. Incentive: his teams across three time zones rely on written decisions, rarely being in the room. Unsaid: his template is plausibly why notes are four times longer (Exhibit 5).
Cheryl Tan — Head of Customer Success, Singapore, who manages Ulwan and the Gulf accounts. Two customers have asked for belief notes on roadmap items affecting them, and sharing one in 2025 saved a renewal. Incentive: renewals. Unsaid: Ulwan's procurement head has begun asking about Upvan's commitments to Udyat, and a candid reflection reaching Dubai would read as confirmation, not candour.
Shabnam Kazi — Head of Pack-house Operations, Nashik, the only leader who must make the tonnage covenant true each quarter. Position: the channel debate is unserious because nobody has costed a pre-cooling changeover, which takes eleven days, not two. Incentive: stability. Unsaid: she stopped writing belief notes in February and signs the template unread.
Abhijit Ranadive — VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Believes the practice has become theatre and should give way to a quarterly audit. Incentive: the four hundred engineering hours a quarter the notes consume. Unsaid: the Aavak rewrite is nine months behind plan, and a rigorous reflection surfaces that before the board sees the roadmap.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the artefact Monday exists to read. Its right-hand column did not exist in March 2025; the strategy team filled it in once the outcome was known.

Exhibit 1 — Project Tarazu belief note (Mar 2025) against outcome (Sep 2026)

Exhibits 2 and 3 describe the same year, revenue and total cost, and reach opposite conclusions about which channel Upvan should be in. The only difference is the allocation base for ₹63 crore of pack-house cost.

7. Voices

“I am not asking anyone to be less honest. I am asking whether a minuted sentence saying we thought verticalisation was three years away belongs in a board pack the week we negotiate with the company that verticalised.” Lukas Brandt, from Berlin at 06:40: “If we move it, we will move it again. There is always a negotiation. That is what a company is.”Leadership call, 24 September 2026
“Sharvari — the FY26 numbers use a different error definition. I raised this in May. If anyone presents the trend as continuous improvement I will say so in the room.”Keerthana Raghunath, email, 26 September 2026, 02:11 IST
“Most belief notes I sign now are written by someone who already knows how the decision will go. We are producing an archive of justifications and calling it learning.”Abhijit Ranadive, engineering channel, 19 September 2026
“Separate the two questions. Was Tarazu wrong, and was Sharvari wrong. Everybody in that room will answer the second while pretending to answer the first.”Shabnam Kazi, to Sharvari, Nashik, 27 September 2026
“I would like the minutes, not a summary. The fund's IC has seen the channel numbers and will ask whether this team saw it coming. Better a document saying we named the risk and mis-dated it than nothing at all.”Neelima Chowdary, email to Mihir Bhagwat and Sharvari Gokhale, 23 September 2026

8. The options as Sharvari sees them

Option A — Hold the session as designed

Nine o'clock, full group, the March note read aloud, each belief marked against Exhibit 1, minutes to the board. The practice survives intact and the record is complete before the negotiation. The cost: the verticalisation sentence enters a written record while a term sheet is live, Keerthana's objection to Exhibit 4 becomes public, and Abhijit's nine-month slip surfaces in the wrong forum.

Option B — Defer three weeks

Move it to 19 October, after the signature and the board. Mihir's argument is narrow and commercial, and the facts will not change. The cost: a practice whose only asset is that it happens on the date written in the note will have been moved for the first time, for the most understandable reason, in the most important case — and everyone who has stopped writing disconfirmers will know what that means.

Option C — Narrow the practice

Keep Monday, but redefine the belief note: confidential to the author and one reviewer, barred from performance reviews and board packs, re-read with only the decision team present. This may restore the candour of FY2024. The cost: what made the practice valuable to Lukas's teams, Cheryl's customers and Neelima's fund was precisely that it was open, and a private reflection is hard to tell, from outside, from none at all.

Option D — Retire it

Replace it with a quarterly decision audit run by the strategy team, with an independent reviewer and no requirement that the decision-maker narrate their own error. Abhijit's four hundred hours come back, and Exhibit 5 arguably supports it. The cost: an audit answers “was the decision right” and never asks “what did I believe, and when did I stop” — and the person best placed to answer the second is the one it works around.

Sharvari had written the four on a page at about nine, then sat looking at them with the sense that it was the wrong page. All four treat this as document governance: who reads the note, when, with what protection. None asks whether the Udyat decision is being argued out under cover of a debate about a ritual, or whether she is, in defending the practice, defending her own authorship of it.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The Second Reading is at 09:00 IST on Monday 28 September; Berlin joins at 05:30, Toronto at 23:30, and the date has held for eighteen months. Udyat requires signature by 16 October. The board meets on 9 October; the pack closes on the 6th. The loan covenant is tested on FY2027 throughput, and on the FY2026 mix only Scenario A clears it. Thirty-eight crore of cross-dock assets are undepreciated. Pre-cooling lines at Nashik take eleven days to reconfigure between the quick-commerce cycle and export grades — a number only Shabnam has stated and nobody has verified. The Pendse matter is unresolved, and counsel has advised, without elaboration, that internal documents assigning individual responsibility for commercial outcomes be reviewed before wide circulation. And Sharvari's own 2023 note carries a re-read date of October 2026.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Take the four beliefs in Exhibit 1 in turn. Was the belief wrong, the test wrong, or the reading late — and does the distinction change what Sharvari should say?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 cannot both guide action. What would you need to know to choose, and what does it mean that each was commissioned by a leader with a stake in the answer?
  3. Exhibit 5 shows a practice degrading. Did the practice fail, did it succeed and then get corrupted by how it was used, or is the measure unreliable? What would distinguish the three?
  4. Several stakeholders want the reflection honest and also safe. Are those reconcilable in one document, or must the record that helps people learn be separated from the one that goes to the board?
  5. Sharvari cannot name a decision that met her own 2023 test. Should that test decide the practice's future, and what does it cost when the person who built a practice must also judge it?
  6. What should Sharvari do at nine o'clock on Monday — and what, on 9 October, should she tell the board about what she believed in March 2025, when she stopped believing it, and why the interval was so long?

It was past eleven. Sharvari opened her October 2023 note, the one with the re-read date a fortnight away, and read its last line: “The test of this is not whether we write these. It is whether anyone ever changes their mind out loud.” She thought about Shabnam signing templates she had stopped reading, and about Mihir's subject line still unanswered. In Nashik the last truck was being sealed for a dark store in Kothrud that opened at six. She did not reply. She did not move the meeting. She sat with the two documents open beside each other, unable to decide which of them she was going to be honest about first.

What I Believed, What Changed: A Reflection at Tijori Money

Mumbai, 21 July 2026

Naveen Bhatia read the calendar invitation for the third time that morning: "Leadership Offsite, Goa, 27–28 July — pre-reads due Friday." He was VP of Product at Tijori Money, and the pre-read the board had asked him to write was not a roadmap or a metrics deck. It was a reflection, no more than four pages, on the Round-Up Boost feature he had championed the previous November and that the company had quietly dismantled in April. Priya Ranganathan, Tijori's co-founder and chief executive, had been specific in her email: "Not a post-mortem of the feature. A reflection on you — what you believed when you built it, what changed, and why." The document would sit alongside the numbers the board would use to decide how the Round-Up story was told to Series C investors in September. Naveen had six days to decide not just what had happened, but how honestly to say so, and to whom.

Tijori Money

Tijori Money was founded in 2019 by Priya Ranganathan and two co-founders from a Mumbai fintech incubator, on a simple promise: round up everyday UPI spends to the nearest ten rupees and sweep the difference into a liquid mutual fund or a digital gold vault. It grew into a savings-and-micro-investing app for first-time investors in tier-2 and tier-3 India — Nashik, Indore, Coimbatore, Jodhpur — a segment Groww, Paytm Money and Jar were also racing to own, and that PhonePe's wealth arm was beginning to court with its distribution muscle. By mid-2026 Tijori had 55 lakh downloads, roughly 9 lakh users who had ever invested, and assets under management of about ₹1,140 crore, earned mostly from a small asset-management fee and a spread on gold purchases. It had raised a Series B from a Mumbai fund and a Singapore-based growth investor, and Priya was preparing the data room for a Series C conversation she hoped to close before Diwali. Engagement — how often a user opened the app and added money — was the number every investor asked about first, because it predicted whether a customer acquired for ₹180 would still be paying fees eighteen months later.

The situation

In November 2025, with the Series C conversation already on the horizon, Naveen had proposed Round-Up Boost: streaks for consecutive days of round-up saving, badges for milestones, a leaderboard visible to a user's contacts, and a push notification timed to land within an hour of salary credit, nudging users to "keep the streak alive." He believed, and said so in the product review, that this was simply good gamification — the same mechanic that made Duolingo and Swiggy's loyalty programme sticky, applied to a habit, saving, that Indian households genuinely needed more of. Daily active users on the savings flow rose 34 percent within eight weeks. The board loved the chart.

By January, Tijori's support queue carried a different signal: users describing anxiety over broken streaks, some admitting they had increased round-up amounts beyond what they could comfortably spare to avoid falling in the leaderboard. A consumer-advocacy group filed a complaint in February. In March, following its broader scrutiny of gamified trading and investment interfaces, the RBI's regional office sent Tijori an informal advisory note asking it to review whether leaderboards and streaks on an investment product met the spirit of fair-practice guidelines for retail investors. No penalty was issued, but the note was unambiguous about the direction regulators were looking. Tijori disabled leaderboards and streak notifications on 9 April; daily actives fell back to roughly where they had started, with two support-heavy weeks before the numbers settled. Naveen wrote the rollback memo himself, in clipped, factual language. He had not, until this pre-read was assigned, written anywhere what he had believed in November, or when precisely that belief had cracked.

The people

Priya Ranganathan — co-founder and CEO, Mumbai. Wants a reflection that is genuinely honest, because she believes Tijori's culture depends on leaders naming their own misjudgments early. She also has a Series C narrative to protect and does not want the document read as an admission that the company knowingly designed an addictive product.

Farid Shaikh — data scientist, Toronto. Built the dashboards that showed both the engagement lift and, three months later, the correlation between streak length and above-average round-up amounts. He is frustrated that the second chart existed in January and was not escalated with the same urgency as the first, and wants the reflection precise about when the data actually turned.

Elena Voss — design lead, Berlin. Flagged in the original design review, in writing, that a visible leaderboard on a savings product risked becoming a dark pattern for stretched users, and was overruled. She is watching whether her dissent will be named in the record at all, because that will tell her whether raising concerns early is worth doing again.

Rohan Kapadia — head of compliance and legal, Bengaluru. Worried a candid written account of what Naveen believed and when could become evidence if the RBI's informal advisory turns into a formal inquiry. Wants the reflection reviewed for language before it circulates beyond the leadership team, without necessarily wanting its substance changed.

Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows how the savings-flow numbers and complaint volume moved together over the six months the feature was live — the evidence Naveen must reconcile with what he told the product review in November.

Exhibit 1 — Round-Up Boost: engagement and complaint trend, Nov 2025–Apr 2026

Exhibit 2 gives the financial context the board reads alongside any reflection: what Round-Up Boost was worth to Tijori while it ran, and what the rollback cost.

Read together, the exhibits do not settle whether Round-Up Boost was a mistake in November — the engagement lift was real, and no one could have been certain in advance how it would evolve. What they settle is when the evidence that it was becoming a problem was available to Naveen — the distinction a reflection has to be honest about: not "was I wrong," but "what did I believe, when did the world tell me something different, and how quickly did I listen."

The options

Option A — Write the full, personal account

Naveen writes exactly what Priya asked for: what he believed in November, the point in January or February when the data and Elena's warning should have changed his mind, and why they did not for six more weeks, naming Elena's dissent explicitly. Upside: genuine reflective practice, most likely to change how the team makes the next such call. Cost: most exposed if the RBI inquiry turns formal, and asks Naveen to be visibly wrong before the board weeks before a fundraise.

Option B — Write a forward-looking lessons memo

Naveen documents what the company will do differently — a gamification review checklist, a lower threshold for escalating support signals — without a detailed personal account of what he believed and when. Upside: safer for Rohan's legal concerns, easier to read at a fundraising-adjacent offsite. Cost: answers "what will change" but not "what did I believe," and Elena is unlikely to read it as real acknowledgment.

Option C — Reframe it as a team retrospective

Naveen convenes Farid, Elena and the product team to co-author a structured retrospective — what we believed, what changed, why — as an institutional document, his own reasoning one voice among several. Upside: spreads accountability accurately, since the decision was never his alone. Cost: dilutes the personal ownership Priya asked to see, and risks reading as diffusion of responsibility if no single name is attached to the original call.

Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, at what point does the data suggest Naveen's original belief — that Round-Up Boost was simply good gamification — stopped being a reasonable read of the evidence?
  2. What does Elena Voss's unresolved design-review warning tell us about how Tijori treats dissent, and what changes if that warning is formally acknowledged versus left unmentioned?
  3. Rohan and Priya both want a defensible document, for different reasons. Can a reflection satisfy legal caution without weakening what makes it honest?
  4. Which option best serves Naveen's growth as a leader, and which best serves Tijori preparing for Series C — are those necessarily the same answer?

A note for the learner

Reflective practice is not a post-mortem. A post-mortem asks what happened to the product; reflective practice asks what the decision-maker believed, what evidence challenged that belief, and why the gap between the two persisted as long as it did. The discipline is dating the belief and the disconfirming evidence separately, then being honest about the interval — exactly what Exhibit 1 makes possible, and what a vaguer memo would let Naveen skip.

A well-reasoned answer does not treat honesty and risk-management as opposites traded off in one direction only. The most defensible path is a version of Option A, written first in full and unfiltered — naming the November belief, marking January as the month the evidence turned, crediting Elena's dissent by name — and only then shared with Rohan for review of phrasing, not for permission to remove the substance. Legal review of language is a normal step for any board document; using it to avoid naming what was believed and when it changed is a different thing, and the one habit that would make this reflection worthless as practice however safely worded. Naveen's task by Friday is to write the honest version first, and negotiate its wording second.

Ghungroo Retail Systems: Three Conversations Before Calibration

1. Sunday night, Banjara Hills

On the evening of Sunday, 27 September 2026, Sunayana Rao sat at her dining table in Banjara Hills, Hyderabad, with three unsent calendar invitations on her laptop and the calibration spreadsheet open behind them. It locked at six the next evening. Once it locked, nine product managers at Ghungroo Retail Systems would carry a rating into the year, one promotion slot worth about ₹18 lakh would be spent or forfeited, and the written record of what their manager had told them would become, for the first time, a document other people read.

The three invitations were addressed to Harshvardhan Doshi in Bengaluru, Ishita Barua in Jaipur, and Devansh Kalita in Guwahati. Sunayana had drafted them on Friday and sent none of them. Each conversation, alone, she knew how to have. Together they contradicted one another: what was fair to Harsh would read, to Ishita, as proof that delivery pain was punished and abrasiveness was not. And at the bottom of her inbox sat the item she had reread four times that afternoon — the anonymised upward-feedback rollup for her own function, in which two of her nine reports had written, in different words, that Sunayana gave feedback in the Thursday roadmap review, in front of everyone, and called it coaching.

Eleven weeks earlier she would have said Ghungroo's product problem was a talent problem. She was no longer sure it lay in the people she was about to grade.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2024

Ghungroo Retail Systems was founded in Hyderabad in 2017 by Srinivas “Seenu” Mudaliar, an enterprise-software salesman whose family ran a two-store gold business in Secunderabad, and an architect who left in 2021. Ghungroo sold point-of-sale, inventory and customer software to jewellery chains of twenty to four hundred stores — the tier below Tanishq and Kalyan Jewellers — who needed HUID-level tracking under BIS hallmarking, GST e-invoicing, old-gold valuation, and above all the gold savings schemes on which the Indian trade runs: eleven monthly instalments, a bonus month, and a customer ledger that must survive audit.

By September 2026 Ghungroo served 310 chains and about 4,100 stores, with recurring revenue of ₹74 crore and a Series C in diligence with Granth Capital Partners. Its product organisation was nine PMs and a head of design; engineering sat in Bengaluru, implementation consultants in Jaipur and Coimbatore, customer success for Asia-Pacific and the Gulf in Singapore, and the Americas sales desk, selling to diaspora-facing chains, in New Jersey.

One decision constrained everything Sunayana could do that Sunday. In April 2024, facing a competitive loss to Lakeer Retail Systems, Ghungroo's leadership chose to sell configurability rather than convention: every chain's scheme logic, valuation rules and store hierarchy would be modelled to its own practice rather than forced into a template. It won deals. It also meant each large implementation consumed a product manager for two to three quarters, writing rules that would never be reused, so that the people doing that work produced almost nothing that looked, in any dashboard, like product. Ghungroo had been trying to unwind the decision ever since, and had not.

3. The industry

Indian organised jewellery retail had been consolidating for a decade, accelerated by mandatory HUID hallmarking, GST, and the collapse of trust in unbranded weight. Tanishq, Kalyan, Malabar Gold and Joyalukkas opened into tier-two cities; CaratLane moved the category online; ONDC began carrying smaller jewellers into digital commerce. Ghungroo sold to the squeezed middle: chains large enough to need real systems, too small to build them. Gold above ₹1 lakh per ten grams had pushed customers toward savings schemes, making scheme software commercially decisive and legally sensitive: schemes attract deposit-like scrutiny, and customer ledgers now sat under the DPDP Act.

Two exposures mattered beyond India. Gauhar Jewellery Trading LLC, a nineteen-store Gulf chain anchored in the Dubai Gold Souk, was Ghungroo's first export logo: ₹2.9 crore signed, a GCC expansion worth an estimated ₹9 crore behind it, and a contracted go-live of 14 December 2026. And Lakeer, better funded since its own raise, had begun quoting fixed-price implementations that Ghungroo could not match under the 2024 decision. Lajwanti Jewels Retail, a fifty-store Gujarat chain, had left for Lakeer in June, citing implementation time.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In March 2026 Ghungroo signed Gharana Jewellers Group — 140 stores across Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka, ₹4.2 crore of annual contract value, the largest deal in the company's history and 42 per cent of it recognised against implementation milestones rather than subscription. The statement of work was written by the sales desk with Gharana's group CIO over four weeks; no product manager saw it before signature. Sunayana, who had joined as Vice-President of Product only in January, did not know then that this was unusual. She learned in May that it was normal.

In April she assigned the rollout to Ishita Barua, a senior PM in Jaipur with the team's best implementation record. Through April and May, Ishita's status notes turned from crisp to defensive. Sunayana's response was to raise the Gharana line in the Thursday roadmap review each week, asking in front of the whole function what had moved. She believed she was holding a standard. In June she recorded in her own notes that Ishita had “a judgement problem: she takes every change request as a commitment.”

In parallel, Harshvardhan Doshi — principal PM in Bengaluru, architect of the scheme engine, the only person who understood the Gulf VAT work Gauhar required — came through his second 360 with rising scores and worsening prose. Two PMs asked to move off his pod in the same fortnight, and a senior designer in Noor Jehangir's Berlin team resigned in July, naming Harsh's review style on her way out. Sunayana met Harsh on 12 June for fifty minutes, and left believing she had delivered clear corrective feedback.

Three things have since turned out to be wrong. First, the meeting. Sunayana's notes from 12 June, retrieved on Friday for the calibration file, record four sentences of praise, one beginning “the only thing I'd watch is…”, and an agreed action about hiring. Harsh's written recollection, submitted to HR in September, is that the conversation was about his promotion track. Both records are accurate. Only one is feedback.

Second, the index. In July, Pallavi Ghatge in Toronto shipped a PM health index built from ticket and cycle-time data (Exhibit 2). Sunayana used it to sort her team in August; it ranked Harsh first, Ishita last. It counts artefacts in the product tracker, and the Gharana configuration work Ishita does lives in the implementation tracker, which the index does not read.

Third, the leavers. HR's exit records list “manager fit” against both PMs who left Harsh's pod (Exhibit 5). An uncirculated pulse survey run three weeks later contains a verbatim from a departing PM describing Harsh as the most useful manager she had had at Ghungroo, and the Thursday review as the reason she left. Policy forbids matching verbatims to individuals.

Figure 1 — Thirty months, two of which Sunayana was present for.

5. The people

Harshvardhan Doshi, Principal Product Manager, Bengaluru — built the scheme and valuation engines; the only person who can hold the Gauhar go-live. Position: the org is slow because nobody says what is actually wrong in reviews, and he says it. Incentive: a Director promotion that has slipped twice, and a competing conversation with Lakeer that two people know about. Not saying: he believed after 12 June that he was already on the track, and has never once been told, in words he recognised as criticism, that his conduct in reviews is a problem.
Ishita Barua, Senior Product Manager, Jaipur — owns the Gharana rollout. Position: she is executing a scope she did not write, against 61 change requests Gharana believes it was sold. Incentive: she wants off Gharana and into platform, and knows a low rating closes that door. Not saying: she asked twice in April for the statement of work to be reopened, was told by the sales desk that the client relationship could not absorb it, and did not escalate because the only forum in which Gharana was ever discussed was the Thursday review.
Devansh Kalita, Product Manager, Guwahati (remote) — two years in, the person Sunayana has invested the most coaching hours in. Position: he has improved and can show it. Incentive: he is the cheapest PM on the roster at ₹31 lakh. Not saying: one of the two upward-feedback comments is his, he assumes Sunayana can work out which, and he interviews elsewhere on Wednesday.
Noor Jehangir, Head of Design, Berlin — lost a senior designer in July. Position: Harsh's behaviour is worse than any score shows, because those most affected rate him politely and leave. Incentive: she is fighting for design headcount in the same calibration and needs the attrition attributed to something other than her own management. Not saying: she has never given Harsh feedback directly either, having concluded it was Sunayana's job.
Cheryl Fonseca, Customer Success Lead, Singapore — owns Gauhar and the Gharana escalation. Position: Ishita is the most reliable person on the account and the delay is entirely scope-driven. Incentive: her retention number depends on Gharana renewing in March. Not saying: she asked Harsh twice to review Ishita's configuration work, and both times he rewrote it instead.
Vikram Seshadri, Head of Sales, Americas, New Jersey — wrote the Gharana scope with the India desk. Position: nothing should be done to Harsh before 14 December, and the change requests are ordinary client behaviour. Incentive: his commission on the GCC expansion is booked against a December go-live. Not saying: he has already promised Gauhar that Harsh will personally run their Dubai cutover week.
Pallavi Ghatge, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto — built the PM health index. Position: it measures throughput in one system and was never meant for individual evaluation. Incentive: it is her visible contribution of the year and is cited in the Series C data room. Not saying: she told Sunayana so in a one-line Slack reply in August that Sunayana acknowledged with a thumbs-up and did not read.
Farida Kotwal, People Partner, Hyderabad — runs calibration. Position: a downward deviation from the prior year's rating requires a documented feedback history, and for Harsh there is none. Incentive: an audit-clean cycle before diligence. Not saying: she thinks the function's real problem is that its manager holds performance conversations in a group forum, and she cannot find a way to say so to a VP.

7. Voices

“I'm not going to pretend a spec is fine when it isn't. If that makes reviews uncomfortable, the alternative is we ship something a jeweller finds at 9 p.m. on Dhanteras.”

Harshvardhan Doshi, product review, 11 September

“Sixty-one change requests. Forty-nine of them were promised before I existed on this account. I have asked three times for someone to tell Gharana no. Instead I get asked every Thursday, in front of everyone, what moved this week.”

Ishita Barua, email to Sunayana Rao and Cheryl Fonseca, 16 September

“Do not touch Harsh before 14 December. I don't care what the 360 says. Gauhar bought him.”

Vikram Seshadri, direct message to Sunayana Rao, 22 September, 02:10 IST

“Please don't rank people with it. It reads one tracker. Ishita's entire year lives in the other one.”

Pallavi Ghatge, Slack, 14 August — acknowledged with a thumbs-up, no reply

“If you want to rate him below last year, I need to see where he was told. A one-line 'the only thing I'd watch' in your own notes is not where he was told.”

Farida Kotwal, calibration prep call, 25 September

“I have watched you coach Devansh for a year and I have never seen you do it anywhere except a room with eight other people in it. He's improved. He's also applying elsewhere.”

Noor Jehangir, video call, 26 September

8. The options as Sunayana sees them

A. Hold the line on Harsh. Rate him at “meets”, defer the promotion, and deliver written feedback on conduct in reviews on Monday. It tells the function that how results are produced counts. It also rates a man down on a record Farida says does not exist, in a week when Lakeer is talking to him, before a ₹2.9 crore go-live Vikram has promised he will run.
B. Promote Harsh, move the people around him. Treat the pod departures as fit, give the slot to the strongest producer, and put juniors elsewhere. Defensible on output. It also spends the only slot on the person whose rater response fell from eleven of twelve to seven of thirteen, and answers Noor's leavers with a seating chart.
C. Reclassify Ishita's year as scope, not judgement. Rate to “meets”, move her to platform in October, and escalate the scope to Seenu as a commercial problem. Probably fairer. It also hands the account to someone new weeks before the Diwali freeze, concedes ₹1.6 crore of stalled recognition into diligence, and tells the sales desk that scoping without product carries no cost.
D. Ask Farida for a two-week extension. Rebuild the evidence: pull implementation data into the index, commission proper verbatims, then rate. Honest about what she does not know. It also misses the cycle, leaves Devansh's rating open the week of his final round, and reaches the 9 October diligence call as a function whose manager cannot grade nine people.

She had written these four out on Friday and had not been able to choose. What she had not written down was the possibility that all four were the same option in different clothes: four ways of deciding what to file about other people, in a year whose one documented fact is that she had not had a single private conversation in which anything difficult was said. Exhibits 2, 3 and 5 all measure her reports. None measures the forum in which her reports were told how they were doing.

9. The deadline and the constraints

Calibration locks at 6 p.m. IST on Monday, 28 September. Downward ratings require a documented feedback history; there is one funded promotion slot and no headcount for backfill until the Series C closes. Gharana's phase 3 cannot start before 20 November, placing the recovery of ₹1.6 crore inside the same quarter as the Gauhar cutover, which carries ₹35 lakh of liquidated damages if it slips past 31 December. Granth Capital's diligence includes a management-quality session on 9 October, at which product attrition, currently 22 per cent annualised, will be raised. Harsh's competing conversation, if it is real, has its own timetable, which Sunayana does not know. Devansh's final round is Wednesday. And the verbatims that would tell her most about Harsh were deleted in August.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Reconcile Exhibits 2, 3 and 5. Which would you allow into a calibration room, and what would you require before using any of them to describe a person?
  2. On 12 June, Sunayana believed she gave Harsh corrective feedback; the notes show praise with one hedged clause. What would have had to be different in that fifty minutes for Harsh to have heard a correction — and whose obligation was it to check that he had?
  3. Ishita, Harsh and Devansh each need something different from Sunayana in the same week, and what serves one signals something unwanted to the others. Sequence the three conversations and state what each is for.
  4. Sunayana reads Harsh as a conduct problem and Ishita as a judgement problem; Cheryl, Pallavi and Farida each dispute part of that. What would change her mind, and what would it cost her to be seen changing it?
  5. Two of nine reports say their manager's feedback happens in public. How should Sunayana receive that, given that acting on it visibly this week would look like a response to her own grading, and that she does not know — and perhaps should not try to learn — who wrote it?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Sunayana file by 6 p.m., which invitations does she send, and what does she say on 9 October when Granth Capital asks her to account for 22 per cent attrition in a nine-person function?

At eleven she closed the calibration file without saving and opened the three drafts again. Harsh's was titled “15 mins”. Ishita's was titled “Gharana — and you”. Devansh's had no title at all. Outside, the last of the visarjan traffic worked its way down towards the tank bund, and somewhere below, a drum. She read Farida's sentence once more — a one-line 'the only thing I'd watch' is not where he was told — and understood that whichever box she ticked by six the next evening, the year she was grading was one in which nobody, including her, had been told anything they could act on. What she did not know was whether that made Monday easier or impossible.
