Coaching and Feedback: The Intervention With a Bimodal Effect

Feedback is not a communication skill. It is a behavioural intervention whose measured effects run in both directions, and the expert's first task is predicting which direction this conversation will run.

1. Two managers, two rooms, September 2026

On 8 September 2026, Kavitha Ranganathan, VP of Product at Raunak Field Robotics in Chakan, outside Pune, was seven weeks from a deadline she could not move. Raunak built autonomous warehouse robots and the software that ran them, on a firmware train that shipped four times a year and locked on 30 October. Her problem had a name: Devansh Kulkarni, her strongest customer-facing group PM, who on 14 July told a Kochi cold-chain customer that multi-aisle handoff would be in the January train. It was neither on the train nor sized. Sunita Rao, the firmware lead, had replanned twice for promises made in rooms she was not in, and a ₹2.4 crore renewal rested on a date no engineer had agreed. Kavitha had raised this in April and in June, in general terms; both times Devansh agreed, thanked her, and continued. She was beginning to suspect the problem was not his listening but her own asking.

In Gurugram, on 22 September, Arvind Pillai opened a 360 review he did not want to read. Arvind ran product at Nishkarsh Underwriting Systems, an enterprise platform Indian general insurers used to price commercial property and marine risk; its newer line put a language model between broker submissions and the underwriter's screen, drafting a risk summary the underwriter accepted or edited. IRDAI-supervised customers adopt only what they can explain to their boards. The review was for Tanya Bhargava, who owned submission intake. Three customer underwriting heads rated her near the top, her squad liked her, her two peer PMs and the risk and compliance leads rated her near the bottom, citing reviews she left early and decisions taken without them. The composite, 3.6 out of 5, described nobody's experience of her. Sridhar Menon, his engineering counterpart, wanted the complaints documented before calibration on 6 October; Juhi Kaul, his design counterpart, wanted nothing written, since a file would push out the best hire in three years.

2. The idea, and the empirical fact that organises it

The terms are routinely conflated. Feedback is information about a specific past action, returned to whoever took it, letting them compare what they did against what they intended. Coaching is the longer practice of turning such information into changed judgement, using questions and not only statements, so the person acts well in a situation nobody anticipated for them.

The history runs through three moments. Kurt Lewin's National Training Laboratories, in the late 1940s, made it a practice to show a group its own process. Douglas McGregor's 1957 essay argued that the appraising manager was forced into playing God over another's worth, the origin of every attempt to separate development from judgement. The third should reorganise everything: Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis pooled 607 effect sizes, found that feedback raised performance on average by about a third of a standard deviation, and found that in roughly 38% of cases performance went down.

Fig. 1 — The Kluger–DeNisi distribution: mean positive and modest, left tail large and real. Feedback is a biased coin whose bias the giver sets.

That result is where the competent practitioner and the expert diverge. The competent practitioner learns a format and applies it consistently. The expert accepts that the average conceals two populations — conversations that move behaviour, and conversations that move attention from the task to the self — and treats the first decision as which population this one will join, declining the obvious form as a live option. The mechanism is attentional, and praise draws attention to the self as easily as criticism does. Four schools sit on that finding and disagree substantively.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Gate zero: predict the sign. Devansh has agreed twice and changed nothing, which is diagnostic: the failure is not informational. Either he does not believe the cost is real, or something rewards the behaviour more than Kavitha's disapproval discourages it — here, a sales organisation that celebrated him for unblocking deals. A third conversation about listening then lands in the left tail.

Gate one: instrument the behaviour before naming it. Kavitha defined something countable — not "over-promising," a disposition, but "naming a ship window for uncommitted scope" — and counted it across twelve forums she had notes on.

Table 2 — Raunak: uncommitted ship-window statements per forum.

1 May – 31 Aug12758%

Difference——36 points

A 36-point drop looks decisive and is not. The standard error of a difference in proportions is the square root of the sum of each proportion's variance over its sample size: 0.58 × 0.42 / 12 = 0.0203, 0.22 × 0.78 / 9 = 0.0191, and the square root of their sum is 0.198 — about 20 points. The shift is 1.8 standard errors: encouraging, not distinguishable from a good run. Resolving it cleanly needs twenty-five forums a side, most of a year here.

Here is the second-order effect that separates the expert: you cannot verify behaviour change on the timescale you must report on. The answer is to change what is measured — Kavitha moved to a weekly leading indicator, whether Devansh's pre-visit brief listed locked scope. Process compliance verifies the short run and outcome rates the long run; confusing them is how managers declare victory in three weeks.

Gate two: price both sides, including your own discomfort.

That is the whole quantitative treatment coaching has: a frame for whether to speak, and an error model for claiming it worked.

Gate three: separate the three things a receiver hears. Feedback arrives as three messages at once — appreciation, coaching, evaluation — and the receiver decides which they hear. Kavitha intended coaching; Devansh, told twice already, would hear evaluation. The expert names the register aloud and honours it: "This is not about your rating. I have been unclear with you twice, and I am going to be specific now."

Fig. 2 — Training teaches the amber box; the variance lives in the green ones.

4. The conditions, stated so they can be falsified

Is the gap an information gap? Feedback is the right instrument only when the person does not already know. Devansh fails it; his is an incentive problem wearing feedback's clothes, and the fix is structural. Tanya passes emphatically: she cannot know her peers experience her as absent, because nobody has put the peer view in front of her.

Can the receiver perform the different thing? Feedback naming a behaviour someone cannot yet produce converts into shame, the reliable route to the left tail. Devansh can obviously refrain from naming a date. Tanya's case is unclear: leaving a review at twenty minutes may be habit, or she may be carrying three accounts of work, in which case feedback about presence is about arithmetic she does not set.

Is there a next repetition, soon, under observation? Devansh has a customer forum most weeks; Tanya's peer interactions are continuous. Contrast a PM whose only repetition is annual planning: feedback given in October is a note to whoever they will be next August, and the deliberate-practice school would say it will not work.

Does trust already exist? It is a precondition, not a product of the conversation. Kavitha has it; five months of restraint bought goodwill even as it cost money. Arvind's is harder, because his material originates with Tanya's critics, and relaying another's judgement without having witnessed the behaviour is how managers spend trust they will later need.

Where is the idea actively misleading? When performance is a system property: telling a PM their cycle time is poor when the constraint is a shared release train teaches them you cannot distinguish them from their environment. When the organisation rewards the behaviour on purpose, as at Raunak. And when the real decision is a staffing one, since coaching someone a manager has already written off withholds the fact they need.

5. Hard edges: seams, regulation, two-sided products and AI

The mechanics assume the manager can see the behaviour; at scale they cannot, and the failures live at organisational seams. At Rozgaar Work Exchange, a Mumbai marketplace matching facilities and hospitality employers with shift workers, a PM owned worker-side liquidity and was outstanding on every metric on her scorecard: fill rate up, time-to-first-shift down. It did not show that her auto-accept default had raised employer no-show disputes by a third. On a two-sided product the behaviour needing feedback is visible only to the counterparty's PM, who does not write her review and escalates rather than telling her. Mature marketplaces answer with a standing cross-side review where each PM presents the other side's damage metric. What such firms say they have is a culture of directness; what they build is a ritual that removes the need for courage.

Regulation cuts differently. At Nazariya Care Systems, a Chennai company running clinical record infrastructure for hospital chains under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, any performance concern touching a privacy incident had to be documented. Managers therefore stopped saying anything informally, and feedback migrated into a channel written for the auditor rather than the recipient. Nazariya's fix was two channels: a documented one for anything with a compliance nexus, an undocumented one for craft, and managers trained to say which they were in. The boundary is judgement-dependent, and it beats a company where nothing unwritten is ever said.

Hardware breaks timeliness rather than visibility. At Raunak the consequence of a specification ambiguity surfaced at integration eleven weeks later, by which point the author had shipped three other things and the causal chain was contestable. Where latency exceeds a few weeks, experts give feedback on artefacts, not consequences: the spec review, not the field failure. AI-native products invert this into present-tense attribution ambiguity. When Nishkarsh's model understated a marine exposure and an underwriter accepted the draft, was that Tanya's acceptance interface, her evaluation set, or unpredictable model behaviour? Feedback given before that is disentangled teaches a PM that uncontrolled outcomes will be attributed to them, the lesson that stops good PMs taking risk on AI surfaces.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Agreement is the commonest false positive. The tell is a conversation that ends warmly, quickly and with thanks; Devansh did this twice. Gracious agreement is what a professional produces to end a conversation, so no objection means the receiver has not engaged enough to find the part they dispute. Experts are reassured by pushback, worried by gratitude.

The composite is the least informative statistic in a 360. The tell is a manager quoting an average; Tanya's 3.6 describes nobody. Averaging eleven views looks like triangulation, but when they are bimodal the between-group difference is the finding: the behaviour is situational, which has a cause you can name.

Specificity is evidentiary, not courteous. The tell is a sentence nobody could check against a calendar. Managers soften by generalising, "sometimes in customer meetings," and think themselves kind; in fact it invites "that's not what happens," and an undated claim is heard as being about character.

Delivering someone else's feedback spends trust you did not deposit. The tell is "some people have mentioned." Relaying looks conscientious, but it makes you author of a judgement you cannot defend, so the receiver discounts it and learns what you carry.

Praise can land in the left tail too. The tell is someone who worsens after public recognition. Praise aimed at the self, you are outstanding, degrades performance for the same reason self-criticism does; praise aimed at the task, the way you sequenced that migration held the release, does not.

The request must be smaller than the problem. The tell is a goal containing an abstract noun: ownership, presence, collaboration. Matching goal to concern feels proportionate, but change is verifiable only at the grain of one action, so the right ask of Devansh is "list locked scope in every pre-visit brief," not "be careful with commitments."

The manager's own receiving sets the ceiling. The tell is a team that gives its manager only procedural feedback, which looks like contentment. A manager who has never visibly changed anything in response has taught the team that the channel is decorative.

Written feedback is a different instrument, not the same one recorded. The tell is a manager who writes what they said. A note is reread by the receiver at their least generous, and by people who were not in the room, and cannot be qualified in real time. Experts write less than they say.

7. What actually differs by product type and stage, and what does not

Much said about context-dependence is decoration; the five-step conversation is the same for a consumer PM and an enterprise PM. Two things genuinely differ. Evidence latency. Consumer products supply shared near-real-time evidence, which anchors the situation step and tempts managers to leap from a metric to a verdict about a person. B2B evidence arrives late, filtered through account teams, often as one escalated anecdote, so the situation step is harder and more often wrong. Hardware is worse. AI products have abundant evidence and contested attribution. Who witnesses the behaviour. On platforms and marketplaces the witness sits in another reporting line, so the manager's information is structurally second-hand.

Stage changes the failure mode, not the method. At fifteen people feedback is continuous, undocumented and usually adequate; the risk is that a founder's offhand remark carries the weight of a verdict. Between fifty and three hundred the characteristic failure appears: managers who once spoke in the moment now save it for a new review cycle, producing exactly the dense retrospective conversation the cycle was meant to prevent. At several thousand, the apparatus that firms such as Infosys and TCS built to keep judgement consistent solves calibration and introduces a new problem: standardised written feedback is optimised for defensibility. What stage changes is which step the organisation quietly destroys.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Nishkarsh: decomposing the 360. Arvind stopped reporting Tanya's composite and looked at the structure instead.

Table 4 — Nishkarsh: Tanya's 360 by rater group, five-point scale.
Rater groupnMeanRecurring content
Customer underwriting heads34.67Understands loss ratios
Own squad44.25Clear priorities; protective
Peer PMs22.50Skips joint planning
Risk and compliance leads22.00Decides alone; leaves reviews early
Weighted composite113.64Nobody's experience

The weighted mean is (3×4.67 + 4×4.25 + 2×2.50 + 2×2.00) ÷ 11 = 3.64. The 2.67-point gap between extreme groups is the actual data. Arvind read it as Tanya optimising for fast-signal parties while starving slow-signal ones — a rational response to her environment, whose fix had to include changing what she was measured on. He asked Sridhar and Juhi each for one dated incident they would stand behind: Sridhar produced two, Juhi none.

Raunak: the intervention that worked and could not be proven. Kavitha delivered the conversation on 15 September, naming the Kochi visit, quoting Devansh's sentence, showing the replan log, then asking what made a date feel necessary in that room. His answer — that the account director had told him a date would close the renewal — located the cause outside him and turned her next action from coaching into escalation. The rate fell from 58% to 22%, which is 1.8 standard errors and unproven; she reported the process change and wrote that the outcome would not be legible before mid-2027.

Rifaqat Retail Cloud: the programme that failed. Rifaqat, a Jaipur company selling storefront software to mid-market retailers, decided in 2025 to build a feedback culture by mandate: each of its 46 PMs and designers would write two peer notes a week in a tool visible to both parties and to managers.

Table 5 — Rifaqat: the mandated programme and its redesign.
PeriodNotesShare datedPM attrition
Month 133841%9%
Month 219122%14%
Month 3629%21%
Month 14, redesigned7178%8%

Volume fell 82% in three months, but the damaging number is specificity, down from 41% to 9%: under a quota the cheapest compliant note is a vague positive, so the mandate selected for precisely the content that does nothing. Worse, two PMs found that a permanent, manager-readable channel was a good place to build a record against a rival, which taught everyone that the tool was political. The recovery removed the quota, made notes visible only to the recipient, and required one field: the date and forum referred to. Specificity rose to 78% at a sixth of the volume. Fewer checkable notes changed behaviour; many unfalsifiable ones changed the weather.

9. Failure modes, with early signs and the cost of delay

Table 6 — Failure modes, earliest sign, catching question, cost of delay.
Failure modeEarly signQuestionCost of delay
Deferral to the cycleAn item is three weeks oldWhy is the oldest still here?One talk carries a quarter; receiver feels ambushed
Coaching an incentive problemAccepted twice, nothing changedWhat rewards this more than I discourage it?Good people follow incentives
Relaying unverified complaintYou say "some people feel"Who will put a name and date on this?Message and messenger discounted
Abstract development goalsA noun no camera recordsWhat would I see next Tuesday?Two cycles of agreement, no change
Writing instead of sayingThe note holds what was never said aloudWould I say this to their face?Trust loss is instant, usually final
Coaching in place of a role decisionYou cannot say what success looks likeIf they did all I asked, would I keep them?Months lost on a settled question

Every early sign there is observable in the manager's own artefacts — their list, their notes, their language — and none requires reading the receiver's mind. Diagnostics that depend on reading the other person fail where they matter most.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The suppressionist position. Buckingham and Goodall argue critical feedback should be largely abandoned, and the evidence is strong: a majority of the variance in one person's rating of another reflects the rater's own scale, and the 38% left tail fits an intervention that often backfires. For this to be wrong, the behaviours that destroy teams would have to be invisible to strengths-focused attention — which both our cases suggest, since no amount of praising Devansh's instinct surfaces the replan cost.

The candour position. Withheld feedback, its practitioners argue, is the manager's cowardice priced as the employee's comfort, and the cost compounds. The evidence is the long tail of people who learn at exit interviews what they could have fixed years earlier, plus Table 3. For this to be wrong, the binding constraint would have to be capability or context rather than information — and for Devansh it demonstrably was.

The documentation position. HR leaders and large-company operators argue that what is not written and standardised is neither fair nor defensible, and they have the better of the fairness evidence: informal feedback is measurably vaguer and more personality-focused when given to women and to second-language speakers. For this to be wrong, writing would have to destroy more candour than standardisation recovers — what Nazariya observed, and what Rifaqat's month-three numbers show. No synthesis reconciles the three; a manager chooses which error to make, and says which.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this gives well-structured feedback promptly. Someone who has internalised it spends more time deciding whether and how to speak than speaking, and can name which of Fig. 1's populations they expect to join. They instrument first, so the opening sentence carries a number or date that survives the receiver's best objection. They hear agreement as a warning, and close by asking the receiver to say back, with a date, what they are changing. They treat their own receiving as the system's constraint: they can point to something they changed because a report told them to, and the team can point to it too. The signature of mastery is not the quality of any one conversation; it is that almost nothing in their team is more than three weeks old.

12. What each of them decided

Kavitha concluded that a third feedback conversation was the wrong instrument, and delivered it anyway in changed form. She made one dated process ask — locked scope listed in every pre-visit brief — and took the incentive conflict to sales leadership as her problem, not his. She wrote nothing in his file. The information test had failed, so the conversation's job was to establish that she now knew the cause; the structural fix belonged at her level.

Arvind declined both positions handed to him. He did not open a documented file, as Sridhar wanted, because two verifiable incidents and a bimodal 360 make an indefensible file. He did not leave it unsaid, as Juhi wanted, because Tanya passed the information test cleanly. He showed her the decomposition rather than the composite, gave her Sridhar's two dated incidents with Sridhar in the room to own them, and changed one objective so the slow-signal stakeholders appeared in what she was measured on. He told Sridhar that recurrence after a named date would bring documentation, and put that date in writing to Sridhar, not Tanya.

Question 1. Kavitha judged Devansh's problem an incentive conflict, not an information gap. Suppose it is instead a capability gap: he cannot hold a customer's pressure without conceding. What in her evidence would look different, and what intervention follows?

Question 2. Arvind acted on Sridhar's dated incidents and discarded Juhi's undocumented concern. Is he rewarding paperwork over judgement, and how should a manager weigh a respected colleague's unevidenced read?

Question 3. The three positions cannot all be honoured. For your own team, which error would you rather make, and what would you tell your reports about the choice?

13. Going deeper

  • Building trust with teams — the precondition test is binding; without it, this is technique without standing.
  • Managing product managers — coaching one report is not building a team where peers do it.
  • Mentoring and being mentored — feedback without authority behaves differently.
  • Influence without authority — Arvind's problem was refereeing peers, not reviewing a report.
  • Conflict and disagreement — the seam rituals work only if the cross-side talk survives a dispute.
  • Psychological safety and team health — why the same words move one team and sink another.
  • Negotiation for PMs — the incentive conflict Kavitha escalated is negotiated, not coached.
  • Working in diverse and global teams — the fairness evidence bites hardest across languages.
  • What makes a great PM — every feedback conversation implies a standard; naming it keeps talk on craft.

Figures are illustrative reconstructions. Raunak Field Robotics, Nishkarsh Underwriting Systems, Rozgaar Work Exchange, Nazariya Care Systems and Rifaqat Retail Cloud are fictional; named regulators, statutes and firms are market context only.

Qatra Agri Systems: The Feedback Before the QBR

1. Opening

Tuesday, 19 August 2026. Baner, Pune. Karan Deshmukh, Group Product Manager at Qatra Agri Systems, read Priya Raghavan's message on the ops channel a second time before replying: "Nine hundred acres in the red blocks, Karan. This isn't a scheduling bug. This is a call Tanvi made and didn't tell any of us." Outside, the monsoon had eased into a drizzle that had already grounded three drone sorties that morning. In four days, on Saturday the twenty-third, Karan would sit in Nagpur across from Ramdas Bhoyar, chairman of the Vidarbha Cotton & Soy Growers' Federation, whose eighteen thousand member-farmers generated ₹9.2 crore of Qatra's annual revenue and whose three-year contract came up for renewal that week. Before that meeting, Karan had a harder one to have first — with Tanvi Kulkarni, the associate product manager who had built the scheduling engine that had just let the federation down, and who did not yet know how much Karan had learned.

2. Company background

Qatra Agri Systems sold drone spraying and crop-health imaging as a service, not as a product a farmer could buy outright. Founded in Nagpur in 2018 by two engineers who had left ISRO's remote-sensing programme, it moved its head office to Pune in 2021 as it professionalised, while keeping its largest operations base in Nagpur, close to Vidarbha's cotton and soybean belt. By the 2026 kharif season Qatra flew sixty-four DGCA-certified drones and a hundred and forty remote pilots certified under the Drone Rules, 2021, covering roughly forty-six thousand acres a season across Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Punjab. Its pitch to a farmer producer organisation was simple: a drone sprayed twelve acres an hour against a labourer's half-acre, at lower pesticide volumes, and the Kisan Drone scheme reimbursed up to half the cost, which made the economics work for growers who could never buy a drone themselves. The market was crowding fast: Garuda Aerospace and IoTechWorld Avigation, both better capitalised, bid aggressively for the same federations. Qatra's edge, Karan liked to say, was that its scheduling software actually worked in the field — it could re-route a fleet around a sudden squall without a human dispatcher on the phone all day. Tanvi had written most of that software herself.

3. The situation

The trouble had started three weeks earlier, when pink bollworm surged early across several blocks in the federation's northern talukas. Qatra's agronomy partner flagged the outbreak as high-severity, meaning those blocks needed spraying within forty-eight hours of a farmer's request. Tanvi, who had spent the previous quarter earning Karan's praise for lifting average acres-sprayed-per-drone-per-day — the efficiency number Qatra reported to investors — had quietly changed the scheduling algorithm's weighting two weeks before the outbreak, favouring route efficiency over farmer-reported severity. She had not asked Priya's team to review the change, and had not asked Marcus D'Souza, Qatra's data scientist in Toronto, whether his spray-efficacy model — built to flag when severity should override efficiency — still applied. Marcus had emailed her on 3 August warning the change would delay high-severity blocks in exactly this scenario; Tanvi replied she would "keep an eye on it" and did not escalate. By 15 August, roughly nine hundred acres in high-severity blocks had been sprayed four to six days late. Several farmers reported worsening pest damage; the federation chairman called Qatra's Nagpur office directly, and word reached Wei Ling Tan, Qatra's Singapore-based customer-success lead, before it reached Karan. When Priya raised the missed service levels in the shared ops channel on 17 August, Tanvi replied publicly that the numbers were "still within monthly tolerance" and that she would "handle the client conversation" herself — a reply that troubled Karan more than the miss itself, the same instinct to centralise and deflect he had watched build in her for months without naming it directly.

4. The people

Tanvi Kulkarni — Associate Product Manager, Nagpur. Built Qatra's scheduling engine from a spreadsheet into production software in under two years, the most technically capable PM on the team. Wants to be trusted with bigger calls, and reads any second-guessing as a vote of no confidence in her judgment.
Priya Raghavan — Engineering Lead, Bengaluru. Shipped the change at Tanvi's request without a design review, on Tanvi's word that it was low-risk. Wants a process where engineering can push back on a PM's call before it reaches farmers, and wants Karan to say so plainly.
Marcus D'Souza — Data Scientist, Toronto. Built the severity-override model specifically to prevent this failure. Wants his warnings to carry consequence rather than sit logged and forgotten, and is losing confidence that Qatra's product function acts on data the way it claims to.
Wei Ling Tan — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Owns the federation relationship end to end and needs, by Thursday, a credible account of what went wrong — one she can give Ramdas Bhoyar without contradicting whatever Tanvi tells him separately.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — High-severity block spraying performance, Vidarbha federation, August 2026

Contract value at stake: ₹9.2 crore annual, three-year renewal. Figures from Qatra ops and pilot logs; farmer damage claims are self-reported and under joint verification with the agronomy partner.

Exhibit 2 — Warning signals in the three weeks before the QBR

Exhibit 2 shows the pattern Karan must respond to: four separate signals, from three time zones, each answered by Tanvi alone rather than brought to him.

Exhibit 3 — Eighteen days from the scheduling change to the renewal meeting; Karan's window to act is under four days.

6. The options

A. Put it in writing, ahead of the QBR

Karan documents the missed service levels and the unescalated warnings in a note to Tanvi, copying HR, setting clear expectations before Saturday. This creates a record that protects Qatra if the pattern continues, and removes ambiguity. Its cost: a copied-in message lands as a verdict, not a conversation — Tanvi may read it as punitive, disengage before the QBR, or leave Karan to face the client without the person who best understands the failure.

B. A private, specific coaching conversation — today

Karan meets Tanvi alone, describes the situation, the behaviour and its impact in concrete terms — the changed weighting, the unescalated warnings, the public deflection — without attacking her competence, and asks her to help design both the fix and her own role at the QBR. This draws on two years of trust to make the feedback land as correction rather than rejection, and keeps Qatra's best technical PM engaged in solving the problem she caused. Its cost is time Karan barely has, and the risk that a still-defensive Tanvi does not hear it as intended.

C. Take over the client relationship, defer the conversation

Karan personally leads the QBR narrative, keeps Tanvi off the client call, and plans to address her judgment after the renewal is secured. This protects the ₹9.2 crore contract in the near term without adding pressure during the critical week. Its cost: Tanvi learns nothing changes if she avoids escalation, Priya and Marcus see their warnings go unanswered again, and Karan quietly absorbs a client-facing role that is not sustainably his.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What evidence shows Tanvi was optimising for the wrong metric, and what made it easier for her not to flag the risk once Marcus warned her on 3 August?
  2. If Karan chooses Option B, how would you word the specific behaviour he needs to name — situation, behaviour, impact — so Tanvi hears it as correctable, not as a character judgment?
  3. Look at Exhibit 2. What does each stakeholder — Priya, Marcus, Wei Ling — need from Karan's decision, and how does their distance from Nagpur shape what they saw and when?
  4. With four days until the QBR, how should Karan sequence the feedback conversation against the client-facing plan Wei Ling needs — and does Tanvi have a role at the QBR itself?

8. A note for the learner

Coaching and feedback exist to change behaviour, not to record blame — and feedback lands only where trust already exists between the two people in the room. Karan and Tanvi have two years of that trust; the case asks whether he spends it well in the four days he has left. Option A is defensible as a record-keeping instinct, but it substitutes documentation for the conversation that changes what Tanvi does next, and a copied-in note spends trust rather than draws on it. Option C avoids the conversation altogether, protecting the deal this week at the cost of teaching Tanvi that escalation is optional — the opposite of what someone being readied to manage other PMs needs to learn.

The stronger path is B, and it works only if Karan separates the person from the behaviour. He names the situation (the unreviewed weighting change), the behaviour (deciding alone, then deflecting questions instead of escalating), and the impact (₹30 lakh in farmer-claimed losses, a ₹9.2 crore renewal at risk) — without attacking a competence the case shows is real. He then gives her a concrete way to act differently at once: co-own the fix, and stand beside him, not behind him, at the QBR, where owning the miss in front of Ramdas Bhoyar may do more for the federation's confidence than any polished excuse alone could. Candour about the behaviour, respect for the person, and a next step that lets Tanvi practise the change, not just hear about it — that combination is what separates coaching from feedback that merely records a failure.

Coaching and Feedback: Giving Feedback That Changes Behaviour

How do I give and receive feedback that changes behaviour — not feedback that merely gets said?

1. A review Meera Iyer cannot postpone again

On the morning of 24 September 2026, Meera Iyer, VP of Product at Ujaas Product Cloud, a Bengaluru-based working-capital platform that lets small manufacturers draw invoice-backed credit lines, opened the mid-year review template for Rohan Dsouza and closed it again without typing a word. Rohan owned the underwriting-decisioning module, which decided, in under four seconds, whether a ₹6-lakh invoice from a Coimbatore auto-parts supplier was creditworthy enough to advance against. He was smart, technically the strongest PM on her team of eleven, and increasingly the reason two engineers had asked to be moved off his squad. The review was due to HR by 3 October. Meera had eleven days.

The material facts were not in dispute. Rohan's squad had missed its last three sprint commitments by wide margins, a junior PM had grown visibly upset in a 1:1 with Meera after a design review Rohan ran, and Rohan's own self-assessment, submitted the previous week, described the quarter as "strong delivery against a difficult roadmap." Meera's dilemma was not whether something needed to be said, but what, exactly, to say, in what order, with what evidence, so that Rohan changed how he ran his squad rather than simply hearing his manager was unhappy with him. Get this wrong and she would either lose a genuinely talented PM to defensiveness, or keep him exactly as he was and lose two more engineers by December. Get it right and his technical strength would compound instead of corrode. Nobody outside the room would ever know how the conversation went, and the team's trajectory for the next year would be decided by it.

2. What coaching and feedback actually is

Feedback, precisely, is information about a specific past action, given to the person who took it, that lets them compare what they did against what they intended or what was needed. Coaching is the broader practice of using that information — plus questions, not just statements — to help someone build the judgement to act differently next time without being told exactly how. Feedback is a data point; coaching is a relationship that turns repeated data points into a changed pattern. Managers who only deliver feedback produce employees who wait to be told; managers who only coach without naming a concrete behaviour produce employees who feel vaguely unsettled but cannot say why.

The most widely taught structure for the feedback half of this pair is Situation–Behaviour–Impact, developed by the Center for Creative Leadership beginning in the 1970s and refined over the following two decades into the compact tool used in most corporate training today. It exists to solve one specific failure mode: feedback that arrives as a judgement about someone's character ("you're not collaborative") rather than a description of an event, which triggers defensiveness before the message is even parsed. SBI forces the giver to anchor in a specific situation, describe an observable behaviour, and state its impact, in that order, before any prescription follows. Layered on top is a second idea, popularised by Kim Scott's 2017 formulation of Radical Candor: the same words land completely differently depending on whether the receiver already believes the giver cares about them personally. The one sentence Meera could say in a meeting without sounding glib is this: feedback changes behaviour only when it is specific enough to be checked against the record and delivered by someone the recipient already trusts to be on their side.

Fig. 1 — The trust axis (care personally) and honesty axis (challenge directly). Both must be present for feedback to change behaviour; either alone fails, and the two failures fail differently.

3. The mechanics: what Meera actually has to do, in order

Practitioners describe SBI as three steps, but the version that produces changed behaviour has five, and the two most often left implicit are the first and the last. Step zero, invisible in every textbook summary, is establishing standing: has Meera, over the preceding weeks, done anything to show Rohan she is invested in his success specifically, not just his output? Without that, step one lands as an attack regardless of wording. Step one is choosing the situation: not "your squad's delivery" but "the sprint review on 15 September, when the checkout-eligibility story was pulled with two days left." Specificity here is evidentiary, not polite; a vague situation cannot be checked against memory and invites "that's not what happened."

Step two describes the behaviour using verbs a camera could have recorded — "you told Ananya, in front of the squad, that her estimate was unrealistic" — never adjectives a camera cannot capture, such as "you were dismissive." Step three states impact, ideally with a number: two engineers requested a move that quarter, completion dropped from near ninety percent to the sixties. Step four, the hardest and most often skipped, is stopping to ask what Rohan's account of the same situation is, before proposing anything — coaching treats the recipient as a source of information about causes, not just a target. Only then does step five arrive: a forward-looking request, checkable at the next 1:1, such as "when you disagree with an estimate, ask a question before stating a verdict."

4. The worked example: reading the sprint record before the conversation

Before Meera said anything to Rohan, she pulled the squad's actual delivery record, because "your team keeps missing sprints" is an opinion and a table of committed-versus-delivered story points is evidence. She looked at the four most recent two-week sprints.

SprintCommitted (pts)Delivered (pts)CompletionNote
Sprint 14322166%—
Sprint 15301963%—
Sprint 16281139%1-day payments-gateway outage
Sprint 17312065%—
Average30.317.858%Company baseline: 91%

Fifty-eight percent against a baseline of ninety-one is a 33-point gap, large enough that Meera's first instinct was to treat it as unambiguous. But Sprint 16 included a payments-gateway outage that consumed roughly a day and a half of capacity through no fault of Rohan's planning, so a fair reading has to isolate that noise first. Recomputing without Sprint 16: (21 + 19 + 20) divided by (32 + 30 + 31), or 60 delivered against 93 committed, gives 65%. That is the second pass — the input changed from "four sprints" to "three, controlling for the outage" — and the answer moved from 58% to 65%, still 26 points under baseline. The arithmetic mattered because it told Meera the pattern was real, not an artefact of one bad week, so the conversation could open with a number Rohan could not simply dismiss by pointing at the outage. Evidence that survives the recipient's best counter-argument is the only evidence worth opening with.

5. Eight distinctions a learner has to hold onto

Feedback is not the same as venting

Telling Rohan "this quarter felt chaotic" discharges Meera's frustration but gives him nothing to act on. The test is whether the sentence names a specific, repeatable behaviour he could recognise doing again; if it names only a feeling, it is venting wearing feedback's clothes.

Trust is a precondition, not a byproduct

Feedback lands only where trust already exists, built through consistent behaviour over time, not manufactured in the moment it is needed. A manager who has never invested in the relationship cannot borrow trust from the conversation itself.

Frequency beats intensity

A single high-stakes review, however well delivered, is a poor substitute for small corrections given close to the moment they happened. Waiting eleven days, as Meera had, concentrates a quarter's pattern into one conversation Rohan will experience as an ambush.

What SBI cannot tell you

The framework structures delivery; it does not diagnose cause. Rohan's behaviour could be arrogance, anxiety about seeming slow, or a habit learned from his first manager. SBI puts data on the table; only the question-asking half of coaching surfaces which it is.

Public correction and private feedback are not the same tool

Naming a mistake in front of the squad, even accurately, often converts a correctable behaviour into a defended identity, since an audience makes retreat feel like humiliation. Reserve the room for recognition, the closed door for correction.

Receiving feedback is a distinct, teachable skill

The instinct to explain or minimise on hearing criticism is nearly universal and has to be named as a skill in its own right — pausing, separating "is this true" from "how it was said" — not assumed to follow from good delivery.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In a consumer product organisation, feedback is often anchored to metrics on a shared dashboard — retention, activation, an adoption curve — which gives the "situation" step an objective anchor but also tempts managers to skip straight from a number to a verdict about the person. In a B2B organisation, evidence is thinner and slower — a lost renewal, an escalation forwarded weeks after the meeting that caused it — so the situation step has to work harder to stay specific rather than collapsing into "clients are unhappy with you." In a marketplace product, feedback has to separate which side's outcome was actually damaged, since optimising too hard for supply can look, from the demand side, exactly like negligence.

Company stage changes the mechanics more than the model. At an early-stage company with a handful of PMs, coaching happens constantly and informally, which builds trust quickly but risks never being repeated with rigor. At a company the size Ujaas Product Cloud was heading toward, with formal review cycles, the risk inverts: feedback gets saved for the scheduled conversation, precisely the pattern behind Meera's own backlog, and the fix is reintroducing small feedback between cycles.

7. Three mistakes that show up from the outside

The sandwich. Symptom: praise, the real point buried in the middle, then more praise. Misunderstanding: that softening protects the relationship, when the recipient remembers the praise and discounts the correction. Diagnostic: ask them, an hour later, to repeat back what they were asked to change.

Feedback as character verdict. Symptom: sentences using "you are" rather than "you did." Misunderstanding: that the goal is describing the person, not a changeable action. Diagnostic: check whether the sentence could be true of the recipient on their best day and their worst day equally — if so, it describes identity, not behaviour.

Feedback without a next step. Symptom: enthusiastic agreement in the room, nothing changes the following sprint. Misunderstanding: that naming the problem is the whole job. Diagnostic: check the notes a week later — no sentence starting "by [date], I will" means no real commitment was made.

Saving it for the formal cycle. Symptom, exactly Meera's own: silence, then one dense conversation carrying a quarter's unaddressed pattern. Misunderstanding: that a scheduled review is a more appropriate venue than the moment itself. Diagnostic: count how many raised behaviours are more than two weeks old — those should already have been said, informally.

8. What good looks like

Two days before the deadline, Meera scheduled thirty minutes with Rohan, not the formal slot but an unlabeled "quick sync." She named the 15 September sprint review and Rohan's exact words to Ananya, then stopped and asked how he remembered it. He said he had been worried the estimate would blow the sprint and had not realised how it sounded until he saw Ananya's face afterward. Meera showed him the three-sprint table, walked him through the outage adjustment herself so he could not dismiss it as unfair, and asked what he thought was driving 65% against baseline. They agreed on one checkable step — a clarifying question before responding to any estimate in front of the squad — reviewed at their next three 1:1s rather than at the next formal cycle.

9. What Meera decided, and two questions to sit with

Meera wrote the review as a description of what she had observed, what Rohan's account added to it, and one specific dated commitment, then scheduled three short follow-ups before the next formal cycle rather than waiting for it to arrive again. What she takes into the next quarter is that the evidence work — the sprint table, the outage adjustment, checking her account against Rohan's — took longer than the conversation itself, and that this was the correct ratio, not over-preparation. What she should study next is managing product managers, because coaching one report well does not yet tell her how to build a team where peer feedback, not just manager feedback, is the default.

Question 1. The last time you gave feedback that did not change anything, was the problem the structure of what you said, or the trust that was or was not already there before you said it?

Question 2. Think of a piece of feedback you are currently sitting on. What is the specific, dated commitment you would ask for if you said it today — and if you cannot name one, is it actually ready to be said?

People, Leadership & Organisation · Leadership & Team · How do I create clarity and energy without becoming the bottleneck?

Creating Clarity and Energy

Two rooms, two opposite failures

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, in Baner, Pune, Aruna Bhatt watched a decision get made for the third time. Bhatt is Principal Product Manager for device software at Mausam Grid Systems, whose GridSense controllers sit beside rooftop solar inverters at 430 industrial sites exporting to utilities such as MSEDCL and Tata Power under net metering. The Central Electricity Authority's revised connectivity standards take effect on 31 March 2027, and all 11,800 installed controllers must first demonstrate updated ride-through behaviour to a BIS-recognised laboratory whose queue runs nine weeks and whose test cycle costs ₹18 lakh. Firmware release 4.2 must therefore freeze on 13 January 2027 and never be reopened.

What went into 4.2 was settled on 14 July, settled again on 6 August, and reopened on 2 September by Harish Pai, head of channel sales, who wanted a Maharashtra net-metering report in the release. Ritwik Sen, director of firmware, had twice agreed to drop a latency fix and twice put it back, and Fatima Zaidi, of regulatory affairs, had said the same sentence in every meeting and watched it lose force. Nobody was confused in the moment; everybody drifted afterwards. Bhatt had no stalemate; she had a decision with a short shelf life.

Nine days later, Sabiha Ansari opened the board her teams used to ask her things, at Umeed Care Exchange in Gurugram — a two-sided marketplace of 9,200 home-care nurses in fourteen cities and 31,000 patient households, ₹268 crore of annualised transaction value on ₹41 crore of net revenue. Ansari directs eleven squads and sixty-eight engineers, and the board held thirty-one open items, each phrased as a question for her. Should the new auto-assignment model place a nurse without a coordinator confirming? Arnav Chaudhary, running supply, believed bad matches drive nurse churn; Lakshmi Prasad, running demand, wanted median fill under four hours; Dr Sameer Gokhale, the medical director, wanted a human in the loop for post-surgical cases.

Ansari was extraordinarily clear. For fourteen months she had been the single place where product intent was current, and everyone had learned to come to her rather than reason it out. Bhatt's decisions dissolved, Ansari's queued, and the failures are linked: almost everything a PM does to make decisions stick harder also routes more traffic through the PM.

Fig. 1 — The two canonical failures: agreement that will not hold still, and agreement that cannot be obtained fast enough. Most advice on this topic cures one and worsens the other.

The idea, and the argument it belongs to

Define the terms precisely, because loose definitions are why this skill is taught as temperament. Clarity is the condition in which everyone who must act holds the same, correct, current decision premises — not the same information, the premises: what was chosen, what ruled out, who owns the next move, and what fact would change the answer. Energy is the rate at which a group converts those premises into action without being chased. Both are properties of a system, not a personality, and both are measurable: clarity by whether independent people write the same sentence a fortnight later, energy by how much work starts unprompted.

The history predates product management. Mary Parker Follett argued in the 1920s that authority should follow the law of the situation; Herbert Simon's Administrative Behavior (1947) supplies the sharpest formulation available, that organisations coordinate by supplying decision premises to people who then decide locally, because no centre holds enough attention. Karl Weick added that organisations enact meaning retrospectively, which is why an unrestated decision acquires a new one, and Amy Edmondson's 1999 hospital study showed reported error rates rising with team safety: openness, not harmony, produces performance. Kim Scott (2017) named the interpersonal half and the sin of niceness; Tanya Reilly's 2018 essay named the labour, uncredited "glue work"; Donald Reinertsen (2009) supplied the physics, that decisions are a queue and queues behave non-linearly.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Decision rights (Simon; Cagan)"Persistent ambiguity is a defect in who decides what.""The PM should absorb it and reconcile meeting by meeting."
Glue work (Follett; Reilly)"Coordination is continuous labour: staff it, credit it, rotate it.""Good structure makes the glue unnecessary."
Candour and safety (Edmondson; Scott)"Most ambiguity is an unsaid sentence; kindness is saying it early.""Directness works whether or not people feel safe."
Motivation (Deci and Ryan; Amabile)"Energy is released by removing obstruction and showing progress.""Energy is an output the PM manufactures."
Flow and queueing (Reinertsen)"Latency has a number on it; utilisation above 0.8 is ruinous.""A fully-utilised decision-maker is efficient."
Tab. 1 — Five positions and the propositions that separate them. Decision-rights and glue-work disagree on whether the work should shrink to zero; the candour and safety literatures disagree about sequence.

Mechanics: raising the half-life, lowering the latency

Experts do two distinct things, and confusing them is the commonest error. The first is raising a decision's half-life: how long before those who must act have drifted into differing accounts of it. The second is lowering decision latency: how long a question waits to be answered. Bhatt has the first problem, Ansari the second, and several remedies trade off.

Half-life is measurable, and Bhatt measured it. After the 6 August meeting she asked the nine attendees, on day 3, day 17 and day 31, to write in one sentence what had been decided, and had a colleague score them blind: nine of nine, six of nine, four of nine. Fitting f(t) = e−t/τ gives τ = 17 ÷ ln(1.5) ≈ 42 days, predicting 48 per cent at day 31 against 44 observed; the half-life is 29 days. Confirming eight weeks out was therefore guaranteed to fail: at 56 days the model predicts 26 per cent agreement, three-quarters of the room arriving with a different decision in their heads and an honest belief that they are being consistent.

Fig. 2 — Bhatt's measured decay (red) against the sawtooth of a ninety-second restatement every fortnight (green). Reinforcement inside the half-life holds the floor near 70 per cent; outside it, the touch merely records the drift.

What raises τ? Four things, in descending order of measured effect at Mausam. Writing down what was not chosen and why, since "no latency fix in 4.2, because a re-test costs ₹18 lakh and nine weeks" is harder to reinterpret than the choice alone. Naming the falsifier, which turns later challenges into factual claims rather than preferences. Naming one owner per next step. And restating inside the half-life: ninety seconds inside an existing meeting, never a new one.

Latency obeys queueing arithmetic. Treat Ansari as a single server: requests arrive at λ a week, she clears μ a week, and the average wait is approximately W = 1 ÷ (μ − λ). Her capacity, net of immovable meetings, was about 34 against 31 arriving.

Requests/week (λ)Wait, working days (W)Open at any moment (λW)Idle cost per year
190.331.3₹10 lakh
250.562.8₹22 lakh
280.834.7₹37 lakh
311.6710.3₹83 lakh
335.0033.0₹2.6 crore
Tab. 2 — Capacity held at 34 a week; idle cost assumes each pending decision idles a quarter of an engineer-day per day of waiting, at ₹14,545 an engineer-day. The model is a caricature; the convexity is the lesson.

Read the table as a second-order effect almost nobody anticipates. Delegating 39 per cent of the traffic, from 31 requests to 19, cuts the average wait fivefold rather than by 39 per cent; adding two squads without changing the decision model pushes λ past 33 and the organisation seizes up for reasons nobody attributes to the hiring. Near saturation the server's experience is linear, the organisation's hyperbolic.

Every technique that makes a decision stick — being the author of the note, the restater, the arbiter of what it meant — also makes the PM the address to which the next question is sent.

Experts split the roles: authorship of the premise stays central, application of it is pushed down. Bhatt did not delegate what 4.2 was for; she delegated every judgement settleable by reading what 4.2 was for. Ansari published the constraint set — complaints under 0.9 per cent, no post-surgical auto-placement — and let squads decide inside it. Simon's formulation is to supply premises, not answers; the test is that a delegated decision is reviewable in retrospect without having been reviewable in advance.

When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

One: the work is interdependent enough that private clarity is insufficient. Test: can any team ship value without another changing something? At Mausam, no — firmware, cloud and regulatory are locked to a certification date; at Umeed, no — supply and demand are one transaction. Where squads genuinely have separate codebases and customers, the claim fails and this becomes over-engineering.

Two: the decision is reversible at a cost worth knowing. Where reversal is cheap, over-clarifying is waste: ship, watch, adjust. Mausam's freeze is the opposite — after 13 January, reversal costs ₹18 lakh and nine weeks and may breach the March date — while Umeed's threshold is reversible within a day. The common error is spending clarity effort evenly.

Three: the PM has standing enough that a written decision is believed. Bhatt passed this on technical ground and failed on commercial ground: Pai did not think she understood the Maharashtra channel, which is exactly why he reopened. Technique cannot manufacture credibility; it only spends it.

Four: the disagreement is about ends, not facts. Where people differ on a fact, get the fact. Where they differ on what the company is for — Chaudhary's retention against Prasad's fill time — no data closes it. The idea is actively misleading in one case: when the ambiguity is a bet the executives deliberately left open. Forcing closure there destroys option value, usually because ambiguity is uncomfortable for the PM rather than costly.

Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

Multi-product. Mahaul Workspace Systems, 1,400 people in Hyderabad, sells desk booking, visitor management and workplace analytics on one shared identity platform, and every real ambiguity in the company lives on that platform team's boundary, the only place three roadmaps meet. Mahaul's stated model is "empowered teams with clear ownership"; its actual model, after two quarters in which 40 per cent of platform capacity went to unplanned seam work, is a published contract of 1.5 platform-engineer-quarters per product, six weeks' notice, and anything beyond the quota negotiated with the other product leads present. Clarity at a seam is a standing negotiation with a price list, not an announcement.

Two-sided. Umeed cannot make one promise. "You will never be auto-assigned outside your skill band" and "median fill under four hours" are both clarity and they contradict at the margin. Expert practice is to publish which side yields under stress: Ansari's rule was that supply constraints bind first and demand promises flex, because an unstated precedence rule is resolved differently by every squad.

Regulated. At Manzil Payments Group in Mumbai, a payment aggregator authorised by the RBI and running on NPCI rails, the clearest sentence cannot be said externally until legal clears it: six working days at the median, nineteen at the ninetieth percentile. The expert move is two-layered: an internal premise stated today without hedging, an external commitment dated and openly provisional. Collapse the layers and you either freeze awaiting legal or retract in public.

Hardware plus software. When part of the system has a long irreversible cycle, the half-life must exceed the cycle time or the cycle is entered with a decision already dissolving. Bhatt's twenty-nine days against a nine-week lab queue is a mismatch goodwill cannot fix.

AI-native. Umeed's decision — auto-assign above 0.82 confidence — has a peculiar property: its referent moves. When Bhaskar retrains in November, 0.82 means something else, and a settled decision becomes unsettled without anyone reopening it. Mature teams therefore bind decisions to observable behaviour rather than model internals, and the eval suite becomes the clarity artefact.

What mature companies do, as against what they describe, deserves saying plainly: nearly all run a shadow reconciliation layer — a chief of staff, a business review, a programme manager with no authority and total information — and the PM's real skill is feeding it accurately rather than pretending the org chart resolves things.

Eight nuances that separate the expert

1. Clarity is premises, not information. The tell is a team that receives more context each week and still asks what it should do. The obvious reading — they need background — is wrong: context widens the choice set, premises narrow it. Experts ship the constraint, not the reading list.

2. Energy is subtraction. The tell is a team visibly energised twenty minutes into a kickoff and flat by Friday. That is not a motivation problem; something structural drains faster than the kickoff filled. Deci and Ryan imply you cannot inject energy into competent adults; Amabile supplies the one reliable source term, visible progress on meaningful work.

3. The bottleneck is convex. The tell is a PM reporting "slightly busier than last month" while three teams independently report being blocked. Small load increases produce large latency increases, and the server notices last.

4. Sequence matters between safety and candour. The tell is a manager proud of his directness whose team has not contradicted him in a quarter. Edmondson and Scott are quoted together but order differently: candour delivered into a team that does not feel safe arrives as verdict, not information.

5. Re-litigation is usually a decision-rights defect. The tell is the same question reopened by a different person each time. The obvious reading is weak documentation; the correct one is that ownership was never agreed, and each reopener sincerely believes they are within their rights — because they are.

6. Consensus-seeking is conflict avoidance in process clothing. The tell is a meeting ending with "let us take it offline" more than once a week. The offline conversation is where the decision happens, settled by whoever follows up hardest; the room's agreement was a measurement artefact.

7. The note must carry its own falsifier. The tell is a decision note that reads as a verdict with no line saying what would change it; such notes are reopened at about twice the rate, because a challenger has no legitimate way to be right except by reversing everything. A second tell is disagreement rising in the fortnight after writing starts: private divergence becoming public, the mechanism working.

8. Glue work must be rotated, and kindness expires. Reilly's tell is that the person everyone calls indispensable has the weakest promotion case, because their output is other people's throughput. The related tell is a hard sentence deferred to "after the release": it gets harder, the other party's sunk investment grows, and the conversation acquires a betrayal component it need not have had.

How it differs by product type and by stage

Some differences are real. In consumer products the half-life is short but reversal is cheap, so the equilibrium is frequent, lightly documented decisions. In B2B, as at Mausam, decisions are carried to customers by account teams and quoted back months later, so they must outlive a sales cycle. In enterprise they must also survive procurement and the customer's change control, and the falsifier line is often all that stops a roadmap slide becoming a commitment. On platforms the precedence rule — who yields — is the real decision; in hardware, irreversibility dominates; in AI products the decided object is non-stationary. Some differences are not real: kind-not-nice is invariant, as are the premise discipline, the falsifier and the named owner.

Stage shifts the balance rather than the technique. Below about thirty people the half-life is long because everyone overhears everything, and formal notes are wasteful. Between fifty and five hundred — both protagonists' companies — it collapses fastest, because the overhearing stops before the writing starts. Above a thousand, artefacts calcify and the skill inverts: deciding which decisions to kill, since a stale premise confidently held is worse than an acknowledged gap.

Three worked examples

Mausam: raising the half-life. Bhatt costed a reopening before arguing for anything. Each of the three consumed six senior people for seventy-five minutes plus three and a half engineering days of replanning: 22 person-hours and 10.5 engineer-days that quarter, annoying but affordable. The number that mattered came after the freeze — a scope change after 13 January means ₹18 lakh of re-test, a queue pushing certification past 31 March, and service credits of ₹40,000 per site per month across 430 sites, or ₹1.72 crore a month. Her single change was a written premise with an explicit not-list and falsifier, restated for ninety seconds every fortnight inside the existing Monday review. Agreement at day 30 rose from 44 to 81 per cent, implied τ from 42 to about 142 days, reopenings from three in eight weeks to one in twelve.

Umeed: lowering the latency. Ansari classified a month of her thirty-one weekly requests. Nine were genuine supply-demand trade-offs only she could make; twelve were applications of a premise she had set and never written down; ten were requests for permission from people who already had it. She published two pages — the precedence rule, the three behavioural bounds, and what each squad lead could decide unaided — and declined, visibly, to answer four questions in the second week. Arrivals fell to 19 a week, the average wait from 1.67 days to 0.33, and estimated idling cost from ₹83 lakh a year to ₹10 lakh, at a price of two poor squad decisions, both reversed.

Urvara Agri Systems: where it failed. Urvara, a Nashik agronomy platform serving 62,000 grape and onion growers on ₹96 crore of revenue, installed the full apparatus in early 2025: a decision log, a responsibility matrix, a Friday alignment forum. Re-litigation rose from 38 per cent of decisions reopened to 52, and median latency from 2.6 days to 4.2. Two causes, both instructive: the forum created a standing re-entry point, so no decision was load-bearing for more than five days, and the founder, Mahendra Salunkhe, kept reversing things in late-night messages, teaching everyone the log was decorative. Devyani Pawar, the head of product, had followed the literature and produced ceremony. Recovery took two quarters and three moves: a twenty-minute review in which only the named owner could reopen an item, and only by stating a new fact; a falsifier line on every note; and Salunkhe, once, publicly declining to reverse a decision he disagreed with. That restraint did more than the apparatus — re-litigation fell to 21 per cent, latency to 1.3 days — but the cost of the failed year was attrition of 19 per cent annualised, which took three quarters to hire back.

Failure modes and their early diagnostics

The recurring debate. Early sign: déjà vu in stand-up. Diagnostic: have three people separately write the decision in one sentence and score the match; below seven in ten it has lapsed. Caught late it surfaces as a missed irreversible date — ₹1.72 crore a month at Mausam.

The heroic bottleneck. Early sign: the PM feels indispensable and slightly flattered. Diagnostic: count decisions arriving against decisions closable per week; above 0.8 utilisation the firm is already paying. Caught late it looks like a team-quality problem — good people leaving because they cannot move — and is misdiagnosed as a hiring gap.

Ruinous niceness. Early sign: a hard sentence rehearsed and undelivered twice in one week. Diagnostic: what do I believe that this person has not heard from me? Caught late, the cost is someone else's wasted quarter plus a conversation that now includes betrayal.

Energy without direction. Early sign: high velocity and falling agreement on what the quarter is for — Umeed in August. Diagnostic: ask two squads what the company is optimising.

Where experts genuinely disagree

Structure versus labour. The decision-rights school holds that persistent glue work is evidence of broken org design, and points to well-bounded teams demonstrably needing less reconciliation. The glue-work school holds that interdependence is irreducible in any complex product, and that denying it pushes the work onto whoever is conscientious — disproportionately women, invisibly. The structural view fails if coordination load stays constant as a well-designed org grows; the labour view fails if a boundary redesign removes the need without displacing it. Neither has a clean measurement.

Write first or talk first. Memo cultures argue that writing exposes muddle speech conceals. High-context founding teams argue that it raises latency and formalises positions before they are ripe, converting explorable differences into defended ones. The falsifier for the first is a team whose documents demonstrably slowed good decisions; for the second, a team whose verbal agreements survive a quarter.

Is energy a leadership output at all? Self-determination theory says no: competent adults arrive motivated and leaders can only remove obstruction. Much of the leadership-development field says yes, citing the effect of framing on discretionary effort. Amabile's progress principle sits between, the strongest evidence that something a leader controls — making progress visible — changes both affect and output.

The open question: the right re-litigation rate. Everyone treats reopening as waste, yet a firm with zero reopenings in a volatile market is committed to stale premises, and where the underlying artefact drifts, decisions arguably should expire. Urvara's 52 per cent was pathological and its 21 clearly better. Whether the optimum is 5 per cent or 25, and how it varies with reversal cost and volatility, no evidence known to this author settles.

What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this writes better decision notes. Someone who has internalised it does three things differently. They instrument: they know their team's decision half-life and their own utilisation because they have counted, and calibrate effort to reversal cost rather than spreading it evenly. They say the hard sentence within days rather than weeks, paired with the reasoning and the falsifier, so the other person can disagree with the argument rather than with them. And they measure success by their own absence, wincing when a team says "we waited to check with you." The competent practitioner builds a system that runs through them; the expert builds one that runs without them.

What Aruna and Sabiha decided

On 11 September, Bhatt held a forty-minute meeting with one named decision on the board and left with a one-page premise: 4.2 contains the CEA-mandated behaviour and nothing else; the latency fix and the Maharashtra report ship in 4.3 in May; the only fact that changes this is a confirmed movement of the 31 March date. She told Pai directly, in front of the others, that his report was a good idea asked for at a bad time and that she would not put ₹1.72 crore a month of exposure behind it, then gave him a dated slot rather than a vague promise.

On 24 September, Ansari published two pages and answered four fewer questions than she was asked. Auto-assignment went live in Tier-1 cities under three behavioural bounds, post-surgical cases excluded at Dr Gokhale's insistence, and each squad lead was told in writing what they could decide alone. She disagreed with two of the month's squad decisions and let both run.

For discussion: Bhatt bought clarity by cutting scope and Ansari by cutting her own involvement — which is better protected against the failure that hit Urvara? If the optimal re-litigation rate is unknown, on what basis should a PM judge a reopening to be discipline rather than learning? And at what exposure does the arithmetic of delegation stop working, known beforehand rather than after?

Going deeper

What makes a great PM places clarity and energy last among the core skills, because it presumes the judgement the others build. Influence without authority supplies what this page assumed, the credibility that makes a premise believed. Conflict and disagreement goes where this page stopped: the dispute about ends that no premise closes. Negotiation for PMs is the seam skill Mahaul's contract is made of. Building trust with teams is the precondition for a hard sentence landing as information, and psychological safety and team health is Edmondson's evidence base for why candour sequenced wrongly makes things worse. Coaching and feedback is how the kind-not-nice sentence changes behaviour instead of merely being accurate.

People, Leadership & Organisation · Leadership & Team · How do I create clarity and energy without becoming the bottleneck?

Creating Clarity and Energy

On Thursday 24 September 2026, Meera Iyer, Group Product Manager at Yantra Systems, a Bengaluru maker of shop-floor scheduling and quality software for discrete manufacturers, opened her calendar and found the same three names on it for the eleventh straight working day: Rohan Deshmukh, VP Engineering; Kabir Anand, VP Sales; and Priya Nair, VP Customer Success. They had been arguing by email since 10 September, and the argument had not moved an inch.

The facts were not in dispute. Yantra's scheduling engine, the core module that plans which machine runs which job in a factory, was showing its age: it generated roughly 140 support tickets a month, at an average resolution cost of ₹3,200 each, and Rohan wanted five sprints of his four-person squad to rebuild it before the debt compounded further. Kabir wanted three sprints from the same squad, immediately, to build a customised sequencing rule that Ashok Leyland's plant team had made a condition of renewing — a ₹4.2 crore account, about 9 percent of Yantra's ₹46 crore annual recurring revenue, due to lapse in six weeks. Priya wanted neither: a freeze, because her desk was already absorbing 140 tickets a month and could not take a rushed, undertested feature on top.

Each VP was right about their own slice, none controlled the squad alone, and none would move without the others agreeing. Meera owned none of the three things at stake — she had no formal authority over any VP. What she did have was the one thing nobody else in the room was explicitly paid to produce: a decision everyone left believing was the same decision, with enough conviction to act on it without her chasing them. Fail, and eleven days of stalemate become twenty, with the renewal or the rebuild the casualty. Over-function — deciding the architecture herself, adjudicating every follow-on ticket — and she would become the very bottleneck a PM in the room was meant to prevent.

Fig. 1 — Three VPs, three defensible asks, one shared squad, and a GPM with no authority over any of them. The scarce resource in this room is not engineering time; it is a decision everyone believes is the same decision.

The idea

Clarity is a shared, correct, and current understanding — among the people who must act — of what has been decided, why, and what happens next. Energy is the collective willingness to act on that understanding without being chased. Neither is a document or a mood; both are properties of a group, and in most organisations no single role owns producing them, because they fall between functions rather than inside one. Software manager Tanya Reilly named this invisible coordination work "glue work" in a widely read 2018 essay, arguing that senior people who do it well are under-recognised precisely because the work leaves no artifact of its own. Around the same time, former Google and Apple executive Kim Scott, in Radical Candor (2017), drew the distinction this topic turns on: being kind — caring personally while challenging directly — produces clarity, while being merely nice — avoiding a hard sentence to protect a meeting's mood — produces what Scott calls ruinous empathy: comfort now, confusion later. Underneath both sits a finding from Harvard's Amy Edmondson, whose 1999 research on psychological safety showed teams move faster and take more ownership when they can disagree openly without being punished for it — the actual source of "energy," rather than enthusiasm or hustle.

The problem this idea solves is specific to product management: a PM sits at the intersection of engineering, sales, and customers, with influence but rarely authority, and the default failure mode is to let ambiguity persist because naming it feels confrontational. The sentence Meera could say in that room without sounding glib is this one:

"My job here isn't to have the best idea — it's to make sure that when we leave, all three of you can say the same sentence about what we decided, and want to go do it."

How it actually works

The mechanics are more deliberate than they look from outside. First, Meera converted a vague agenda item — "scheduling engine priorities" — into one decision statement: which of the two, rebuild or custom feature, gets the squad's next three sprints. Vague topics produce vague meetings; a named decision gives everyone something concrete to agree or disagree with.

Second, and this is the step most practitioners skip because it feels risky, she surfaced the disagreement in the room rather than letting it stay in email threads and hallway asides. This is exactly why the best classrooms teach this skill through role-played stakeholder conflict rather than through reading about it: a case with no real disagreement in it teaches a student nothing about the actual job, since the job only exists when people in the room want different things. Meera asked Rohan and Kabir to state their case to each other, not to her, and asked Priya to name the specific failure she feared, in tickets and hours, not in general anxiety.

Third came the kind-not-nice move: Meera told Rohan directly that the rebuild would not get this quarter's sprints, rather than letting him leave with a hedge he could reinterpret later. Fourth, she made the decision portable: a one-page note, timestamped, naming the decision, the reasoning, the owner of each next step, and the date the rebuild would be revisited. Fifth, she closed the loop with the why, not just the what, because people execute what they understand and merely comply with what they're told. Sixth — the step nearly everyone leaves implicit — she scheduled a five-minute check three weeks out, since clarity decays; an unreinforced decision quietly reverts to whoever argues loudest next. Seventh, she declined to approve every subsequent ticket on the custom feature herself, handing that back to Kabir's and Rohan's teams — the difference between being glue and being cement.

A worked example

The arithmetic Meera used was simple enough to say out loud. Kabir's custom rule needed three sprints from all four engineers: twelve engineer-sprints. At a fully loaded cost of roughly ₹28 lakh per engineer per year, one sprint (two weeks of twenty-six) costs about ₹1.08 lakh per engineer, so twelve engineer-sprints cost roughly ₹12.9 lakh. Delaying Rohan's rebuild a quarter, meanwhile, was projected to push the 140 monthly tickets up 15 percent as debt compounded, adding roughly ₹2 lakh across the quarter. Against a ₹4.2 crore renewal, that was not a close call, and saying so out loud, in rupees, did more for clarity than any relationship-building would have.
