Fig. 2 — The same two costs, run against a smaller renewal. Below roughly ₹1–1.5 crore, the ₹12.9 lakh feature cost and the compounding technical debt stop being a close call in Kabir's favour — which is precisely why Meera named the numbers instead of letting seniority or volume decide.

Change one input — make the account ₹90 lakh, a small, non-strategic customer rather than a top-ten one — and the same arithmetic flips the recommendation: the rebuild's compounding cost now dominates a much smaller renewal, and the kind-not-nice conversation runs the other way, toward Kabir. The mechanics of creating clarity did not change; what changed was which side of the room needed to hear a direct "no."

The nuances a learner must notice

Clarity is not consensus

Rohan did not agree the rebuild should wait. He left clear about the decision, the reasoning, and the date it would be revisited, without agreeing it was correct. Waiting for everyone to agree before calling something decided produces neither clarity nor a decision.

Energy is not enthusiasm

Nobody applauded. Energy here meant both teams could start Monday without another meeting, because friction and ambiguity, not morale, stood between the decision and the work.

Glue work should shrink, not grow, over time

Reilly's original point was that uncredited coordination work is bad for the person doing it and the organisation depending on it. A PM who is still personally reconciling the same three VPs a year from now has converted a role into a chore; the one-page decision note and the three-week check are how Meera tried to make the process outlive her presence in the room.

Kind and nice are routinely confused

Telling Rohan "not this quarter" felt less comfortable than telling him "let's see how it goes," but the second sentence is the unkind one: it spends his time on false hope. Scott's quadrant treats bluntness without care as its own failure, called obnoxious aggression, which this is not — Meera's directness was paired with acknowledging that Rohan's technical case was sound.

The idea needs real decision rights to work

If Meera had no credibility with the three VPs — if her note carried no weight because nobody trusted her judgment or data — the same steps would look like theatre. Creating clarity presumes the room already grants the PM enough standing to be believed; it is not a technique for manufacturing authority that was never earned.

It is often confused with holding more alignment meetings

The eleven days of email were, in effect, an unstructured meeting that never ended. More syncs would not have fixed it; naming one decision statement did. Clarity is a property of the decision, not of how often it was discussed.

It cannot tell you whether the decision itself was right

Suppose the rebuild really was the more important bet and Meera deferred it under commercial pressure anyway. A clearly communicated, energetically executed wrong call is still wrong — only efficiently so. This topic governs execution conditions, not strategic judgment; ask separately whether the call was right, and whether everyone understood it the same way.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and scale

At Yantra, a B2B seller to manufacturers, clarity has to survive a long chain: from Meera's squad through Kabir's account team to Ashok Leyland's own plant manager, weeks before the renewal signs. In a consumer product, the equivalent scene might involve a fintech app like Yatharth Networks, where a small squad argues daily over one retention metric and energy shows up as same-day shipping rather than a quarterly commitment. In a marketplace, clarity must be created on both sides of a transaction at once — a logistics platform balancing driver supply against shipper demand cannot resolve ambiguity for one side while leaving the other guessing. The job also changes with size: in a ten-person startup, glue work is personal and constant, done in hallway conversations; at a four-hundred-person company like Yantra, a PM who stays personally involved in every reconciliation becomes the bottleneck the role was meant to prevent, which is why a written decision and a scheduled check-in matter more, not less, as headcount grows.

Common mistakes

The same debate resurfaces every sprint. The symptom is déjà vu in standups; the error is treating a verbal agreement as self-executing instead of writing and distributing it. Diagnostic: ask three stakeholders a week later to state the decision in one sentence, and see if they match.

The PM is copied on every thread and approves every ticket. This looks like diligence but is usually fear of the conflict delegation would surface. Diagnostic: a calendar audit of what share of meetings exist only to relay information the PM adds no judgment to.

The room nods, then nothing moves. Polite silence is mistaken for agreement, when someone left with an unspoken objection. Asking one-on-one "what part of this do you still disagree with?" catches what the group setting suppressed.

What good looks like

Run the same meeting well and it looks unremarkable: forty-five minutes, one decision on the whiteboard, Rohan and Kabir arguing to each other rather than through Meera, a direct "not this quarter" landing without a raised voice, a one-page note in every inbox within the hour, and a diary invite three weeks out with no agenda beyond "did this hold." Nobody leaves cheering. Both squads start Monday without asking Meera anything first.

Closing

Meera deferred the rebuild by one quarter, committed the squad to Kabir's feature with a written ticket ceiling Priya signed off on, and gave Rohan a dated slot for the rebuild plus the ₹2 lakh figure as the acknowledged cost of waiting. Nobody got everything; everyone knew exactly what they'd gotten. The next thing worth studying is influence without authority — the companion skill for situations where the PM's credibility itself is still in question. Two questions worth sitting with: when you last called a meeting "aligned," could every person there have written the same one-sentence decision afterward? And where has being nice quietly cost someone the clarity that being kind would have given them sooner?

Case · People, Leadership & Organisation · Leadership & Team

Qanat Jal Analytics: Twelve Days to Clarity

Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh · 14 October

At 8.40 on a Tuesday morning, Barkha Srivastava stood at the whiteboard in Qanat Jal Analytics' Gomti Nagar office with forty-seven sticky notes in front of her — one for every decision waiting on her personal sign-off. In twelve days, on 26 October, Qanat's founder-CEO Bhaskar Oberoi would present to the board of Uttar Pradesh Jal Nigam (Urban) — UPJN(U) — asking it to convert an eight-town pilot into a forty-five-town, statewide rollout worth roughly ₹14 crore in annual recurring revenue. Barkha, promoted eight weeks earlier from senior product manager to Head of Product, was not deciding what to tell the board. She was deciding something narrower and more consequential: how the next twelve days would actually run, and whether she would spend them approving every ticket herself or find another way to give four scattered teams clarity without becoming the one thing they were all waiting on.

Company background

Qanat Jal Analytics was founded in 2017 by Bhaskar Oberoi and a co-founder-CTO to sell software, not pipes: a metering, billing and non-revenue-water (NRW) analytics platform for India's urban local bodies and state water boards. Qanat did not manufacture meters — it ingested readings from whatever hardware a client already had, from Secure Meters' bulk flow meters to Itron's AMR units — and turned them into billing, leak alerts and NRW dashboards showing, town by town, how much treated water a board produced versus how much it was actually paid for. That gap routinely ran above 35% in Indian cities against a global benchmark near 15%, and AMRUT 2.0, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs scheme funding 24x7 water supply in mid-sized cities, made NRW reduction a scored condition for further grants — useful to a city engineer and legible to a funding agency at once.

By October, Qanat was live in 41 towns across Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar, with ₹18 crore in ARR (Exhibit 1), competing against L&T Smart World's utility arm, Itron entering directly, and eGov Foundation's free, government-preferred DIGIT platform, which ULBs defaulted to unless a vendor showed it clearly did more. A small Singapore-routed pilot with a Sharjah-area municipality, arranged through a Gulf systems-integrator partner, was Qanat's first step outside India. The company had never lost a live client, and had never operated at the scale the UPJN(U) deal implied.

The situation

In August, Manish Trivedi, the co-founder-CTO who had quietly made most of engineering's calls since 2017, left for a Bengaluru startup. No one had been named to replace him. That same week, the July-August billing cycle — Qanat's heaviest, timed to monsoon meter readings — overloaded the ingestion servers mid-sync for three UPJN(U) pilot towns, producing four days of stalled bills and a testy call from the client's Executive Engineer. Since then, Rajeev Bisht, the engineering lead in Nagpur, had been holding the platform together while fielding requests he had no mandate to refuse.

Those requests were multiplying. Wei Chen, Qanat's data scientist in Toronto, was building the AI-based leak-detection model that David Fernandes, the sales head in New Jersey, had already promised UPJN(U)'s board as the centrepiece of the 26 October demo — but Wei's model needed a cleaned data pipeline only Rajeev's team could build, and Rajeev kept bumping it behind stability fixes. Farah Ansari, the customer-success lead in Singapore covering both the India accounts and the Sharjah pilot, was fielding ticket volume up 60% since Manish left, most undocumented product knowledge having lived in his head. Unable to get a straight answer from each other, all three had taken to escalating straight to Barkha — Slack from Toronto at 11 pm IST, a call from Singapore at 7 am, in person from Nagpur. Barkha had been personally approving engineering exceptions, pricing carve-outs and ticket priorities for six weeks, sleeping four hours a night, and the queue kept growing (Exhibit 2).

The people

Rajeev Bisht — Engineering Lead, Nagpur. Wants a freeze on new asks until billing is provably stable; feels every team treats his backlog as infinitely elastic.
Wei Chen — Data Scientist, Toronto (9.5 hours behind IST). Wants ten uninterrupted days of pipeline support for the demo; her requests to Rajeev sit unanswered across the time-zone gap.
Farah Ansari — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Wants budget to hire a contract associate now, and fears the ticket backlog will cost Qanat the Sharjah renewal and two Indian ULB contracts.
David Fernandes — Sales Head, New Jersey. Wants the leak-detection demo delivered as promised, plus the discounted per-connection rate he has already floated to UPJN(U) to close the deal.

Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — Qanat's growth, FY2023–FY2025 (projected)
MetricFY23FY24FY25 (proj.)
Towns live92441
States123
ARR (₹ crore)4.110.618.0
Avg. NRW reduction (pts)61114

Source: Qanat internal MIS. NRW reduction measured against each town's baseline at go-live, averaged across live towns.

Exhibit 2 — Decisions queued for Barkha's personal sign-off, by week since Manish's exit
Week ofEng. exceptionsPricing/contractFeature scopeAvg. days pending
1 Sep6241.5
15 Sep11472.8
29 Sep15593.6
13 Oct196114.4

36 items open as of 14 October; row totals do not equal 47 sticky notes as some items span categories.

Exhibit 1 shows why UPJN(U) takes the pitch seriously: Qanat has quadrupled ARR and roughly doubled NRW-reduction performance in two years. Exhibit 2 shows the cost of the last six weeks — the queue in front of Barkha has more than tripled, and items sit nearly three times as long. The timeline below shows why: four workstreams that each look manageable alone collide in the same twelve days.

Exhibit 3 — The collision point: Wei's model cannot start until Rajeev's team frees pipeline capacity, which Rajeev will not release until billing is stable, while Farah and David run continuously in the background, both routing exceptions through Barkha.

The options

Option A — Keep deciding everything herself

Barkha continues as she has for six weeks: every exception and scope call comes to her, and she works whatever hours it takes to clear the queue before 26 October. Upside: nothing gets decided badly by a team missing the full picture. Cost: Exhibit 2's queue is already growing faster than she can clear it; Qanat's throughput is capped at what Barkha alone can approve, and the pattern survives 26 October intact, guaranteeing the same crisis next quarter.

Option B — Step back and let each lead decide independently

Barkha tells the four leads to use their judgement and stop escalating, trusting each to act in Qanat's interest. Upside: immediate relief for Barkha; a clear signal of trust. Cost: none has visibility into the others' constraints — Rajeev does not know Wei's demo is board-promised; David does not know Rajeev has no spare capacity. Without a shared frame, independent "good" decisions collide, as Exhibit 3 already shows happening even with Barkha in the loop.

Option C — Set the frame, assign the calls, hold one daily review

Barkha spends the morning writing a one-page ranking of the four workstreams against the single 26 October goal, states plainly what will not happen in the next twelve days (no further pricing promises, no new feature commitments), and hands each lead real decision rights inside that frame: Rajeev owns all engineering trade-offs within an agreed stability floor; he and Wei run a three-day joint sprint to unblock the pipeline first; Farah gets standing authority to hire a contract associate up to ₹60,000 without further approval; David is told directly that no pricing exceptions go out before her one daily review. A 15-minute daily cross-time-zone sync replaces continuous Slack escalation. Upside: throughput no longer depends on Barkha alone, and the Wei-Rajeev collision gets sequenced rather than argued about. Cost: an uncomfortable, explicit conversation with David, and the risk that Barkha's ranking is wrong.

Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 tell you about what six weeks of personal decision-making has cost Qanat?
  2. Look at each stakeholder's request from their own city and vantage point. Which conflicts are genuine trade-offs, and which are simply nobody having the full picture?
  3. Evaluate Options A, B and C against "creating clarity and energy." Which one increases how many good decisions Qanat can make per day, rather than moving the bottleneck around?
  4. What, specifically, would you say to David about the pricing exception he has already floated — and how does kindly-but-firmly differ from simply being nice?

A note for the learner

This topic asks how a PM becomes the glue holding a team together without becoming its ceiling. Bringing order to chaos does not mean making every call personally — that is Option A, and Exhibit 2 shows the arithmetic fails: the queue grows faster than one person can clear it. Nor does it mean stepping back and hoping good people make good calls — that is Option B, which fails for a subtler reason: without a shared frame, reasonable people optimising locally produce Exhibit 3's collision, not clarity. The skill this case tests is narrower and harder: make a few visible, decisive calls quickly — what will not happen, who decides what, one cadence to stay coordinated — and hold people to them with kindness rather than niceness. Kindness tells David plainly, to his face, that the pricing promise was premature; niceness would avoid that conversation and let the ambiguity fester into the client relationship.

The defensible path is Option C. It shrinks the categories driving Exhibit 2's growth by moving pricing and engineering exceptions to named owners instead of Barkha's inbox, and resolves Exhibit 3's collision by sequencing the pipeline handoff explicitly rather than letting Rajeev and Wei negotiate it through escalations. It costs Barkha one hard conversation with David and the risk of a wrong ranking — real but bounded, unlike Option A's unbounded arithmetic or Option B's uncoordinated drift. A strong answer names that trade-off honestly rather than presenting Option C as costless.

Case · People, Leadership & Organisation · Leadership & Team

Ashmaka Mine Systems: The Operating Model Vrinda Deshmukh Did Not Have

Indore, Madhya Pradesh · Sunday, 4 October, 10.50 pm

The rain over Vijay Nagar had stopped an hour earlier, and Vrinda Deshmukh could hear the generator next door still running. On her dining table were three printouts labelled Product Operating Model — v1, each by a different person, none by her. The first was Prabhat Ranade's: four slides headed One Roadmap, One Owner. The second was Shabnam Qureshi's, eleven pages of engineering governance with a decision-rights table running to forty-one rows. The third had arrived at 9.14 that evening from Girish Nalawade in Hospet, a single scanned page in his handwriting, saying in effect that the field would keep doing what the field had always done.

At 11 the next morning, Vrinda would sit in a room off AB Road with Prabhat, the chief financial officer down from Mumbai, and two partners from Ashvattha Growth Partners, and be asked the question put to her at every monthly steering meeting since June: is the product organisation now able to make decisions without you in the room? In June she had said, honestly, not yet. In July she had shown them a plan. In August, a dashboard. It was now October, the dashboard said things were better, the field said they were worse, and Vrinda no longer trusted her own read of which was true.

Company history

Ashmaka Mine Systems was founded in Indore in 2015 by Prabhat Ranade, a former mine planning engineer, and two colleagues who had spent their twenties reconciling weighbridge slips against dispatch registers around Katni. Their first product was unglamorous and immediately sellable: a haul-cycle dispatch board telling a shift in-charge which tipper went to which face, and a weighbridge reconciliation module matching gross and tare weights against transit passes, so a mine manager saw where tonnage had gone missing before the auditors did. Blast planning and statutory production reporting came in 2018, when customers began asking Ashmaka to generate their monthly returns.

The decision that shaped everything after it was made in November 2019. Shortlisted for a fourteen-site contract with a private minerals group, Ashmaka won by agreeing to configure the platform site by site — every weighbridge protocol, shift pattern, royalty and transit-pass workflow built to that site's existing practice rather than to a product standard. It worked. Revenue tripled in two years, the reference sold eleven more accounts, and site-shaped became a compliment inside the company. By October 2025 those 58 sites rested on 23 long-lived configuration branches no single engineer fully understood. Prabhat still described the branches as a moat. Shabnam described them, in a document she had not yet sent to the board, as 23 products with one revenue line.

Vrinda had joined in February 2025 from a Pune analytics firm, as Ashmaka's first VP Product and first senior hire from outside mining. Prabhat's offer letter gave her a two-sentence mandate: bring order to the roadmap, and make the product org run without heroics. She spent four months learning the difference between a limestone site and an iron-ore site, and the next four discovering that the heroics were not a bug in the system but the system itself.

The industry

Mining software in India sits between two kinds of buyer and two kinds of regulator, and Ashmaka was exposed to all four. Its customers were limestone and aggregate producers feeding cement plants, iron-ore lessees in the Hospet–Ballari belt, and contractors working captive coal blocks auctioned since 2020. All filed statutory returns to the Indian Bureau of Mines and worked under Directorate General of Mines Safety inspections; all moved mineral under state e-permit systems — Madhya Pradesh's e-Khanij, Odisha's i3MS — that Ashmaka had to integrate with, each on its own release calendar, each capable of changing a field format without notice. GST e-way bills had to tie to transit passes; the Mining Surveillance System could flag a lease-boundary anomaly that Ashmaka's software was then asked to explain.

Above Ashmaka sat the global fleet-management incumbents — Komatsu's Modular Mining, Caterpillar's MineStar, planning suites such as Deswik and Micromine — strong on the deep-pit engineering problem, expensive, and indifferent to the statutory layer that consumed most of a mine manager's paperwork. Beside it sat the enterprise stacks: Tata Steel, JSW and Hindustan Zinc ran SAP-centred landscapes a dispatch product had to fit into, and NMDC and Coal India subsidiaries ran tender-driven procurements. Below it, and rising, were Mehnat Fleet Systems of Ranchi, selling a cheaper dispatch-only product to contractors, and Amaanat Weighbridge Systems of Raipur, narrow on reconciliation and faster than Ashmaka into e-Khanij. A third, Manthan Mine Analytics of Nagpur, sold prediction dashboards to the same buyers and had raised more money.

Ashmaka's global exposure was newer. Maqbool Minerals Trading LLC, a Muscat-based aggregates trader, had tendered for eleven quarry sites in Oman and the UAE; Ashmaka's bid, roughly ₹6.8 crore over three years, was due on 12 October. The tender asked for multilingual shift reporting, a data-residency commitment, and an audited uptime history that the site-shaped branches made genuinely hard to produce on one page.

Exhibit 1 — Market map, drawn by Vrinda for the July steering pack and not revised since. Positions reflect Ashmaka's win/loss notes from 31 competitive FY25 deals; five were lost without a recorded reason.

The situation in detail

In February, when Vrinda arrived, the diagnosis seemed obvious. Ashmaka had 34 people in product and engineering, 58 live sites, no written prioritisation, and a founder answering technical questions on customer WhatsApp groups. Escalations reached whoever replied first. Vrinda's instinct was a single channel: one intake tracker, one weekly triage, one published roadmap. By April it existed and it visibly worked — median time from a field escalation to a decision fell from 6.4 days in March to 3.1 in June (Exhibit 3).

In April she believed the bottleneck was the absence of a process. By June she believed the bottleneck was her: everything flowed through the triage she chaired, and she sat in 31 recurring meetings a week. So in July she pushed the decisions down. She published a decision-rights charter — Shabnam drafted it, hence the forty-one rows — naming an owner for each class of decision: site configuration to the regional solution leads, platform architecture to Shabnam, statutory-module scope to Bipin Mahato in Dhanbad, pricing exceptions to Prabhat, analytics scope to Shonali Guha in Toronto, anything touching a customer commitment to Vrinda.

Through August the dashboard improved further, and the August pulse survey put the product org's clarity score at 3.9 out of 5 against 3.1 in May (Exhibit 4). Prabhat forwarded it to the Ashvattha partners with one line: this is what a product org looks like.

Three things have since turned out to be wrong. First, on 12 September, Grace Tan in Singapore, preparing the Maqbool tender response, asked for a list of every configuration change made to the four largest accounts in the previous quarter. Girish's team produced 267; the tracker held 53. The charter had not stopped the old channel, it had merely made it unofficial, and the shadow log Grace assembled (Exhibit 5) showed that where the records disagreed the field record was almost always the accurate one. Second, the pulse survey's improvement was narrower than it looked: the response rate had fallen from 86% in May to 41% in August, and eleven of the fifteen people who stopped responding sat in field or solutions roles. Third, on 24 September, Angaar Minerals Group — Ashmaka's largest account at ₹4.2 crore of annual recurring revenue, eight sites, limestone and captive coal — raised a formal notice: at its Singrauli-area coal site the weighbridge reconciliation module had been reporting a 2.3% variance against a contracted tolerance of 0.7% for at least six weeks, roughly ₹38 lakh a month in disputed tonnage. Nobody had escalated it, because the site had asked Girish's engineer directly and he had, in good faith, applied a local tare-weight patch on the branch, which held for a fortnight and then stopped holding.

On 29 September Shabnam sent Vrinda a note asking to be relieved of the platform role by January, giving no reason beyond one sentence: I have written governance twice and nobody is governed by it.

The people

Prabhat Ranade — Founder and CEO, Indore. Position: one roadmap, one owner, and that owner is Vrinda. Incentive: a bridge round priced on ARR growth, and the Maqbool tender as proof of an export story. Not saying: he is still on nine customer WhatsApp groups and made four site commitments in September that entered no tracker.
Shabnam Qureshi — Head of Platform Engineering, Nashik. Position: consolidate the 23 branches onto one configurable core before taking new geography; she has costed it at 14 engineer-months. Incentive: judged on incidents, owns none of the revenue. Not saying: two of her best engineers have interviews elsewhere, and her note is partly a bid to force the consolidation decision.
Girish Nalawade — Director, Field Operations, Hospet. Position: sites are not identical and never will be; the charter is an office fantasy applied to a mine. Incentive: renewals at 97%, built on his personal credibility with mine managers. Not saying: he knew of the Singrauli variance on 8 September and expected to fix it quietly, as he had fixed forty things before.
Bipin Mahato — Lead, Statutory & Compliance, Dhanbad. Position: statutory reporting must be centrally owned, because a wrong return is a regulatory exposure, not a customer preference. Incentive: he is the only person who can sign off a return-format change, and likes it that way. Not saying: he has been quietly declining field requests he considers unsafe, and those declines appear nowhere.
Shonali Guha — Analytics Lead, Toronto. Position: haul-cycle prediction is the only thing separating Ashmaka from Mehnat, and it needs clean data from ten sites that the branches do not give her. Incentive: hired to build a differentiator, has shipped nothing to production in five months. Not saying: her accuracy numbers come from the three cleanest sites and may not generalise.
Grace Tan — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Position: Ashmaka cannot bid Muscat credibly until there is one documented product; she compiled the shadow log herself. Incentive: she carries the Gulf pipeline and the renewal risk on Indian accounts inherited in July. Not saying: she has told the Maqbool contact that Ashmaka's uptime history is "being consolidated", which is generous.
Kaushik Rane — Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai. Position: no net headcount before the bridge closes; the ₹1.9 crore for six product roles is contingent on the Muscat bid landing. Incentive: a clean ARR-per-engineer chart. Not saying: Angaar's service-credit clause is capped at ₹35 lakh a quarter, and he has not modelled the variance being found to predate September.

Exhibits

Exhibit 2 — Scale and shape of the business, FY23–FY26

Exhibit 3 — Decision latency and escalation volume, March–September

Exhibit 4 — Product org pulse survey (1–5 scale)

Exhibit 5 — Tracker versus field record, Q2 FY26 (four largest accounts)

Exhibit 6 — Timeline of belief and correction, reconstructed from Vrinda's notes, the tracker export and Exhibit 5. The parallel channel's start date is unknown; Girish dates it to 2017.

Read together, the exhibits settle nothing. Exhibit 3 is the cleanest evidence Vrinda has that the operating model works; Exhibit 5 is the cleanest evidence that Exhibit 3 measures a channel most of the work has left. Exhibit 2 shows a business that has stopped adding sites while ARR still rises, which finance reads as pricing power and Shabnam reads as capacity exhaustion. Exhibit 4's clarity gain is real for those who answered and unknown for the eleven field staff who did not.

Voices

“Put the tracker aside a minute. My engineer at Singrauli got a call at 4 am because the night shift's tippers were queued and the board showed stale allocations. Should he have raised a ticket and waited for a named owner in Nashik to wake up?”Girish Nalawade, field operations review, 26 September
“No. He should have fixed it and told us. What he should not have done is edit a tare weight on a branch and tell nobody, because that is not a fix, that is a liability with a two-week fuse.”Shabnam Qureshi, same review
“The Maqbool clarification round wants one architecture diagram and a 24-month uptime series. I have 23 branches and four uptime definitions. I can send something. I would rather send something true.”Grace Tan, email, 2 October, 07.40 SGT
“Three clean sites give me 81% haul-cycle accuracy. They do not tell me it holds at Hospet. If I present the 81% on Monday it becomes a promise and I spend FY27 defending it.”Shonali Guha, chat thread, 3 October, 22.10 IST
“The charter says statutory scope is mine. In practice a site asks Girish, Girish asks me, I say no, the site hears nothing. I am the reason for nine delays this quarter and nobody wrote that down, including me.”Bipin Mahato, one-to-one with Vrinda, 30 September
“Do not walk into Monday with twenty-three branches as a problem. Walk in with one roadmap and one owner. Ashvattha funds growth, not reorganisations. Muscat is growth.”Prabhat Ranade, call to Vrinda, 4 October, 19.30 IST

The options as Vrinda sees them

A. Consolidate first

Accept Shabnam's plan: freeze new geography, put 14 engineer-months into collapsing the 23 branches onto one configurable core, and tell Maqbool that Ashmaka will bid next cycle. This removes what Exhibit 5's parallel channel exists to serve, and is the only option that addresses the Angaar variance at its root. It also forfeits a ₹6.8 crore tender, hands Kaushik a flat-growth story mid-bridge, and asks the board to fund invisible work for two quarters on the word of an engineering lead who has just asked to step down.

B. Make the charter real

Keep the structure and enforce it: close the unofficial channel, route every configuration change through the tracker, publish declines as well as approvals so Bipin's nine silent refusals become visible, and hold the weekly triage as the single forum. Cheap and fast. It is also what Girish has told her in writing the field will not follow — and Exhibit 5 suggests it has not been following since July while the dashboard said otherwise. Enforcement without added field capacity may simply drive the channel further underground.

C. Push ownership to the sites

Invert the charter: give each regional solutions lead real authority over their sites, including tare and configuration changes, against a standard that states only what must never vary — statutory return formats, audit trail, reconciliation tolerance. Girish would sign it tomorrow. Shabnam would read it as ratifying the 23 branches and leave in January; Bipin would be enforcing regulatory limits without being able to see what sites are doing.

D. Buy the difference

Ask the board for the ₹1.9 crore now rather than contingent on Muscat, hire six — two field engineers, a technical writer, three platform engineers — and attempt consolidation and the tender together. This is Prabhat's instinct and the only option nobody in the room will argue against on Monday. It also assumes 34 saturated people can absorb, train and supervise six new ones during Angaar's remediation window, and Vrinda has no evidence for that.

What unsettles her is a suspicion that all four share a premise: that the problem is where decisions are made. Girish's handwritten page argues something else — that a mine runs on trust built face to face at the site, that his engineers act because they are trusted to, and that every instrument Vrinda has built measures the flow of paper rather than the flow of judgement. She is not sure he is wrong, and not sure what she would build if he is right.

The deadline and the hard constraints

The steering meeting is at 11 am on Monday, 5 October. The Maqbool bid closes on 12 October; Grace's clarification response is due on the 7th. Angaar's notice requires a written remediation plan within fifteen working days of 24 September, and its service-credit clause exposes Ashmaka to ₹35 lakh a quarter; whether the variance predates September may be decided by the Singrauli site's own registers. The quarterly statutory return also falls on 12 October, and Madhya Pradesh has announced an e-Khanij field change effective 1 November that Bipin estimates at three engineer-weeks across the affected branches. Hiring is frozen at 34 until the bridge closes, expected December. Shabnam's stated last month in the platform role is January; there is no second platform lead inside the company, and two recruiters have told Vrinda the role takes four to six months to fill in Indore.

Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly did Vrinda's April intervention fix, and what did it only appear to fix? Use Exhibits 3 and 5 together.
  2. Exhibit 4 went to investors as evidence of a functioning product organisation. What should a careful reader have asked before forwarding it?
  3. Girish's renewals run at 97% and his team made 214 unlogged changes in a quarter. How should Vrinda think about a person whose behaviour is both why customers stay and why she cannot see the business?

Sunday night

At 11.40 Vrinda stacked the printouts and wrote one line on a notepad: what do I know on Monday that I did not know in July? Under it, honestly: that the thing I built measured itself. Then her phone lit with a message from Girish — Singrauli's night shift had run clean for the third consecutive shift, tare corrected, no queueing — and a second from Shonali in Toronto, where it was still Sunday afternoon, asking whether the 81% slide should go into the pack or stay out. The generator next door was still running. Vrinda did not reply to either.
